The next day, September 5, the Tlaxcalan army appeared, no less terrible to the sight by its innumerable multitude (A) than beautiful for the lovely variety of their plumes and other military ornaments. It was divided into five squadrons of ten thousand men each; each carried its own standard, and in the rear guard, according to the custom of that nation, came the common standard of the republic, which was, as we have said elsewhere, a golden eagle with outspread wings. The arrogant Xicotencatl, to show the little account he made of the Spaniards, and that he did not wish to take them by hunger but to conquer them by arms, sent them a refreshment of three hundred turkeys and two hundred baskets of tamalli, exhorting them to restore their strength for the battle. Shortly afterward he detached two thousand courageous men, so that they should

(A) Cortés says that the army of the Tlaxcalans was of more than 149,000 men. Bernal Díaz affirms, as a thing certain and well known to him, that it consisted of only 50,000 men, namely 10,000 of Maxixcatzin, 10,000 of Xicotencatl, 10,000 of Tlehuexolotzin, 10,000 of Chichimecatecuhtli, one of the most distinguished lords of that republic, and 10,000 of Tecpanecatl, lord of Topoyanco, a considerable city of the same republic, although these names have been much altered by this author. This number seems more probable; that which is read in the letter of Cortés may be believed to be a mistake of the first printer of it. [p. 46] assault the camp of the Spaniards. This assault was so violent that, Bk. VIII. forcing the entrenchments, they entered the camp and fought hand to hand with the Spaniards. The Tlaxcalans might have been victors this time, not so much because of the far superior number of their troops as because of their bravery and the quality of their arms, which were pikes, lances, swords, and darts with two and three points, had not the discord that arose among them made victory easier for their enemies. The son of Chichimecatecuhtli, who was commander of the body of troops of his father (*), having been insulted with words by the arrogant Xicotencatl, conceived such great indignation that he challenged him to a duel, which should decide the question of their courage and of their fortune; and not being able to obtain this satisfaction from him, in order to take some vengeance he withdrew from the field the troops who were under his orders, and induced the same course in those of Tlehuexolotzin. Despite so great a diminution of the army, the battle was very obstinate and bloody. The Spaniards, after having courageously repulsed the troops that had assaulted their camp, marched in battle order against the main body of the Tlaxcalan army. The slaughter which the artillery made in the crowded multitude was not enough to make the Tlaxcalans turn their backs, nor to prevent them from promptly filling those gaps which the dead left; indeed with their firmness and intrepidity they had thrown the Spaniards into confusion, in spite of the clamors and reproaches of Cortés and his captains. At last, after four hours of fighting, the Spaniards returned victorious to their camp, although the Tlaxcalans did not cease to assault them often on that same day. Of the Spaniards only one man was lost, and sixty were wounded, and all the horses. Of the Tlaxcalans very many were killed; but not even one corpse

Xicotencatl, disgusted at the unfortunate outcome of this expedition, had the diviners of Tlaxcala consulted, and they replied that those strangers, as children of the Sun, were invincible during the day; but as soon as night arrived, together with the vital heat of that planet their strength to defend themselves also failed. In consequence of such an oracle that general resolved to make an assault upon the Spanish camp by night. Meanwhile Cortés sallied forth once more to commit hostilities in the neighboring villages, of which he burned ten, and among them one of three thousand hearths, and returned with some prisoners.

Xicotencatl, so that the blow he was planning against the Spaniards should not fail, wished first to inform himself of the disposition and strength of their camp. He therefore sent fifty men to Cortés with a gift accompanied by courteous expressions of goodwill, charging them to observe everything; but they could not make their observations with so much dissimulation that Teuch, one of the three principal Cempoalans, did not notice it and at once warn Cortés. That general, having called some of the spies aside, forced them with threats to declare that Xicotencatl was preparing to make the assault the following night, and that they had been sent expressly to observe by what part of the camp entry would be easiest for him. Cortés, having heard their confession, had the hands of all fifty cut off (B), and sent them back to Xicotencatl, charging them to let him know that whether he came to his camp by day or by night, he would always make him know who the Spaniards were; and, these circumstances appearing to him very opportune for battle, before the enemy had completed all their preparations for the assault, he sallied forth at nightfall with a good number

[p. 49] 49 Configlieri alcuni abbracciarono il parere del Re di Tezcu- ==co, ed altri quello del Signor d' Iztapalapan, al quale aderì Liu. VIIL ancora Motezuma . Questo sventurato Re non trovava da per tutto, se non oggetti, e motivi, onde temere. L' imminente confederazione de' Tlascallesi cogli Spagnuoli lo teneva in una somma inquietudine, Da una altro canto inquietavalo l' alleanza di Cortès col Principe Ixclilxochitl suo ni: pote e nemico giurato, il quale dacchè congiurò contro il Re di Tezcuco suo fratello, non avea mai lasciate l' armi, ed allora appunto fi trovava in Otompan alla testa d’ un esercito formidabile. Accresceva questi timori la ribellione di parecchie Provincie, che aveano seguito l' esempio de’ Totonachi, Mandò dunque sei Ambasciatori a Cortés con mille vesti curiose di bambagia , ed una buona quantità d'oro, e di vaghe penne, e gl’incaricò di congratularsi con lui delle sue vittorie, d' offerirgli altri più grandi regali, e di difsuaderlo del viaggio a Messico rappresentandogli la malagevolezza della strada ed altri ostacoli difficili da superarsi, Partirono prontamente questi Ambasciatori con un seguito di + di dagento uomini, ed arrivati al campo degli Spagnuoi eseguirono appunto quanto era stato loro ordinato . Cortés gli ricevè con tutto l'onore al loro carattere dovuto, e fi protestò sommamente obbligato alla bontà di sì gran Monarca ; ma trattenne a bella posta gli Ambasciatori , sperando che frattanto occorrefse qualche zuffa co' Tlascalleli , la quale accredirafle d'avanti a’ Messicani la bravura delle sue truppe, e la superiorità delle armi Europee ; o pure fatta la pace colia Repubblica fossero testimonj della severità, colla quale voleva rimproverare a' Tlascallesi Ia loro ostinazione . Non ilstette guari, che gli capitò l’ occasione , che tanto desiderava . Tre squadroni nemici piombarono sul campo degli Spagnuoli con urli spaventevoli, è con una tempesta di frecce, e di dardi. Cortès, con ruttochè avesse tolto quello stesso giorno una purgante, montò a cavallo, ed uscì intrepidamente contra i Tlascallesi , i quali senza troppa fati- Sroria del Messico Tomo III, G ca [p. 50] 592 ca furono sconfitti a vista degli Ambasciatori: Messicani. Lis. Vil, Persuafsi alla fine i partigiani del vecchio Xicotencatl, che non era spediente alla Repubblica la guerra cogli Spa. pala a gouoli ; è temendo inoltre , che questi s' alleaflero co' confede- Meslicani , risolvettero di comun consenso di far la pace, de Ti € presero per mezzano d'essa colui medesimo, ch'era staro scallei Generale in quella guerra. Xicotencarl, benchè da principio cogli Spa-rifiurafle di farlo per lo rofsore che avea dell' esito iofausto gnuoli. della guerra, fu alla fine obbligato a incaricarsli della com» messione. Portolli al campo degli Spagnuoli con una nobile e numerosa comitiva, salutò Cortèàs a nome di tutta la Re» pubblica, fi scusò delle già fatte oltilità col pretesto d' averlo creduro Alleato di Motezuma, tanto a cagione de' superbi presenti mandatigli da Messico, quanto per la gran truppa messicana , che conduceva seco, promise una ferma pace ed una eterna alleanza tra gli Spagnuoli ed i Tlascalleli , e gli presentò un poco d' oro ,ed alcune balle di vesti di bambagia , scusando la scarsezza dell' oflerta colla povertà del loro paese cagionata dalla perpetua guerra co' Messicani, i quali impedivano loro il coinmercio con altre Provincie, Cortés non tralafciò veruna dimostrazione di rispetto verso Xicotencatl: fece sembiante d' eflere soddisfatto delle sue scuse ; ma richiese, che la pace fosse finczra e durevole; poichè le giammai la rompevano , prenderebbe una sì terribile vendetta di loro, che fofle per servir d' esempio agli altri Popoli, Fatta la pace, e congedato Xicotencatl, fece Cortès celebrare il Santo Sacrifizio della Mela in rendimento di grazie all’ Altissimo. Ognuno porrà immaginare il dispiacere, ch' ebbero gli Ambasciatori Messicani nel veder conchiuso sì fatto accomodamento . Lagnaronsi con Cortès, e gli rinfacciarono la sua troppa facilità nel dar credenza alle promesse d’uomini sì perfidi, come i Tlascallesi . Dicevangli, che quelle apparenze di pace non ad altro fine s' indirizzavano , che a quello d' inspirargli della confidenza per tirarlo alla loro Capitale, e far quivi senza loro pericolo ciò , che non avea» [p. 51] 51 aveàno potuto ottenere colle armi în campagna : che para-2==gonafse la condotta di quel Senato con quella della Corte Liu. VUI, di Messico. I Tlascalleh , dopo d' aver accordato loro con mostre di pace il permesso d' entrare nel loro paese, non cessarono di fare ad essi la guerra , finchè non riconobbero affatto inutili tutti i loro sforzi... Da' Messicani pel contrario non aveano sofferra niuna ostilità, anzi aveano. avuro la più distinta accoglienza, ed i più grandi ossequj, e serviz) In tutti i luoghi de' loro dominj, dov' erano capitati , e dal loro Sovrano, le più rilevanti prove di benevolenza, e d'a» micizia .. Cortès rispose, che non credette mai di far verun torto con quell'accomodamento alla Corte di Messico, acui si protestava sommamente obbligato ; poichè egli voleva aver pace con tutti: che del resto e' non temeva i Tilascallesi ia caso che efler volessero suoi nemici: che per lui, e per gli altri Spagnuoli tanto valeva l'efler affaliti nella Circà, quanto nella campagna; tanto di dì, quanto di notte, mentre (apevano vincere in qualunque luogo e tempo ; che anzi per quel medesimo , che coloro dicevano de’ Tlascalleli , egli voleva portarsi alla loro Città , per aver occasione di far quivè una strepitosa vendetta della loro perfidia.

Bk. VIII.

> Non fu l'alleanza de' Tlascalless l’unico frutto, che raccolsero, gli Spagnuoli dalle loro vittorie . Nel medesimo campo, nel quale avea ascoltato I’ Ambasciatore di iaia

breast-straps, and went to meet the enemy, who were just then marching toward the Spanish camp. The sight of the punishment inflicted on the spies, and the noise of the bells in the silence and the darkness of the night, so frightened the Tlaxcalans that they at once fell into disorder and fled by various roads; and Xicotencatl himself returned in shame to Tlaxcala. Maxixcatzin therefore took the occasion to press his first opinion, adding now to the reasons already adduced by him the disastrous experience of so many expeditions that had turned out unhappily: which moved all the minds of the senate to peace.

§ 20.     While this affair was being debated in Tlaxcala, in Mexico they New embassies and

gifts from were consulting about what should be done with those strangers.

Moctezuma to Moctezuma, aware of the victories of the Spaniards, and fearing by

Cortés.

now their confederation with the Tlaxcalans, summoned the king of

Texcoco, his nephew, Prince Cuitláhuac, and other councilors, set before them the state of affairs, revealed his fears, and asked their counsel. The king of Texcoco held to his first opinion, namely that those strangers should be magnificently treated in all the places through which they passed; that they should be graciously admitted into the court, and their proposals heard, as those of any vassal would be heard, the king always displaying his superiority and observing that decorum which befits the majesty of the throne; that if they should ever plot anything against the person of the king or against the state, force and severity should be employed against them. Prince

Cuitláhuac repeated what he had said in the other conference, namely that it was not expedient to receive those strangers in the court; that a good gift should be sent to their leader, he should be asked what he liked in that country for the great lord in whose name he came, and the friendship and good understanding of the Mexicans should be offered him; but that at the same time new entreaties should be made to him to return to his own country. Among the other [p. 49] councilors some embraced the opinion of the king of Texcoco, and

Bk. VIII. others that of the lord of Iztapalapa, to which Moctezuma also adhered. This unhappy king found everywhere only objects and reasons to fear. The imminent confederation of the Tlaxcalans with the Spaniards kept him in extreme disquiet. On another side, Cortés’s alliance with Prince Ixtlilxochitl, his nephew and sworn enemy, disquieted him, who since he had conspired against the king of Texcoco, his brother, had never laid down his arms, and just then was in Otompan at the head of a formidable army. These fears were increased by the rebellion of several provinces which had followed the example of the Totonacs.

He therefore sent six ambassadors to Cortés with a thousand curious cotton garments, and a good quantity of gold and of lovely feathers, and charged them to congratulate him on his victories, to offer him other, greater gifts, and to dissuade him from the journey to Mexico by representing to him the difficulty of the road and other obstacles hard to overcome. These ambassadors set out promptly with a retinue of more than two hundred men, and, arriving at the camp of the Spaniards, carried out exactly what had been ordered them. Cortés received them with all the honor due to their character, and declared himself extremely obliged to the goodness of so great a monarch; but he purposely detained the ambassadors, hoping that in the meantime some skirmish with the Tlaxcalans might occur which would establish before the Mexicans the bravery of his troops and the superiority of European arms; or else that, peace having been made with the republic, they might be witnesses of the severity with which he wished to reproach the Tlaxcalans for their obstinacy. It was not long before the occasion he so greatly desired presented itself. Three enemy squadrons fell upon the camp of the Spaniards with frightful yells and a tempest of arrows and darts. Cortés, although he had taken a purge that very day, mounted his horse and sallied out intrepidly against the Tlaxcalans, who without too much effort [p. 50] were defeated in sight of the Mexican ambassadors.

Bk. VIII.

The partisans of old Xicotencatl being at last persuaded that war

§ 21. with the Spaniards was not expedient for the republic, and fearing bePeace and confederation of the Tlaxcalans

sides that these might ally themselves with the Mexicans, resolved by with the Spaniards. common consent to make peace, and took as mediator for it that very man who had been general in that war. Xicotencatl, although at first he refused to do so for the shame he felt at the unfortunate outcome of the war, was in the end obliged to take charge of the commission.

He betook himself to the camp of the Spaniards with a noble and numerous retinue, saluted Cortés in the name of the whole republic, excused the hostilities already committed with the pretext that he had believed him an ally of Moctezuma, both on account of the superb gifts sent him from Mexico and because of the great Mexican troop that he brought with him, promised a firm peace and an eternal alliance between the Spaniards and the Tlaxcalans, and presented him with a little gold and some bales of cotton garments, excusing the scantiness of the offering by the poverty of their country, caused by the perpetual war with the Mexicans, who prevented their trade with other provinces. Cortés omitted no demonstration of respect toward

Xicotencatl: he made a show of being satisfied with his excuses; but he required that the peace be sincere and lasting; since if they ever broke it he would take so terrible a vengeance on them that it would serve as an example to the other peoples.

The peace made, and Xicotencatl dismissed, Cortés had the Holy

Sacrifice of the Mass celebrated in thanksgiving to the Most High.

Everyone can imagine the displeasure which the Mexican ambassadors felt on seeing such an accommodation concluded. They complained to Cortés, and reproached him for his too great readiness in giving credence to the promises of men so perfidious as the

Tlaxcalans. They told him that those appearances of peace were directed to no other end than that of inspiring him with confidence in order to draw him to their capital, and to do there without danger to themselves what they had not [p. 51] been able to obtain by arms in the open field; that he should compare the conduct of that senate with that of the court of Mexico. The Bk. VIII. Tlaxcalans, after granting them with show of peace permission to enter their country, had not ceased to make war on them until they recognized all their efforts as wholly useless. From the Mexicans, on the contrary, they had suffered no hostility; indeed they had had the most distinguished reception, and the greatest attentions and services in all the places of their dominions where they had arrived, and from their sovereign the most notable proofs of goodwill and friendship. Cortés replied that he had never believed that he did any wrong by that accommodation to the court of Mexico, to which he declared himself extremely obliged; since he wished to have peace with everyone; that for the rest he did not fear the Tlaxcalans in case they should choose to be his enemies; that for him and for the other Spaniards it was all one to be assailed in the city as in the open country, by day as by night, since they knew how to conquer in any place and time; that indeed for the very reason that those men said about the Tlaxcalans, he wished to go to their city, in order to have occasion to take there a resounding vengeance for their perfidy.

The Tlaxcalans were far from that disloyalty which the Mexicans imputed to them; for from the very moment in which the senate decreed peace they were always the most faithful allies of the Spaniards, as will be seen in the course of this history. The senate was eager to have Cortés in Tlaxcala with all his troops in order to bind still closer the mutual friendship and to treat seriously of the confederation against the Mexicans, and they had already, by means of their messengers, invited that general to take lodging in their houses, declaring the regret they felt at seeing such illustrious friends of the republic in so great discomfort.

The alliance of the Tlaxcalans was not the only fruit which the Spaniards gathered from their victories. In the same camp in which he had heard the ambassador of Tlaxcala,

Cortés, when he had become sufficiently informed of the quality, the pretensions, and the forces of that prince, gladly accepted his alliance, and offered to place him on the throne of Acolhuacan.

At the same time the Mexican ambassador, who was expected, returned from the court with a gift of gold jewels worth fifteen hundred sequins, and of two hundred precious garments of feathers, and with fresh entreaties from Moctezuma to turn that general aside from the journey to Mexico and from friendship with the Tlaxcalans: vain efforts of the faint-heartedness of that monarch, since to spend so much gold on gifts to those strangers was in truth nothing other than to buy at a higher price the chains which were soon to bind his liberty.

VIII. enlisted in Cuba, and the survivors were for the most part wounded or ailing; and such was the dismay this had caused among the soldiers that they not only spoke ill of their general in private, but even begged him to go back to Veracruz. But Cortés rallied them, and with effective reasons of honor, and with his own example of courage and constancy in perils and in hardships, rekindled them for that bold undertaking. At length they took fresh heart, with the hope of a happy outcome, founded on the confederations then made.

The Mexican ambassadors, who still kept with Cortés, declined to § 24. accompany him to Tlaxcala; but he persuaded them to go with him, Entry         of the

Spaniards into promising them that at his side they would be perfectly safe. This dif‐ Tlaxcala. ficulty overcome, the army marched, well ordered and prepared for any eventuality. In the cities of Tecompantzinco and Atlihuetzian it was received with all possible magnificence, though not comparable with that of the capital, from which the four lords of the republic came out to meet the Spaniards with a fine and numerous dance of the nobility, and with so great a throng of people that some estimated it at more than a hundred thousand persons: a number not improbable, considering the population of Tlaxcala and the surprising novelty of those extraordinary men, who aroused the curiosity of all those peoples. In all the streets of the city there had been set up, according to the custom of those nations, arches of branches and flowers, and everywhere there resounded a confused music of instruments and acclamations, with such great demonstrations of joy that it seemed rather the triumph of the republic that was being celebrated than that of its enemies. This day, so memorable in the annals of Tlaxcala, was September 23, 1519.

The Tlaxcalans had prepared for the Spaniards, and for all their allies, a fine and comfortable lodging. Cortés wished the Mexican ambassadors to lodge in an apartment near his own, as much to do them honor as to remove from their minds the distrust of the Tlaxcalans. The chiefs of the republic, to give the Spaniards a new proof of their sincere friendship, presented to Cortés, according to the custom of those peoples, three hundred beautiful young women. Cortés at first refused them, alleging that the Christian law forbade polygamy; but then, in order not to displease them, he accepted some of them as maids to Doña Marina. In spite of such a refusal they soon presented him with five virgins of the first nobility, whom Cortés did accept, in order to strengthen still more the friendship with that republic. These virgins, together with the others, were promptly instructed, and, renouncing the superstition of their parents, were solemnly baptized in a temple, which was cleaned and made ready for the celebration there of the most holy mysteries of our religion. One of the five ladies was a daughter of Prince Maxixcatzin, who took at baptism the name of Doña Elvira, and she fell to Captain Juan Velázquez de León. Another, a daughter of the elder Xicotencatl, was called Doña Luisa Techquihuatzin, and was given to Captain Pedro de Alvarado, (C) and the other three

> {*) Fiume di Tlascalla .

Encouraged by so happy a beginning, Cortés wished to persuade the chiefs of the republic and the nobility to detest their superstition and to acknowledge the one true Deity; but they, though convinced by his reasons, and confessing the goodness and the power of the God whom the Spaniards worshiped, were nevertheless not induced to renounce their so-called gods, because they considered them necessary for human happiness. “Our god Camaxtle,” they said, “grants us victory over our enemies; our goddess Matlalcueye sends the rain necessary to our fields, and defends us from the inundations of the Zahuapan. (*) To each of our gods we are indebted for a part of the happiness of our life, and their wrath, provoked by our ingratitude, could bring down the most terrible punishments upon the state.” Cortés, animated by a zeal too ardent and violent, wished to do to the idols of Tlaxcala what he had done with good success to those of Cempoala; but Father Olmedo and other persons of standing dissuaded him from so rash an attempt, representing to him that such violence, besides being unsuited to the peaceful promulgation of the Gospel, could cause the total ruin of the Spaniards in a city so populous and so attached to superstition. Nevertheless, during the twenty days that he stayed there he never ceased to reproach them with the abominable cruelty of their sacrifices, and to inculcate the purity and the holiness of the Christian religion, the falsity of the gods they worshiped, and the existence of a Supreme Being, who rules all natural causes and watches with admirable providence over the preservation of his creatures. These exhortations, made by a man of such authority, of whom the Tlaxcalans had formed too exalted an idea, though they did not produce all the fruit that was desired, were nevertheless quite useful, since the senate

Thus every day the alliance of the Tlaxcalans was established more firmly by new demonstrations, in spite of the repeated suggestions of the Mexican ambassadors to break it. Cortés, although well persuaded of the sincerity of the Tlaxcalans, had given orders to his troops to remain constantly under arms against whatever might happen. The senate took offense at this, and complained bitterly of Cortés’s distrust after so many and such clear proofs of their good faith; but

Cortès quantunque ben persuaso della fincerità de' Tiascallesi , avea dato ordine alle sue truppe di mantenersi ognora ia arme per cid che avvenir potesse. Spaniards. The senate was appeased by the reply, and such discipline in soldiers so pleased them that Maxixcatzin wished to introduce it among the troops of the republic.

At last Cortés, having procured during the time he stayed in

Tlaxcala a more exact knowledge of the situation of the city of

Mexico, of the forces of that kingdom, and of everything that could serve his purpose, determined to continue his journey; but before departing he gave the Tlaxcalans, as a gift, a great number of the finest garments that the King of Mexico had sent him. He was in doubt about the road he should take to go to that court. The Mexican ambassadors wished him to go by way of Cholula, where good lodging had been prepared for all his men. The Tlaxcalans dissuaded him from such a course, representing the perfidy of the Cholulans, and counseled him to take the road by Huexotzinco, a state likewise confederated with the Tlaxcalans and with the Spaniards; but Cortés resolved to go by way of Cholula, as much to please the ambassadors as to show the Tlaxcalans how little account he made of the efforts of his enemies.

The hatred kindled in the hearts of the Tlaxcalans by so detestable a treachery was seeking some occasion to avenge it, and none seemed to them more opportune than this, now that they found themselves confederated with the Spaniards. Now, in order to inspire the same hatred in Cortés, and to move him to war against that state, they made him aware of the conduct of the Cholulans toward him; for they had not sent their messengers to pay him compliments, whereas the Huexotzincas had sent theirs, although they were somewhat farther away than the Cholulans. They told him, moreover, of the message which they said they had received from the Cholulans, reproaching them for the alliance made with the Spaniards, calling them cowards and base, and threatening them that if they attempted anything against that Holy City they would all die drowned; for among their other errors they were persuaded that whenever they pleased they could, merely by scraping the walls of the sanctuary of Quetzalcoatl, make great rivers spring from it, which in a moment would flood the city; and though the Tlaxcalans feared such a misfortune, the desire for vengeance surpassed their fear.

Moved by such suggestions, Cortés sent four Tlaxcalan nobles to Cholula to learn from those lords the reason why they had not shown toward him the regard that the Huexotzincas had shown. The Cholulans excused themselves on the ground of their enmity with the Tlaxcalans, whom they could never trust. (D) This reply was brought by four commoners, which

(D) Torquemada adds that the Cholulans detained the chief of the Tlaxcalan messengers, called Patlahuatzin, and with unheard-of cruelty flayed [p. 58] was a manifest demonstration of contempt. Cortés, warned of this by the

Bk. VIII. Tlaxcalans, had those lords told, through four Cempoalans sent there by him, that the embassy of a monarch so great as the King of Spain was not to be entrusted to such base messengers, since not even they themselves were worthy to hear it; that they should know that the Catholic King was the true lord of all that country, and that in his name he was coming to exact the homage of those peoples; that those who submitted to him would be honored, and the rebels would be punished according to their deserts; that they should therefore appear within three days in Tlaxcala, to render obedience to their sovereign; otherwise they would be treated as enemies. The Cholulans, although among themselves they mocked, as may be believed, so arrogant an embassy, nevertheless, in order to dissemble their malign intent, presented themselves the next day to Cortés, begging him to excuse their failure, caused by their enmity with the Tlaxcalans, and protesting that they were not only friends of the Spaniards but vassals as well of the King of Spain.

§ 26.

Entry of the   Having therefore resolved on the journey by way of Cholula, Cortés left Spaniards into

Cholula. Tlaxcala with all his men and with a great number of Tlaxcalan troops (E), which he promptly dismissed, except six thousand men whom he took with him. A little before arriving at Cholula, the principal lords came out to meet him, and the priests with censers in their hands and with music of instruments, and after performing the customary ceremonies of respect they told the general to enter, by all means, with all his Spaniards and his face and arms, and cut off his hands; but this account is certainly false, for such an atrocity could not have been unknown to the Spaniards; yet neither Bernal Díaz, nor Cortés, nor any other of the first historians makes mention of it. Cortés would not have omitted it in his letter to Charles V to justify the severity of the punishment inflicted on the Cholulans; nor is it likely that after such an outrage committed against one of his messengers he would have waited for other signs of the perfidy of the Cholulans in order to punish it.

Bk. VIII. their enemies, to enter. Cortés consented in order to please them, and the Tlaxcalans remained encamped outside the city, imitating in the arrangement of the camp, in the order of the sentinels, and in other things the military discipline of the Spaniards. On the entry of the Spanish army into Cholula there was a similar throng of people, and the same ceremonies, acclamations, and courtesies as there had been in Tlaxcala, but not so sincere.

At that time Cholula was a populous city, eighteen miles distant from Tlaxcala to the south, and about sixty from Mexico to the east, and no less celebrated for the commerce of its inhabitants than for its religion. It was situated, as it is at present, in a beautiful plain, and not far from that cluster of high mountains which surround the valley of Mexico on the east. Its population at that time was, according to Cortés, about forty thousand houses, and almost as many more were in the surrounding villages, which served it in place of suburbs. Its commerce consisted in cotton manufactures, in gems, and in earthenware, and the jewelers and potters of Cholula were very famous. As for religion, it may be said that Cholula was the Rome of Anahuac. The celebrated Quetzalcoatl’s having stayed so many years in that city, and his having so greatly favored its citizens, brought it about that after the apotheosis of this god a special worship was dedicated to him there. The astonishing multitude of temples that it had, and above all the great temple, erected upon a mountain made by hand, which still survives, drew to that place, held to be holy, endless pilgrims, not only from the neighboring cities but even from the more distant provinces.

Cortés was lodged with all his troops in certain large houses, where for the first two days they were abundantly supplied with provisions; but soon these began to run short, until nothing was furnished them but water and wood. This was not the only proof of their malign disposition,

plotting. The Cempoalan allies observed that in the streets of the city there were some pits, in which they had planted sharp stakes and covered them with earth, which seemed made for no other purpose than to disable the horses. Eight men, moreover, who came from the camp of the Tlaxcalans, warned him that they had seen the city emptied of women and children: a sure sign among those nations of some imminent war. Besides, it was known that in some streets they had built entrenchments, and had made great heaps of stones on the flat roofs of the houses. Finally, a Cholulan lady, who had fallen in love with the beauty, the wit, and the discretion of Doña Marina, begged her to save herself in her house from the danger that threatened the

> Vedendosi Cortès in sì grave rischio di perire , determinò adoperare i mezzi più opportuni per salvarli , Fece venire alla sua presenza le persone principali della Città, e disfle loro, che sz aveano qualche querela contro gli Spagnuoli , l'’esponessero schiettamente, ficcome fi conveniva ad uomini onorati , e lor darebbe una convenevole soddisfazione, Risposero coloro , ch' erano ben soddisfatti della sua condotta, e pronti a servirlo: che qualora determinafie la spa partenza, farebbe abbondantemen-

Spaniards; whereupon Doña Marina had occasion to learn the whole contrivance of the conspiracy, and at once informed Cortés. He learned by word of mouth from the same Cholulan lady that her fellow citizens had agreed to make a general slaughter of the Spaniards with the help of twenty thousand

Mexicans (*) who were encamped near the city. Not content with these reports, he charged Doña Marina to use all her arts to bring to his lodging two priests, who confirmed everything that the lady had declared.

Seeing himself in so grave a risk of perishing, Cortés resolved to employ the most suitable means to save himself. He had the principal persons of the city come into his presence, and told them that if they had any complaint against the Spaniards they should state it frankly, as befitted honorable men, and he would give them fitting satisfaction. They replied that they were well satisfied with his conduct and ready to serve him; that whenever he determined on his departure, he would be abundantly provided

The Cholulans went away content, because it seemed to them that everything was going well for the happy success of their treachery; and to make it more sure, they sacrificed to their gods, so they say, ten children, five of each sex. Cortés assembled his captains, disclosed to them the perverse designs of the Cholulans, and bade them state their opinion. Some wished that the danger be avoided by withdrawing to the city of Huexotzinco, barely nine miles from Cholula, or else to Tlaxcala; but the greater part left the matter to the determination of their general. Cortés gave the orders that seemed to him most suited to his purpose, protesting that he would never think himself safe in Mexico without leaving that perfidious city well punished. He ordered the auxiliary troops of Tlaxcala to fall upon the city the next day at sunrise, putting to the sword all the citizens, sparing none, save only the women and children.

order to give you satisfaction; but you, with detestable perfidy, have contrived under the semblance of friendship the most cruel treachery, to make me perish with all my men: I am ignorant of nothing of your malign designs.” And calling aside four or five Cholulans, he asked them what reason they had had for resolving upon so execrable an attempt. They replied that the Mexican ambassadors, to please their sovereign, had induced them to plot his death. Cortés then, with a countenance full of fire, spoke thus to the ambassadors who were present: “These wicked men, to excuse their crime, blame for the treachery both you and your king; but I neither believe you capable of such villainy, nor can I persuade myself that the great monarch

Moctezuma would wish to play the cruel enemy toward me at the very time when he gives me the most weighty proofs of his friendship, or that, being able to oppose my claims by open force, he would avail himself of traitors to thwart them. Rest assured that I shall have your persons respected in the massacre that we are about to carry out. Today these traitors will perish, and their city will be thrown into ruin. I call Heaven and Earth to witness that it is their perfidy that arms our hands for a vengeance so contrary to our inclination.”

That said, and the signal to attack having been given by the firing of a musket, the Spaniards hurled themselves with such fury upon those wretched victims that of all those who were in the courtyard, although they were many, not one was left alive. The streams of blood that ran through that courtyard, and the piteous laments of the dying, would suffice to cause horror and pity in any heart that was not driven on by the fury of vengeance. Having no more to do within the house, they went out into the streets, bloodying their swords with the same severity on as many Cholulans as presented themselves to them.

The Tlaxcalans for their part entered the city like hungry lions, reviving their ferocity with the hatred [p. 63] of their enemies, and with the desire to please their new allies. A blow so fierce and so unexpected at once threw the citizens into dis‐ Bk. VIII. order; but having gathered in several squadrons they made for some time a vigorous resistance, until, seeing the slaughter that the artillery was working among them, and recognizing the superiority of European arms, they were again thrown into confusion. The greater part of them sought escape in flight; some resorted to the superstition of scraping the walls of the temple in order to flood the city; but finding such effort wholly useless, they tried to fortify themselves in the houses and in the temples. Even this was of no avail; for behold, their enemies set fire to all the buildings where they meet with any resistance. The houses burn, and the towers of the temples: nothing is seen in the streets but bloodied or half-burned corpses, nor is anything heard but the insulting and threatening clamors of the confederates, the feeble sighs of the dying, imprecations against the victors, and laments to their gods for having abandoned them in so great a calamity. Of the many who took refuge in the towers of the temples there was but one who surrendered to the victors: all the others either perished, burned to ashes, or procured a less painful death by throwing themselves down from that height.

(F) In the writings of Monsignor de las Casas this event at Cholula is read very much distorted. It is true that the vengeance was too rigorous and the massacre made there horrible; but the Spaniards did not lack, for punishing the Cholulans, those reasons that we have adduced, and this prelate makes no mention of any, nor did those odious circumstances attend it which he recounts, and which are not found in any ancient historian. To make us believe that the Spaniards carried out that massacre merely out of caprice, and that while the soldiers made rivers of blood flow the general cheerfully sang I know not what verses, it would be necessary at least that the same prelate testify to it as an eyewitness, or that he allege such documents as would suffice to efface that idea of Cortés which all who knew him give us, and make probable what is wholly incredible. But Monsignor de las Casas was neither present, nor does he adduce proofs sufficient to merit our belief. Without due caution he availed himself of some information given him by one of the many enemies of Cortés. I am no panegyrist of this Conqueror, to excuse [p. 64] more than six thousand Cholulans, the city was left depopulated. The

Cortés, moved to pity, caused the fury of arms to cease, and a general pardon to be proclaimed. On the announcement of this decree there were seen to rise at once from among the slain some who had feigned death in order to escape it, and troops of fugitives came toward the city, weeping, some for the death of a son or a brother, some for that of a husband. Cortés had the corpses, which by now were beginning to stink, removed from the temples and the streets, and set the noble prisoners at liberty.

his faults; but I am a historian, I am a man, and I am a Christian, and therefore I will not affirm what I do not believe, nor believe so great a wickedness in an individual of my species without grave grounds. I describe the event at Cholula as I find it in the most truthful historians, who were present or informed themselves as well from the ancient Spaniards as from the Indians.

[p. 65]

Within a few days that city was so well populated again that not one of its inhabitants seemed to be missing. There Cortés received the Bk. VIII. compliments of the Huexotzincas and of the Tlaxcalans, and the oath of fidelity to the Crown of Spain from the Cholulans themselves and from the people of Tepeyacac; he settled the differences that existed between the two republics of Tlaxcala and Cholula, and restored their ancient alliance and friendship, which from then on never failed. Finally, to satisfy the duties of humanity and of religion, he had the cages in the temples broken open, and set at liberty all the prisoners and slaves who were destined for sacrifice. He also had the great temple cleaned, and raised upon it the standard of the cross, after having given the Cholulans, as he did to all the other peoples among whom he stayed, some idea of the Christian religion.

The ambassadors replied that before taking such a resolution he should make more diligent inquiries into the affair of the Cholulans, to be certified of the good intentions of their sovereign; that if it seemed good to him, one of them would go to the court to present to the king his complaints. clear up the truth in this particular, nor can we refrain from blaming the levity of our authors in affirming so confidently what they altogether did not know. Why should credence be given to the Cholulans, men double-dealing and dissembling, as all confess, and not to the

Mexicans, and to Moctezuma himself, who by the eminence of his character was more worthy of trust? The constantly peaceful conduct of that monarch toward the Spaniards, in that he did them no harm on so many and such fine occasions as he had to overwhelm them, and the moderation with which he always spoke of them (which the historians themselves do not deny), make the excuse of the Cholulans improbable; but on the other hand certain indications, though obscure, of Moctezuma’s displeasure, and above all the hostilities committed at this same time on the garrison of Veracruz by a powerful feudatory of the Crown of Mexico, give it some appearance of truth.

§ 30. Uprisings in     Cuauhpopoca, (*) lord of Nauhtlan (called by the Spaniards Almería), Totonacapan. a city situated on the coast of the Mexican gulf, thirty-six miles north

of Veracruz and near the borders of the Mexican empire on that side, had orders from Moctezuma to reduce the Totonacs to due obedience as soon as Cortés should withdraw from that coast. In order to do his duty he demanded with threats from those peoples the tribute which they were bound to pay to their sovereign. The Totonacs, grown insolent through the favor of their new allies, replied arrogantly that they owed no homage to one who was no longer their king.

Now Cuauhpopoca, seeing that his demands availed nothing to restore to subordination men who had too much confidence in their allies and no respect for their sovereign, put himself at the head of the Mexican troops that were in the garrison of those frontiers, and began to make raids through the

> (*), Bernal Diaz I' appella Quetzalpòpoca, il quale è ancora. nome MeMi= #200. > [p. 67] 67 li luoghi di Totonacapan, «<astigando coll’armi la loro ribel- ==lione. 1 Toronachi porzarono i loro lamenti a Giovaniitas. VUL d' Escalante, Governatore del presidio della Veracroce, e lo pregarona d' opporsi alla crudeltà de' Messicani , esibendosi ad ajutarlo con un buon numero di truppe. Elscalante mandò al Capo de' Mefficani un'ambadciata cortese per distorlo da quelle ostilità , le «quali non potevano , secondo che egli credeva, efler gradite dal Re di Meslico , che tanto s' era impegnato nel favoric gli Spagnuoli protettori de' Totonachi . Quaubpopoca rispose, ch’ egli meglio di lui sapeva, fe era o no, spiacevole al suo Re il pgastigo di que' ribelli: che se gli Spagnuoli volevano sostenergli, egli colle sue truppe gli aspetterebbe nelle pianure di Nauktlan , acciocchè l'armi decideflero della loro sorte. Non potè comportare una tal rif. posta il Governatore: onde marciò incontanente verlo il luogo prefiflo con due cavalli, e due piccoli cannoni, con cinquanta pedoni Spagguoli , € con dieci mila Toronachi in circa. Nel primo attacco de' Messicani subito fi scompigliarono i Toronachi, e per la maggior parte fi misero a fuggire ; ma ad onta della loro codardia gli Spagnuo» li continuarono coraggiosamente la zuffa , facendo non poco male ai Meslicani . Costoro, come quelli che non aveano mai sperimentata la violenza dell’artiglierìa, e la maniera di combattere depli Europei , fi traflero impauriti alla vicina città di Navwhrlan. Gli Spapnuoli gl’ incalzarono con furia, e attaccarono il fuoco ad alcuni edifizj ; ma questa vittoria lor costò la vita del Governatore , il quale infra tre giorni morì delle ferite, di sei o sette soldati, e di mol» ti Totonachi., Un di questi soldati, il quale aveva la testa grofla e l'asperto fiero , fu fatto prigione , e mandato a Mesfico da Quauhpopoca; ma eflendo morto per le ferite nella strada , non portarono altro a Motezama, che la testa, la cui sembianza fece ranto ribrezzo a quel Re, che non vol. le che fofle a suoi Dei offerta in alcun tempio della Corte, : Ebbe Cortès la nuova di queste rivoluzioni prima di I 2 par[p. 68] partir da Chololla; (G) ma non volle dire allora niente;

(*) Bernal Díaz calls him Quetzalpopoca, which is also a Mexican name. [p. 67] the districts of Totonacapan, chastising their rebellion with arms. The Totonacs carried their complaints to Juan de Escalante, governor Bk. VIII. of the garrison of Veracruz, and begged him to oppose the cruelty of the Mexicans, offering to help him with a good number of troops. Escalante sent to the chief of the Mexicans a courteous embassy to dissuade him from those hostilities, which could not, as he believed, be agreeable to the King of Mexico, who had so committed himself to favoring the Spaniards, protectors of the Totonacs. Cuauhpopoca replied that he knew better than Escalante whether or not the punishment of those rebels was displeasing to his king; that if the Spaniards wished to support them, he with his troops would await them in the plains of Nauhtlan, so that arms might decide their fate. The governor could not endure such a reply; so he marched at once toward the appointed place with two horse and two small cannon, with fifty Spanish foot, and with about ten thousand Totonacs. At the first attack of the Mexicans the Totonacs were at once thrown into confusion, and the greater part took to flight; but in spite of their cowardice the Spaniards continued the fight courageously, doing no little harm to the Mexicans. These, as men who had never experienced the violence of artillery and the manner of fighting of the Europeans, withdrew in fright to the nearby city of Nauhtlan. The Spaniards pressed them furiously, and set fire to some buildings; but this victory cost them the life of the governor, who within three days died of his wounds, and of six or seven soldiers, and of many Totonacs. One of these soldiers, who had a large head and a fierce aspect, was taken prisoner and sent to Mexico by Cuauhpopoca; but having died of his wounds on the road, they brought nothing to Moctezuma but the head, whose appearance caused such horror in that king that he would not allow it to be offered to his gods in any temple of the court.

§ 31.   Now, having no more to do in Cholula, he resumed the journey to Journey of the

Spaniards to Mexico with his Spaniards, with six thousand Tlaxcalans, and with Tlalmanalco. some Huexotzinca and Cholulan troops. At Izcalpan, a village of

Huexotzinco, fifteen miles distant from Cholula, the Huexotzinca lords came again to pay him their compliments, and advised him that from that place there were two roads to Mexico: one open and well kept, which led to certain ravines where some ambush of the enemy was to be feared, and the other recently obstructed and encumbered with trees purposely cut down, which was also the shorter and the safer. Cortés profited by the advice, and in spite of the Mexicans had the obstructions removed from the road, under the pretext that the difficulty of the way was rather an incentive to the courage of the

Spaniards; and he continued his journey through that great forest of pines and oaks until he climbed to the summit of a high mountain called Ithualco, between the two volcanoes Popocatepetl and

Iztaccihuatl, where they found large houses intended for the lodging of Mexican merchants. Here they became aware of the daring feat of

Captain Diego de Ordaz, who a few days before, to make known to those peoples the courage of his nation, had climbed, together with nine other soldiers, almost to the very summit of Popocatepetl, although he could not observe the mouth, or vent, of that great volcano, on account of the deep snow that was there, and of the clouds of smoke and ashes that it hurled from its entrails. Meanwhile Moctezuma, dismayed by the event at Cholula, retired to the palace Tlillancalmecatl, set apart for the time of mourning, and stayed there eight days, fasting and practicing his usual austerities to obtain the protection of his gods. From this same retreat he sent to Cortés four personages of his court with a gift, and with fresh entreaties and pretexts to turn him aside from the journey, offering to pay a certain tribute annually to the King of Spain, and to give the Spanish general four loads of gold, (*) and one to each of his captains and soldiers, if from the place where they then were they would return to their own country. So great was the horror that the Spaniards caused in that superstitious prince! He would not have made more anxious efforts to avoid their sight, had he foreseen all the harm they were to do him. Cortés paid them every possible courtesy, and replied, thanking the king for his gift and for his magnificent promises, to which he hoped to respond with good services; but at the same time protesting that he could not turn back without making himself guilty of disobedience to his sovereign, and promising to do the state not the slightest harm by his coming: that if, after he had set forth by word of mouth to His Majesty the embassy he bore, and which he could not entrust to any other person, he should judge that the sojourn of the Spaniards at the court was not conducive to the good of his kingdom, he would without delay take the road again to return to his own country.

Moctezuma’s disquiet increased through the suggestions of the priests, and especially through the report they gave him of certain oracles of their lying gods, and of I know not what frightful visions which they said they had had in those days. This put his mind in such consternation that, without awaiting the outcome of the last embassy sent to the Spaniards, he held council again with the King of

> (ID' Amaquemecan dagli Spagnuoli derta Mecameca è presentemente un viliaggio non per altro rinomato... che per essere ivi nata la celebratissima Monaca, Giovanna' Agnèse della: Croce, donna di prodigioso-ingegno,.e di pon volgar-letceratura ,

Texcoco, with his brother Cuitláhuac, and with the other personages whom he was accustomed to consult, all of whom held to their first opinion: Cuitláhuac in that of not permitting the Spaniards to enter the court, and of making them leave the kingdom, willingly or by force, and Cacamatzin in that of receiving them as ambassadors, since the King of Mexico did not lack forces to repress them, should they plot anything against the royal person or against the state.

Moctezuma, who until then had always adhered to the opinion of his brother, now embraced that of the King of Texcoco, but at the same time charged this same king to go to meet the Spaniards and to endeavor to dissuade the general from the journey to the court. Then

Cuitláhuac, turning to the king his brother, said to him, “May the gods grant, lord, that you not receive into your house one who will drive you out of it, and that when you wish to remedy the evil you may have time and means to [p. 71] do so.” “What are we to do,” replied the king, “when our friends, and

Bk. VIII. what is more, our very gods, instead of favoring us, make our enemies prosper? I am now resolved, and I could wish that all would resolve not to flee, nor to show any cowardice, come what may; but I pity the old men and the children, who have no strength to defend themselves.”

Cortés, having dismissed the Mexican ambassadors, set out with his troops from Ithualco, and took the road by Amaquemecan and Tlalmanalco, two cities about nine miles apart from each other, situated on the slopes of those great mountains. Amaquemecan, together with the neighboring hamlets, contained twenty thousand inhabitants. (I) In these places the Spaniards were well received, and several lords of that province visited Cortés and presented him with a certain quantity of gold and some slave women: they complained bitterly of the vexations they suffered from the King of Mexico and his ministers, in the same terms in which those of Cempoala and of Chiahuitztla had already done, and at the suggestion of the Cempoalans and of the Tlaxcalans who accompanied Cortés, confederated with the Spaniards for the sake of liberty. So that the farther the Spaniards advanced into that country, the more their forces went on increasing, like a stream which, with the waters it receives in its course, goes on swelling until it becomes a great river.

From Tlalmanalco the army marched to Ayotzinco, a village situated on the southern shore of Lake Chalco, (L) where was the port for the merchant boats which traded

news that the King of Texcoco was coming to visit the Spanish general in the name of the King of Mexico, his uncle. Not long after, the king himself arrived, carried in a litter adorned with handsome feathers on the shoulders of four of his servants, and followed by a numerous and brilliant retinue of Mexican and Texcocan nobility. As soon as he came in sight of the Spanish general he alighted from the litter, and began to walk on foot, preceded by some of his servants, who went along removing from the road everything that might offend his eyes or his feet. The Spaniards were amazed at such grandeur, and from it conjectured how great that of the King of Mexico would be.

Cortés came out to meet him at the door of the lodging, and greeted him with a profound bow, to which the king responded by touching the ground with his right hand and then carrying it to his mouth. He entered with a lordly and majestic air one of the halls, and having sat down, congratulated that general and his captains on their happy arrival, and professed the great desire which the King of Mexico, his uncle, had to form a friendship and to have good relations with the monarch of the East, by whom they had been sent to that country; but at the same time he exaggerated the difficulties that would have to be overcome in order to go to the court, and begged Cortés to change his purpose, if he wished to please the king. Cortés replied that if he were ever to turn back without delivering his embassy, he would fail in his duty, and would give great displeasure to his sovereign, who had sent him and and it is plainly seen from the description of Cortés, and no one before Solís has said that it took place at Amaquemecan. Iztapalatenco; but this is a manifest mistake caused by a lapse of memory. [p. 73] and all the more since he found himself now so near to the court, af‐

Bk. VIII. ter having overcome the perils of so long a journey. If it is so, then, said the king, we shall meet at the court: and taking courteous leave, after having been presented with some European trinkets, he left behind a part of his nobility to accompany Cortés on the journey.

From Ayotzinco the Spaniards marched to Cuitláhuac, a city founded on a small island in Lake Chalco, which, although small, was nevertheless, according to Cortés, the most beautiful he had seen until then. This city communicated with the mainland by two broad and convenient causeways built on the lake: one to the south, two miles long, and the other to the north, which was more than two miles in length. The Spaniards went along very cheerful at seeing the multitude and the beauty of the cities that were on the lake, the temples and the towers that rose above the other buildings, the groves that adorned the inhabited places, the kitchen gardens and gardens floating on the waters, and the innumerable boats that plied them, but no less fearful at seeing themselves surrounded by an immense throng of people who came from all those places to observe them: whereupon Cortés commanded his men to go well ordered and ready, and warned the Indians not to encumber the road, nor approach the files, if they did not wish to be treated as enemies. In Cuitláhuac they were well lodged and given gifts. The lord of that city complained secretly to Cortés of the tyranny of the King of Mexico, confederated with him, and made known to him the convenience of the road for going to the court, and the consternation into which the oracles of the gods, the phenomena of the sky, and the success of the Spanish arms had thrown Moctezuma.                                                            § 33.

From Cuitláhuac they set out by the other causeway toward Visit of the princes of

Texcoco, and entry of Iztapalapa; but on the way Cortés was detained by a new piece of the Spaniards into good fortune. Prince Ixtlilxochitl, seeing that Cortés had not wished that court. to make the journey by way of Calpulalpan, where he was awaiting him, resolved to come to meet him on the road to Iztapalapa. Cortés, seeing so many armed troops coming, felt some uneasiness; but when he was informed of the quality of the personages who were coming to find him, and of the motive of their coming, he went out to meet them, and, the due compliments having been paid on both sides, both princes invited Cortés to betake himself to the court of Texcoco, and he allowed himself to be easily persuaded by the great advantage he hoped to derive from Prince Ixtlilxochitl, whose attachment to the

Spaniards had already been made sufficiently evident.

Texcoco was at that time, although somewhat inferior to Mexico in magnificence and splendor, the largest and most populous city of the country of Anahuac. Its population, including that of the cities of

Huexotla, Coatlichan, and Atenco (which, being contiguous to it, might be reckoned its suburbs), was, according to Torquemada, a hundred and forty thousand houses. To the Spaniards it seemed twice as large as Seville. The grandeur of the temples and of the royal palaces, the beauty of the streets, the fountains, and the gardens furnished abundant matter for their admiration.

The population of Iztapalapa was then more than twelve thousand houses, built for the most part on a number of small islands very near one another and contiguous to the same peninsula, near which there were innumerable floating kitchen gardens and gardens. The city was then governed by Prince Cuitláhuac, brother of Moctezuma and his immediate successor on the throne of Mexico, who together with his other brother Matlatzincatzin, lord of the city of Coyoacán, received Cortés with the same demonstrations as had already been used by the other lords through whose places he had passed. They also assert that Cacamatzin accompanied Cortés to Texcoco; but it is clear to us that this is not true, both from Cortés’s account and from the ancient manuscripts cited by Don Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl. (N) An Indian historian cited by Don Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl says that on this occasion Prince Ixtlilxochitl was baptized, together with two hundred other nobles of that court; but this is a story so improbable that it needs no refutation. [p. 76] devised, and lodged him and all the troops that accompanied him in Bk. VIII. his own palace. This was a vast edifice of stone and lime, newly built

and not yet furnished. Besides its many halls and rooms convenient for living in, whose roof was of cedar and whose walls were covered with handsome cotton hangings, and besides the large courts where the troops allied with the Spaniards had their quarters, it had a garden of surprising size and beauty, described by us above, where we treated of the agriculture of the Mexicans. After dinner the prince led his guests to this garden, in which they greatly enjoyed themselves, and there formed a great idea of Mexican magnificence. In this city the Spaniards observed that, in place of the complaints and murmurs which they had heard elsewhere, nothing was heard but praise of the government, because the nearness of the court made people more cautious in speaking.

The next day, very early, the Spaniards marched along that great causeway which joined, as we have said, Iztapalapa with Mexico, and which was cut by seven small canals for the passage of boats from one lake to the other; over these there were bridges of beams for the convenience of travelers, which were easily raised whenever they wished to bar the passage to enemies. After passing through Mexicaltzinco, and seeing Colhuacan, Huitzilopochco, Coyoacán, and Mixcoac, cities all founded on the shore of the lake, they arrived, amid an incredible throng of people, at a place called Xoloc, where the causeway from Coyoacán joined this one. In the angle formed by these two causeways, not more than half a league distant from the capital, there was a good bulwark with two small towers, surrounded by a wall more than ten feet high with its crenellated parapet, with two gates and a drawbridge: a place memorable in the history of Mexico because the camp of the Spanish general was there during the siege of that great city. Here the army halted to receive the compliments of more than a thousand Mexican nobles, all uniformly dressed, who as they passed before the Spanish general bowed to him with the [p. 77] usual ceremony of touching the ground and kissing the hand.

When these compliments were over, in which they spent more Bk. VIII. than an hour, the Spaniards continued their march as well ordered as § 35. if they were going to give battle. A short time before arriving at the Entry of the

Spaniards into city Cortés received word that the King of Mexico was coming to Mexico, and demonmeet him, and shortly afterward he let himself be seen with a distin‐ strations     of the king

and of the nobility. guished and numerous retinue. Three nobles went before, carrying in their hands gold rods held aloft, as insignia of majesty, by which the people were warned of the presence of the sovereign. Moctezuma came richly dressed, on a litter covered with plates of gold, which four nobles carried on their shoulders, and under an umbrella or sunshade of green feathers adorned with a number of gold ornaments. He wore hanging from his shoulders a mantle adorned with very rich jewels of gold and gems, on his head a thin crown of the same metal, and on his feet soles, likewise of gold, tied with straps of leather studded with gold and gems. Two hundred lords, much better dressed than the other nobles but all barefoot, accompanied him two by two, keeping close on either side to the walls of the houses to show the respect which they bore to their sovereign. As soon as the king and the Spanish general saw each other, both dismounted, the latter from his horse and the former from his litter, and the king began to walk leaning on the arms of the King of Texcoco and of the lord of Iztapalapa. Cortés, after making the king a deep bow, drew near to him to put around his neck a gold cord on which were strung little glass balls that looked like gems, and the king bowed his head to receive it; but when Cortés wished to embrace him, he was not permitted by those two lords, who served as his supporters. That the two lords who accompanied Moctezuma did not permit Cortés to put the band around his neck. 3. That they did this with some disdain. 4. That they were, however, reproved by the king. VIII. and the pleasure he had in having come to know so great a monarch.

Moctezuma answered him in a few words, and having made the usual ceremony of touching the ground and kissing the hand, he repaid the gift of the glass beads with two necklaces of fine mother-of-pearl shells, from which hung some large prawns of gold made true to nature. He charged Prince Cuitláhuac with conducting Cortés to his lodging, and himself returned with the King of Texcoco.

Both the nobility and the immense crowd, who from the flat roofs, doors, and windows of the houses were watching everything that happened, were amazed and bewildered no less at the novelty of so many extraordinary objects presented to their eyes than at the unprecedented condescension of their king, which contributed greatly to enhancing the reputation of the Spaniards. These marched, themselves full of wonder at the sight of the greatness of the city, the magnificence of the buildings, and the multitude of the inhabitants, along that great and broad street which, without deviating at all from the straight line, continued that causeway of Iztapalapa built on the lake, as far as the south gate of the great temple, while in their minds there alternated with admiration fear for their fate, seeing themselves so few in the center of a foreign kingdom. Thus they walked a mile and a half into the city to the palace that had once been King Axayacatl’s, not far from the west gate of the said temple, which was assigned to them as their lodging. There Moctezuma was awaiting them, having however gone on ahead. When Cortés arrived at the gate of that palace, the king took him by the hand and led him into a great hall, made him sit on a dais similar in form to those of our altars and covered with a handsome cotton rug, beside a wall likewise covered with a rug adorned with gold and gems, and, taking courteous leave, said to him: “You and your companions are now in your own house: dine and rest, for I shall shortly return.”

Era sì grande questo edifizio , che vi s' alloggiarono comodamente e gli Spagnuoli , ed i loro Alleati, i quali infieme colle donne e colla servitù, che quelli seco loro conducevano , trapassavano i sette mila. Da per tutto v'era una gran pulizia: quasi rutte le stanze aveano letti di stuoje di giunco , e di palma, giusta la loro usanza, con altre stuoje arrotolate per guan- *ciali, e sotto cieli di bambagia, e scranne fatte d’ un solo pezzo . Alcune stanze aveano il pavimento coperto di stuoje, e le muraglie parimente coperte di tappeti di cotone di varj colori. Le mura erano asflai grofle, ed in certe distanze v'erano alcune torri. Sicché gli Spagnuoli vi trovarono quanto ne potevano bramare per la loro sicurezza . Il diligente e cauto Generale distribuì subito le guardie, formò una batterìa de’ suoi cannoni dirimpetto alla porta del palazzo, ed adoperò tanta diligenza per fortificarsi , come se quello stesso giorno asperrafse qualche affalto da’ suoi nemici . Imbandisli quel giorno a Cortès ed a' suoi Capitani un magnifico pranzo servito dalla Nobiltà, e pel resto dell’ esercito fi portarono diverse e copiole vivande, benchè d' inferior qualità. Questo dì “tanto memorabile non meno per gli Spagnuoli, che per li Messicani fu li 8. Nov. 1519. dopo sette mesi ch' erano arrivati gli Spagnuoli nel paese d’ Anahbuac,

The king went off to his palace; and Cortés at once caused [p. 79] a salvo of all the artillery to be fired, to frighten the Mexicans with

Bk. VIII. such a noise. Meanwhile he went to see all the rooms of the palace in order to assign quarters to his men. This building was so large that both the Spaniards and their allies were comfortably lodged in it, who together with the women and the servants whom they brought with them numbered more than seven thousand. Everywhere there was great cleanliness: almost all the rooms had beds of rush and palm mats, according to their custom, with other mats rolled up for pillows, and under canopies of cotton, and seats made of a single piece. Some rooms had the floor covered with mats, and the walls likewise covered with cotton hangings of various colors. The walls were very thick, and at certain intervals there were some towers. So the Spaniards found there all that they could wish for their security. The diligent and cautious general at once posted the guards, formed a battery of his cannon facing the gate of the palace, and used as much diligence in fortifying himself as if he expected some assault from his enemies that very day. A magnificent dinner, served by the nobility, was set out that day for Cortés and his captains, and for the rest of the army various and plentiful dishes were brought, though of inferior quality. This day, so memorable no less for the Spaniards than for the Mexicans, was November 8, 1519, seven months after the Spaniards had arrived in the country of Anahuac.

“Valiant general, and you his companions, all my domestics and courtiers are witnesses of the pleasure which I have had at your happy arrival at this court: and if until now I had made a show of reluctance, it was only [p. 81] to humor my subjects. Your fame has magnified things and disturbed

Bk. IX. minds. It was said that you were immortal gods; that you came mounted on beasts of portentous size and ferocity, and that you wielded thunderbolts with which you made the whole earth tremble. Others spread the report that you were monsters cast up by the sea; that the insatiable hunger for gold had made you abandon your country; that you were too much given to delights, and such gluttons that one of you ate as much as ten of our own people. But all these errors have vanished through the acquaintance that my subjects have had with you. It is now known that you are mortal men like us, although somewhat different in color and in beard. We have already seen with our own eyes that those beasts, so renowned, are nothing but deer more corpulent than ours, and that your so-called thunderbolts are nothing but a better-contrived kind of blowpipe, whose balls are driven with greater noise and do greater harm. As for your personal qualities, we are well informed by those who have had dealings with you that you are kindly and generous, that you bear hardships patiently, that you use severity only against those who provoke your indignation by their hostilities, and that you use arms only for the just defense of your persons.”

“I have no doubt that you likewise will already have driven from your minds, or will soon drive out, those false ideas which the flattery of my vassals or the malevolence of my enemies has made you conceive. There will also be someone who has told you that I am one of the gods, and that I take at my pleasure the form of a lion, or a tiger, or some other animal; but you see already (here, as he said this, he took the skin of his arm between his fingers) that I am of flesh and bone like other mortals, though more noble by my birth and more powerful by the height of my dignity. Some will have complained to you of my cruelty and tyranny; but they call tyranny the legitimate use of supreme authority, and they call cruelty the necessary severity of justice.”

“Having set aside, then, both on our side and on yours, every disadvantageous idea caused by false information, I accept the embassy of that great king who sends you, I hold his friendship dear, and I offer to his obedience my whole kingdom; since, considering the signs which we have observed in the heavens, and what we see in you, it seems to us that the time has now arrived for the oracles of our ancestors to be fulfilled, namely, that there should come from the east certain men, different from us in dress and in customs, who should be lords of all these countries; for we are not natives of this land: it is not many years since our ancestors came here from the northern regions, and we have not until now ruled these peoples otherwise than as lieutenants of Quetzalcoatl, our god and lawful lord.”

Cortés replied, thanking him greatly for the singular favors he had until then received from him, and for the honorable opinion which he had formed of the Spaniards. He told him that he was sent by the greatest monarch of Europe, who, although he might aspire to something more, being a descendant of Quetzalcoatl, nevertheless was content to establish a confederation and perpetual friendship with

His Majesty and with his successors; that the purpose of his embassy was not to take from others what they possessed, but rather to announce to them the true religion, and to communicate to him certain important counsels for improving the government and making his vassals happy: which he would do on another occasion, if His

The next day, Cortés, wishing to return the king’s visit, sent to ask § 2. him for an audience, and obtained it so promptly that those who Cortés’s visit to the

king. brought him the answer were the very men who served as introducers of ambassadors, and who were to conduct him and instruct him in the ceremonial of that court. Cortés dressed in the most splendid finery he had, and took with him the captains Alvarado, Sandoval, Velázquez de León, and Ordaz, and five soldiers besides. They went to the royal palace amid an immense crowd of people, and as soon as they reached the first gate, those who accompanied them drew up in two files, one on each side; for to enter it crowded together was reckoned a lack of respect to His Majesty. After passing through three courts and some halls to the last antechamber leading to the audience hall, they were there courteously received by a number of lords who kept guard, and were obliged to remove their shoes and to cover their showy garments with coarse robes. When they entered the audience hall, the king took a few steps toward Cortés, and taking him by the hand, and turning an affectionate glance to the others, had them all sit down. The conversation

(a) The learned and judicious Father Acosta, speaking of this first conference of Moctezuma, in bk. VII, ch. 25 of his History, says thus: “Many are of the opinion that, given the state of things on that first day, it would have been easy for the Spaniards to do with the king and with the whole kingdom whatever they wished, and to communicate to them the law of Jesus Christ with great peace and the contentment of all; but the judgments of God are profound, and many were the sins of both parties; whence it came about otherwise, although in the end the Lord accomplished His design of showing mercy to that nation, after having judged and punished those who in His sight deserved it.” [p. 84] was long, and on diverse subjects. The king put several questions, as Bk. IX.

> Ehs, IX mande, tanto sul governo politico, quanto sulle cose natutali di Spagna, è Cortès dopo' avergli in tutto soddisfatto s' introdusse scaltramente in materie di Religione. Gli espose

much on the political government as on the natural things of Spain, and Cortés, after having satisfied him in everything, cunningly entered upon matters of religion. He set forth to him the unity of God, the Incarnation of the divine Word, the creation of the world, the severity of God’s judgment, the glory with which He rewards the just, and the eternal pains to which He condemns sinners. Then he spoke of the rites of Christianity, and in particular of the bloodless sacrifice of the Mass, in order to compare it with the inhuman sacrifices of the

> Punità di Dio, l'Incarnazione del Verbo divino, la creazione del Mondo, li severità del giudizio \di Dio, la gloria, ton cui premia i giusti, e le pene eterne, a cui condanna i peccatori . Indi ragionò de’ riti del Cristianesimo, e particolarmente dell'incruento sacrifizio della Mesla per farne il paragone cogl’ inumani sacrifizi de' Messicani, declamando fortemente contra la barbara crudeltà d' immolar vittime umane, e di cibarsì della loro carne . Motezuma rispose ,' che intorno alla creazion del Mondo erano d'’ accordo ; poichè quello stesso, che avea detto Cortès, l'’ aveano già inteso da' loro maggiori : che del resto s' era più informato da' suoi

Mexicans, declaiming strongly against the barbarous cruelty of immolating human victims and of feeding on their flesh. Moctezuma answered that on the creation of the world they were in agreement, since the very thing that Cortés had said they had already heard from their elders; that for the rest he had already been informed by his ambassadors of the religion of the Spaniards. “For my part,” he added, “I do not doubt the goodness of the God whom you worship; but if He is good for Spain, our gods are likewise good for Mexico, as the experience of so many centuries has shown us. Spare yourselves, therefore, the trouble of wishing to induce me to abandon their worship. As for the sacrifices, I do not know why it should be blamed to sacrifice to the gods those men who, whether by their own crimes or by their fortune in war, are already destined to death.” But although Cortés did not succeed in persuading him of the truth of the Christian religion, he obtained at least, so they say, that human flesh should no longer be served at the royal table; either because by Cortés’s arguments the natural loathing for such food was awakened in his mind, or else because he wished at least in this to please the Spaniards. He also made his royal beneficence toward them conspicuous on this occasion, giving to Cortés and to the four captains several works of gold and ten bales of very fine cotton garments, and to each soldier a necklace of gold.
