IX, sa, e risolvette di conciltrarli gli animi della Nobilrà con una buona condotta, e con maniere offequiole , ed amorevoli ed ordinò alla sua gente, che in tal maniera fi regolafse, che non potessero lagnarsi di loro i Messicani; ma mentre che pareva badare colla maggior diligenza alla pace, rivolgeva nella sua mente de’ penfieri arditi e temerarj, alla pace aftatto contrarj, ed efsendogli d'uopo par marurarli l' înformarli prima co' suoi occhj delle fortificazioni di Messico, e delle forze de' Messicani, addimandò al Re il permetffo di vedere i palazzi Reali, il tempio maggiore, e la piazza del mercato . Accordollo benigoamente il Re, come quegli che nulla sospettava dello scaltro Generale, nè previde le conseguenze della sua troppa indulgenza, Videro pure gli Spagnuoli tutto ciò che vollero, trovando da per tutto abbondante materia d'ammirazione .

Cortés having returned to his quarters (so we shall henceforth call the palace of King Axayacatl, where were lodged [p. 85] the Spaniards) he began to reflect on the danger in which he found himself in the center of a city so strong and populous, and resolved to Bk. IX. win the minds of the nobility by good conduct and by courteous and affectionate manners, and ordered his men to behave in such a way that the Mexicans could have no complaint of them; but while he seemed to attend with the greatest diligence to peace, he was turning over in his mind bold and rash designs, entirely contrary to peace, and, since to ripen them it was necessary for him first to inform himself with his own eyes about the fortifications of Mexico and the forces of the Mexicans, he asked the king’s leave to see the royal palaces, the great temple, and the market square. The king kindly granted it, as one who suspected nothing of the cunning general, nor foresaw the consequences of his excessive indulgence. The Spaniards also saw everything they wished, finding everywhere abundant matter for admiration.

(b) Dr. Robertson puts in place of the causeway of Tepeyacac that of Texcoco, which, in the place where he describes Mexico, he situates toward the northwest, and where he speaks of the posts of the Spanish army in the siege of that capital, toward the east, having already said that toward the east there was no causeway on the lake; but there was not, nor could there ever be, any causeway on the lake from Mexico to Texcoco, because of the very great depth of its bed in that part, and had there been one, it would not be of three miles only, as this author affirms, but of fifteen, which is the extent of the lake between. A queste quattro parti nelle quali fu divisa quella Città infino dalla sua fondazione s'aggiuns2, come una quinta parte, la Città di Tlatelolco firuata a Maestro , restando dopo la conquista del Re Axajacatl unita a quella di Tenochtitlan, e compolta di tutte due quella di Mellico .

Chapultepec. The circuit of the city, not including the suburbs, was more than nine miles, and the number of houses at least sixty thousand. (c) The city was divided into four quarters, and each quarter into several wards, the Mexican names of which are still preserved among the Indians. The dividing lines of the four quarters were the four broad streets corresponding to the four gates of the court of the great temple. The first quarter, called Tecpan (today San Pablo), comprised all that part which lay between the two streets corresponding to the south and east gates. The second, Mojotla (today San Juan), between the south and west streets. The third, Tlaquechiuhcan (today

Atzacualco (today San Sebastián), between the north and east streets.

To these four parts, into which that city was divided from its very foundation, there was added, as a fifth part, the city of Tlatelolco, situated to the northwest, which after the conquest of King Axayacatl remained united to that of Tenochtitlan, and the two together made up that of Mexico.

There

(c) Torquemada affirms that the population of the capital was 120,000 houses; but

the Anonymous Conqueror, Gómara, Herrera, and other historians agree on the number of 60,000 houses, not of 60,000 inhabitants, as Robertson says; since there was no ancient author who estimated it so small. It is true that in the Italian translation of the account of the Anonymous Conqueror one reads sixty thousand inhabitants; but this was without doubt a mistake of the translator, who, having perhaps found in the original sesenta mil vecinos, translated 60,000 inhabitants, when he should have said 60,000 hearths; for otherwise it would have to be said that Cholula, Xochimilco,

Iztapalapa, and other such cities were larger than that of Mexico. But in the aforesaid number the houses of the suburbs are not included. We know from the testimony of Herrera and of Bernal Díaz that toward the west the houses continued on one side and the other of the causeway of Tlacopan all the way to the mainland, that is, for a space of 2 miles. Toward the southwest there was the suburb of Aztacalco, toward the south those of Acatlan, Malcuitlapilco, Atenco, and Iztacalco, and toward the northwest Zancopinca, Huitznahuac, Xocotitlan, Coltonco, and others. It is to be believed that Torquemada meant to count the houses of the suburbs as well; but for all that the number of 120,000 houses seems to me excessive.

> 1 Verano attorno alla Città molti argioi, e chiuse per =—trattener: l’acque, quando era d'uopo, e dentro d' essa tanti L' » IX. canali , che appena v'era contrada , dove non fi potesse andar “in batta: ciò “che non meno conrribuiva ad abbellir la Città , ed-a render più agevole il trasporto delle vettovaglie, e di- tutte l'altre derrate del loro commercio, che-ad assicurar vieppiù i Cirradini contro a' tentativi de' loro nemici Le strade principali erano larghe e dritte. Quanto all’ altre alcune erano meri canali, dove non fi poreva andar altrimenti che in barche ,altre erano felciate,-e senza verun' acua, ed altre aveano un canaletto tra due terrapieni, i quali farvi alla comodità de' viandanti, ed allo scarico delle barche, o pur erano giardinetti, con alberi piantativi, e fiori.

There were around the city many dikes and sluices to hold back the waters when need required, and within it so many canals that there Bk. IX. was hardly a ward where one could not go by boat: which contributed no less to the beautifying of the city, and to making easier the transport of provisions and of all the other goods of their trade, than to making the citizens still more secure against the attempts of their enemies. The principal streets were wide and straight. As to the others, some were mere canals, where one could not go otherwise than in boats, others were paved and without any water, and others had a little canal between two embankments, which served for the convenience of passersby and for the unloading of the boats, or else were little gardens, with trees planted in them, and flowers.

As for the buildings, besides the many temples and the magnificent royal palaces of which we have spoken elsewhere, there were also other palaces or large houses which the feudatory lords had built for their dwelling at the time when they were obliged to reside at court. On top of all the houses, except those of the poor, there were flat roofs with their parapets, and on some even battlements and towers, though much smaller than those of the temples: so that the Mexicans provided for their defense no less in the streets and in the houses than in the temples.

Besides the great and renowned square of Tlatelolco, where the principal market was held, there were other small squares distributed throughout the city, where ordinary provisions were sold. There were also in several places fountains and fishponds, especially near the temples, and many gardens, partly planted at ground level and partly on high flat roofs.

The many large buildings, neatly whitewashed and polished, the high towers of the temples scattered through the quarters of the city, the canals, the avenues of trees, and the gardens formed a whole so beautiful that the Spaniards never seemed to tire of looking at it, especially when they viewed it from the upper court of the great temple, which overlooked not only the habitations of that court but also the lakes, and the fine and large

[p. 88] cities that were round about. They were no less amazed at the sight

Bk. IX.

of the royal palaces, and of the surprising variety of plants and animals that were kept there; but nothing else filled their minds with greater astonishment than the great market square. There was not a

Spaniard who did not celebrate it with singular praises, and some of them, who had traveled through almost all of Europe, declared, as

Bernal Díaz attests, that they had never seen in any square in the world either so great a number of merchants, or so great a variety of merchandise, or so fine an order and arrangement in everything.

§ 4.    When the Spaniards went up on the great temple, they found the Outbursts of Cortés’s

zeal for religion.

king there, who had gone there beforehand in order to prevent by his presence any attempt that might be made against his gods. After having observed the city from that height, at the urging of the king himself, Cortés asked his permission to see the sanctuaries, and he granted it after consulting the priests. The Spaniards entered them, and contemplated, not without compassion and loathing, the blindness of those peoples, and the horrible slaughter that the cruel superstition of their sacrifices wrought among them. Cortés then, turning to the king, said to him: “I wonder, my lord, that a monarch as wise as you are should worship as gods these abominable figures of the Devil.”

“Had I known,” replied the king, “that you were to speak with such contempt of our gods, I should never have yielded to your requests.”

Cortés, seeing him so indignant, asked his pardon, and took leave to return to the quarters. “Go in peace,” said the king, “for I shall remain here to appease the anger of our gods, provoked by your blasphemies.”

> Malgrado questo disgusto ottenne Cortés dal Re non solamente il permesso di fabbricare dentro” il reciato del quartiere una cappella ad onor del vero Dio, ma ancor gli operaj ed i materiali per la fabbrica , nella quale fi celebrò la Santa Mesla, finché vi fu del vino, e giornalmente vi con[p. 89] 89 tevano È Soldati a far le loro divozioni. Voleva inoltre consacrare al culto del vero Dio lo steffo santuario d' Huitzilopochili, ed allora fo trattenuto dal rispetto del Re e de’ Sacerdoti ; ma l' eseguì alcuni mesi dopo , eflendosi acquistara, una, maggior autorità coll’ imprigionamento del Re, e con altre azioni non méno temerarie , che oramai vedremo. Spezzò gl’ Idali, che vi fi veneravano, fece ripulire ed acconciare il santuario, vi collocò ‘un. crocifillo , ed una immagine della Madre di Dia, (4) e meslo inginocchione innanzi a queste sacre, immagini ringraziò l' Altissimo d' aver loro accordato di adorarlo in quel luogo già per tanto tempo destinato alla più abominevole , e crudele idolatrìa. Que- Îto medesimo zelo per la Religione l' indufle a replicar spesso al Re i suoi ragionamenti sulle sfantissime verità del Cristianelimo; ma quantunque Motezuma non fofle disposto ad abbracciarle , nondimeno mofso dalle ragioni di lui comandò , che d'allora innanzi“non fi facrificaflero più vittime “umane; e benchè non compiacesse al Generale Spagnuolo nel rinunziar alla idolatria, lo carezzava ognora, e non v' era piorno, nel quale non facefle nuove finezze e regali agli Spagnruoli, L'ordine, che diede il Re a' Sacerdoti intorno a' sacrifizj non fu costantemente cslervato ; e quella grand' armo» na, che v'era stara fin’ allora , fi turbò per l’inaudito atten» raro del Generale Spagnuolo,

Despite this displeasure, Cortés obtained from the king not only permission to build within the enclosure of the quarters a chapel to the honor of the true God, but also the workmen and the materials for the building, in which Holy Mass was celebrated as long as there was wine, and daily there gathered [p. 89] the soldiers to perform their devotions. He also planted in the principal court a great cross, so that the Mexicans might see the supreme Bk. IX. veneration in which that holy instrument of our redemption was held among the Spaniards. He wished, moreover, to consecrate to the worship of the true God the very sanctuary of Huitzilopochtli, and was then restrained by respect for the king and the priests; but he carried it out some months afterward, having acquired greater authority through the imprisonment of the king and other actions no less rash, as we shall presently see. He smashed the idols that were venerated there, had the sanctuary cleaned and repaired, placed in it a crucifix and an image of the Mother of God, (d) and, kneeling before these sacred images, thanked the Most High for having granted them to adore Him in that place, so long devoted to the most abominable and cruel idolatry. This same zeal for religion led him to repeat frequently to the king his discourses on the holiest truths of Christianity; but although Moctezuma was not disposed to embrace them, nevertheless, moved by his arguments, he commanded that from then on human victims should no longer be sacrificed; and although he did not comply with the Spanish general in renouncing idolatry, he was ever affectionate toward him, and there was no day on which he did not show the Spaniards new kindnesses and gifts. The order which the king gave to the priests concerning the sacrifices was not constantly observed; and the great harmony that had existed until then was disturbed by the unheard-of attempt of the Spanish general.

(d) The image of the Mother of God which Cortés placed in the sanctuary of Huitzilopochtli is believed to be the very same one that is now venerated under the title of Our Lady of los Remedios, or of Succor, in a magnificent temple about eight miles distant from the capital toward the west. It is said that a soldier of Cortés named Villafuerte brought it with him to Mexico, and that on the day after that terrible night in which the Spaniards were defeated he hid it in the place where some years later it was found, that is, in that very place where it is now venerated. (e) That Cortés’s aim was to seize Moctezuma by whatever means, and that the

uprisings at Veracruz were nothing but a mere pretext for putting his design into effect, is evident from his letter to Charles V of October 30, 1520. “Six days having passed, most invincible Prince” (he says in ch. 23 of this letter, or account), “since I entered the great city of Temistitan (he should have said: Tenochtitlan), and having seen some things of it, though few, in comparison with what there is to see and note:

from those, and even from what I had seen of the land, it seemed to me that it was fitting for the royal service, and for our security, that that lord (Moctezuma) should be in my power, and not in complete freedom; lest he should change the purpose which he showed of serving Your Highness, the more so as we Spaniards are somewhat intolerable and importunate, and because, if angered, he could do us much harm, so much that no memory of us would remain, given his great power; and also because, having him with me, all the other lands that were subject to him would more readily come to the knowledge and service of Your Majesty, as afterward happened.” Still more plainly he reveals it in ch. 2 of the same letter, citing another written by him to the same king from Veracruz: “I assured Your Highness,” he says, “that

I would have him (Moctezuma) either captured, or dead, or subject to the Royal

They answered that the Mexican commoners were at that time entertained in the public rejoicings which the king had ordered to celebrate the arrival of such noble strangers; but that among the nobility they noticed a certain suspicious demeanor, and that among other things they had heard them say that it would be easy to remove the bridges from the canals, which seemed to indicate some secret conspiracy against the Spaniards.

> Non potà Corrès dormire quella notte per l'inquietudine , e pasflolla. tutta girando pensieroso pel quartiere , Una sentinella gli fece sapere allora , che in una stanza v' era un uscia dì fresco murato. Cortés could not sleep that night for anxiety, and spent it all walking about the quarters, lost in thought. A sentry then informed him that in one room there was a door that had been freshly walled up. Cortés had it opened, and on entering found many rooms in which was deposited the treasure of the late King Axayacatl. He saw there many idols, a great quantity of works of silver, gold, gems, feathers, and cotton, and several other things, which the tributary provinces paid to the Crown, or the feudatory lords presented to their sovereign. After observing with amazement so great a wealth, Cortés had the door walled up again, leaving everything then as it was before.

The next morning he assembled his captains, and represented to them the hostilities committed by the lord of Nauhtlan against the garrison of Veracruz and against the Totonacs, their allies, which, according to what the allies themselves said, would not have been committed without the order or permission of the King of Mexico. He set forth with the greatest energy the most grave peril in which they found themselves, and declared to them his design, exaggerating the advantages that were to be expected from its execution, and minimizing the evils that might result from it. Their sentiments were various. Some rejected the general’s counsel as rash and impracticable; and said that it would be better to ask the king’s permission to withdraw from the court; since he who with so much eagerness, and with such great gifts, had sought to dissuade them from the resolution of going to Mexico would readily

> La matrina seguente ragund i! suoi Capitani, rappresentò loro le cstilivà Eatò dal Signor di Nauhtlan contro il prefidio della Veracroce, e contra i Totonachi loro alleati , le quali secondo che dicevano gli stessi Allsari, non fi sarebbono fatte senza l’ordine, o il permesso del/Re di Meslico. Espose co!la maggior energ\ìa il gravissimo” pericolo, in cui si trovavano, e dichiarò loro il suo disegno , esagerando i vantaggi, che doveansi aspettare dalla esecuzione’, e diminuendo i mali, che potrebbono cagionarli . I lot fentimenti furono varj . Alcunt rigettavano il consiglio del Generale, come temerario ed impraticabile; e dicevano, che sarebbe meglio il domandar permefso al Re di ritirarsi dalla Corte; poichè chi con tanta premura, e con sì pran presenti avea cercate di distornargli dalla risoluzione di portarsi a “2° "ah [p. 92] facilmente accorderebbe loro la partenza. Altri stimavano Lis. M2 [p. 92] grant them leave to depart. Others thought departure indeed necesBk. IX. sary, but believed that it should be done secretly, so as not to give the

Mexicans occasion for some treachery; but the greater part of them, drawn beforehand by the general himself to his side, as is to be believed, consented to his counsel, rejecting the others as ignominious and more perilous. “What will be said of us,” they said, “seeing us leave at once a court where we have been loaded with honors? Who will not be persuaded that it is fear that drives us out? And if once we lose our reputation for courage, what security can we promise ourselves either in those places of the Mexicans through which we shall necessarily have to pass, or among our allies, who will no longer be restrained by respect for our arms?” The resolution was finally taken to seize Moctezuma in his palace and take him prisoner to their quarters: a resolution barbarous and extravagant to excess, suggested by fear for their fate and by experience of their own good fortune, which more than anything else encourages men to advance to the most arduous enterprises, and often sends them headlong.

For the execution of so perilous an attempt Cortés put all his troops under arms and distributed them in the suitable places. He commanded five of his captains and twenty-five soldiers, in whom he most trusted, to proceed to the palace two by two, but in such a manner that all should arrive at the same time, as if by chance; and he went there with Doña Marina as interpreter, having first obtained the king’s consent for that hour at which he was accustomed to visit him.

He was introduced with the other Spaniards into the audience hall, where the king, very far from foreseeing what was to happen to him, received them with his usual affability. He had them sit down, gave them some gifts of gold, and moreover presented to Cortés one of his daughters. Cortés, after expressing to him his gratitude in the briefest terms, excused himself from accepting her, alleging that he was married in Cuba, and that according to the law [p. 93] of God among the Christians he was not permitted to have two wives; but in the end he admitted her into his company, so as not to Bk. IX. displease the king, and to have an opportunity of making her a Christian, as indeed he obtained. To the other captains the king likewise gave some daughters of Mexican lords from among those that he had in his seraglio. They then conversed for some time on various subjects; but Cortés, seeing that these discourses distracted him from his purpose, said to the king that that visit was directed to informing him of the conduct of the lord of Nauhtlan, his vassal: he complained of the hostilities committed by that lord against the Totonacs on account of their friendship with the Spaniards, of the war made on the Spaniards of Veracruz, and of the death of the governor Escalante and of six soldiers of that garrison. “I must,” he added, “give an account to my sovereign of the death of these Spaniards, and in order to be able to give him a suitable satisfaction, I have made inquiry into so irregular a conduct. All blame you as the principal author of such uprisings; but I am far from imagining such perfidy in so great a monarch as that of persecuting us as an enemy in that province at the same time that he loads us with favors at court.” “I do not doubt,” replied the king, “that those who blame me for the war of Nauhtlan are the Tlaxcalans, my sworn enemies; but I assure you that I had no influence in it. Cuauhpopoca ventured to make it without my order, indeed against my own will: and so that you may be assured of the truth, I shall have him come at once to the court, and shall deliver him into your hands.” He called at once two of his courtiers, and, handing over to them a certain gem in which was carved the image of the god of war, which he wore always hanging from his arm, and which served as a seal for the mark of his commands, ordered them to set out with the greatest possible speed toward Nauhtlan, and then to bring to the court Cuauhpopoca and the other principal persons who had taken part in the death of the Spaniards, and gave them authority to raise troops, and

The two courtiers set out at once to carry out their commission, and the king said to Cortés: “What more can I do to assure you of my sincerity?” “I do not doubt it,” replied Cortés; “but to dispel the error into which even your own vassals have fallen, that the outrage of

Nauhtlan was carried out by your order, an extraordinary demonstration is required, which shall make manifest your benevolence toward us; and no other seems to me more fitting to this end than that of deigning to come and live with us until the culprits are brought, and by their confession your innocence is made manifest. This will serve to satisfy my sovereign, to justify your conduct, and to honor us, and to put us under cover in the shadow of Your Majesty.” In spite of the artful words with which Cortés tried to gloss over his bold and injurious pretension, the king perceived it at once, and was disturbed.

“Where has it ever been seen,” he said, “that kings let themselves be led off prisoners? And even though I were willing to degrade my person and my dignity in such a manner, would not all my vassals at once take up arms to deliver me? I am not a man who could hide or flee to the mountains. Without submitting to such an infamy, I am here still ready to satisfy your complaints.” “The house, my lord,” said Cortés then, “to which we invite you is one of your own palaces: nor will it be a wonder to your subjects, accustomed already to seeing you frequently change your abode, to see you now come to dwell in the palace of your late father Axayacatl under the pretext of showing us your benevolence. And if your subjects should dare to do anything against you or against us, we have courage enough, strong arms, and good weapons to repress their rashness. For the rest, I pledge you my word that you will be as much honored by us, and as well served, as by your own subjects.” The king persevered in his reluctance, and

Cortés in his urgings, until one of the Spanish captains, too bold and inconsiderate, [p. 95] taking it ill that the execution of their design was being delayed, said

> Io non dubito, che i Leggitori sentiranno nel leggere, e nel considerare le circostanze di questo straordinario avve» nimento quel medesimo dispiacere , ch' io sento nello scriverlo; ma è d'uopo non meno in questo, che in altri avvenimenti di questa storia levar la mente al Cielo, e riverire col più profondo rispetto gl' altissimi configlj della Divina Provvidenza, la quale prefe gli Spagnuoli per istromenti del, la sua giustizia, e della sua misericordia , castigando in alcuni la superstizione e la crudelcà, ed illuminando gli altri col- Ia luce del Vangelo. Bk. IX. angrily that they should drop the talk and resolve to drag him off by force, or kill him. The king, who in the Spaniard’s countenance perceived his purpose, asked Doña Marina what that furious stranger was saying. “My lord,” she replied discreetly, “as your subject I desire your welfare, and as the confidante of these men I know their secrets and know their temper. If you deign to do what they require, you will be treated by them with all that honor and distinction which is due to your royal person; but if you persist in your refusal your life is in danger.” That unhappy king, who ever since he had the first news of the arrival of the Spaniards had been overcome by a superstitious fear, and became more pusillanimous from day to day, seeing himself now in such straits, and persuaded that before his guards could arrive to succor him he might already have perished at the hands of those men so bold and resolute, yielded at last to their entreaties. “I will trust you,” he said, “let us go, then, let us go; since the gods so will it”; and he at once ordered that they should prepare his litter, and got into it to be carried to the quarters of the Spaniards.

I do not doubt that the readers will feel, in reading and in considering the circumstances of this extraordinary event, that same distress which I feel in writing it; but it is needful, no less in this than in other events of this history, to raise the mind to Heaven and to revere with the deepest respect the most high counsels of Divine Providence, which took the Spaniards as instruments of its justice and its mercy, chastising in some the superstition and cruelty, and enlightening others with the light of the Gospel. We shall never cease to inculcate this truth, and to make known even in the most irregular actions of creatures the goodness, wisdom, and omnipotence of the Creator.

Moctezuma finally left his palace, never to return [p. 96] again. He left, protesting to his courtiers that for certain reasons al‐

> Lis. IX,

Bk. IX.

> S. 6. Vita del Re nella prigione.

ready consulted with the gods he was going of his own good will to live for some days with those strangers, commanding them to make it so known throughout the court. He was borne with all that train and magnificence which he was accustomed to display whenever he let himself be seen in public, the Spaniards walking beside him guarding him under color of honoring him. The news of this extraordinary event was at once spread throughout the city, and the people flocked together in crowds: some, moved to tenderness, wept, and others threw themselves on the ground like people in despair. The king tried to calm them, signifying to them the pleasure with which he was going to stay among those friends of his; but fearing some great disturbance, he gave orders to his ministers to drive the rabble from the street, and imposed the penalty of death on anyone who should cause any disquiet. On arriving at the quarters he greeted warmly the

Il Re procurava acchetargli, fignificando loro il piacere, col quale andava a stare tra que' suoi amici; ma temendo qualche grande scompiglio, diede ordine a’ suoi Ministri di scacciar dalla strada la ciur» maglia, -ed impose peva di morte a chiunque cagionasse qualche inquietudine, Giunto al quartiere carezzò gli Spagnuoli, che vennero ad incontrarlo, e prese per la sua abitazione l'appartamento , che più gli piacque, il quale addobbarono prontamente i suoi dimeltici co'più fini tappeti di cotone, e di penne e co' migliori mobili del Real palazzo . Spaniards who came to meet him, and took for his dwelling the apartment which pleased him most, which his servants promptly furnished with the finest hangings of cotton and of feathers and with the best furnishings of the royal palace. Cortés posted a guard at the entrance of that apartment, and doubled those that ordinarily were there for the security of the quarters. He ordered all the Spaniards and allies to treat him and serve him with all that respect that was due to His

Majesty, and permitted Mexicans to enter to visit him, as many as wished, provided they were few at a time: so that nothing of what he had in his palace was lacking to him except liberty.

> Vedendo Cortès la liberalità , o piuttosto prodigaliv® di lui, gli difle un giorno, che alcuni soldati furfanmi aveano tolto dal tesoro del fuo defunto Padre Axajacatl certi pezzi d'oro; ma che gli farebbe subito riporre, dov'erano. ,, Pur- 5» chè non tocchino difle il Re, le immagini degli Dei, nè » ciò che è destinato al loro culto, prendano quanto vo- » gliono. ,, Avutone un tal permesso rraflero quindi gli Spagnuoli più di mille abiti fini di corone, Cortès comandò, che vi si riponeffero ; ma "Motezuma s' oppose dicendo , ch' egli non riprendeva giammai ciò, che una volta avea dato, Fece altresì Cortés “imprigionare alcuni Soldati, perchè aveano pigliato dal medesimo tesoro certa quantità di Îliquidam-

Cortés, on his part, showed such zeal that his men should show him the respect that was due to him, that he had a Spanish soldier flogged because he answered him brusquely, and would have had him hanged, as some historians affirm, if the king himself had not interposed in favor of the culprit. But if he was worthy of such a punishment for having failed, by such an answer, in the respect due to the majesty of that king, what punishment did he deserve who had rashly deprived him of his liberty? Whenever Cortés went in to visit him, he showed him the same reverence, and the same compliments, as he was wont to do when he went to the palace. To divert him in prison he had the soldiers perform the exercise of arms, or even had them play games before him, and the king himself sometimes deigned to play with Cortés and with Captain Alvarado at a game which the Spaniards called the bodoque, and showed pleasure in losing for the sake of having occasion to exercise his liberality. Once he lost after dinner forty pieces of unworked gold, that is, as far as we can conjecture, at least a hundred and sixty ounces. Thus easily do those squander their riches who have acquired them without their own labor.

Questa” Principessa siccome l'altra già presentatagli, furono prontamente india:

Cortés, seeing his liberality, or rather prodigality, said to him one day that some rascally soldiers had taken from the treasure of his late father Axayacatl certain pieces of gold; but that he would have them put back at once where they had been. “Provided,” said the king, “that they do not touch the images of the gods, nor what is destined for their worship, let them take what they wish.” Having this permission, the Spaniards then drew from it more than a thousand fine cotton garments. Cortés commanded that they be put back; but Moctezuma opposed, saying that he never took back what he had once given. Cortés also had some soldiers imprisoned because they had taken from the same treasure a certain quantity of liquidambar; [p. 98] but at the king’s request they were soon set at liberty. Not content

Cortés another daughter of his, whom this general accepted in order to marry her to Cristóbal de Olid, master of the camp of the Spanish troops. This princess, like the other already presented to him, was promptly instructed and baptized without any objection from their father.

Cortés, no longer doubting the king’s good will, which had been made plain no less in the extraordinary demonstrations of liberality than in the pleasure he showed at being among the Spaniards, allowed him after some days of imprisonment to leave the quarters, and urged him to go whenever he wished to amuse himself with hunting, of which he was exceedingly fond. That humbled monarch did not refuse this wretched use of the liberty that was granted him: he went out often, and betook himself now to the temples to perform his devotions, now to the lake to hunt waterfowl, now to the wood of

Chapultepec, or to some other place of recreation, always guarded by a good number of Spanish soldiers. When he went out on the lake, very many boats escorted him, or else two brigantines which Cortés had had built as soon as he entered that court. (*) When he went to some wood, two thousand Tlaxcalans accompanied him, besides the numerous retinue of Mexicans that always attended him for his service; but he never spent the night outside the quarters.

Cortés put the due questions to them, and they frankly confessed the deed without at first accusing the king, until, seeing themselves threatened with torments and believing their execution unavoidable, they declared that all they had done had been commanded them by the king, without whose orders they would never have dared to attempt anything whatever against the Spaniards.

Cortés, having heard their confession, and making a show of not believing their excuse, condemned them to be burned alive before the royal palace as guilty of lese majesty. He went at once to the king’s apartment with three or four of his captains and a soldier who carried irons in his hand, and without omitting even this time the usual ceremonies and compliments, said to the king: “The accused have now been examined, lord, and all have confessed their crime, and they accuse you as the author of the death of my Spaniards. I have condemned them to the punishment they deserve, and which you also deserve, in view of their confession; but having regard, on the other hand, to the great benefits which you have done us until now, and to the affection which you have shown toward my sovereign and toward my nation, I wish to grant you the favor of life; but I cannot avoid making you feel a part of the punishment you deserve for your

went away. So great was the king’s amazement at seeing his person subjected to such an outrage that it left him neither any movement of resistance nor any word to express his grief. He remained for a good while almost senseless. The servants who attended him declared their grief with silent tears, and, throwing themselves at his feet, lightened the weight of the irons with their hands, and took pains to spare him the contact of them by interposing bands of cotton. Having recovered from his stupor, he broke out into some acts of impatience, but promptly regained his calm, ascribing his misfortune to the sovereign ordinance of the gods.

Scarcely had he done this so bold a deed when Cortés passed on to carry out another undertaking no less rash. After giving orders to the guards of the quarters not to permit any Mexican to enter to see the king, he commanded that Cuauhpopoca be led to execution with his son and the other culprits. The same Spaniards led them, armed and drawn up in battle order to hold the people in check in case they should wish to prevent the execution; but what could that little troop have done against the immense multitude of Mexicans who were to be spectators of that great event, had not God, who disposed everything for the execution of his most lofty designs, restrained the effects which the unheard-of attempt of those few men ought to have caused? The fire was kindled before the principal palace of the king.

The wood used for it was a great quantity of bows, arrows, darts, lances, swords, and shields that were in an armory; for Cortés had asked it of the king in order to free himself from the disquiet which the sight of so many weapons caused him. Cuauhpopoca, his feet and hands bound and himself placed on the wood on which he was to be burned, protested anew his innocence, and said again that all he had done had been by the express command of his king; he then made prayers to his gods, [p. 101] and encouraged his companions to suffer death. The fire was lit, and

Cortés’s conduct cannot be justified in any way, since, besides arrogating to himself an authority that did not belong to him, if he truly believed that the king had been the author of the uprisings at Veracruz, why condemn to death, and to so bitter a death, men whose only crime was that of punctually carrying out the orders of their sovereign? If he did not believe the king guilty, why subject him to so great an ignominy, setting at naught the respect due to his character, the gratitude that was fitting toward his beneficence, and the immunity that was owed to his innocence? I conjecture that Cuauhpopoca had received from the king the precise order to bring the Totonacs back under obedience to that crown; and, unable to carry out such an order without becoming entangled with the Spaniards, who protected the rebels, he carried things to the extremes that we have seen.

As soon as the culprits had been executed, Cortés went to Moctezuma’s apartment, and greeting him affectionately, and boasting of the favor he did him in granting him his life, had the irons removed. The joy that Moctezuma then felt was proportioned to the vexation which the ignominy

had

(f) Solís, where he mentions Cortés’s sentence against Cuauhpopoca, says thus: “The case was tried by military procedure, and sentence of death was passed on them, with the provision that their bodies should be burned publicly.” In which, without stating the kind of punishment to which they were condemned, he gives it to be understood that the culprits were not burned, but only their corpses: which does not befit the truthfulness that is required of a historian. He took pains to dissemble what did not accord with the panegyric of his hero; but his dissembling avails little, since not only the other historians but Cortés himself candidly affirms it in his letter to Charles V. See especially the chronicler Herrera in his Decades, Dec. 2, bk. 8, ch. 9. [p. 102] had caused him. His fear of losing his life vanished entirely, and he re‐

Bk. IX.

ceived his liberty as an incomparable benefit. To such a degree had the spirit of that king been debased! He embraced Cortés with the utmost affection, expressed his gratitude to him with singular demonstrations, and that day showed extraordinary kindnesses to the

Spaniards and to his own vassals. Cortés withdrew the guards who were there, and told the king that whenever he wished he might return to his palace, well assured that the king would not do so; for he had often heard from him that it did not suit him to return to his palace while the Spaniards were at the court. Indeed he would not leave the quarters, protesting the danger which the Spaniards would run if he abandoned them; but it may be believed that his own danger also deterred him from resuming his liberty, since he was not unaware how ill his vassals took the abasement of his spirit and his excessive compliance toward the Spaniards.

It is very probable that the execution of Cuauhpopoca caused

§ 8. some ferment among the nobility; for within a few days Cacamatzin, Attempts of the King king of Acolhuacan, no longer able to bear the authority which the of Acolhuacan against

the Spaniards. Spaniards were acquiring at the court of Mexico, and ashamed to see

King Moctezuma, his uncle, so wretched, sent word to him that he should remember he was a lord, and not wish to make himself a slave to those strangers; but seeing that Moctezuma refused to yield to his counsel, he resolved to make war on the Spaniards himself. Their ruin would have been inevitable if the esteem in which Cacamatzin was held among the Mexicans and the Texcocans had been equal to his intrepidity and resolution; but the Mexicans suspected that under color of zeal for the honor of his uncle he concealed some subtle ambition, and the design of usurping the crown of Mexico. Among the

Texcocans, his subjects, he was not much liked, on account of his pride and the harm he had done to his brother Prince Cuicuitzcatzin, who, to escape persecution, had taken refuge in Mexico, and was better liked for his agreeable and popular character.

[p. 103]

Cacamatzin therefore betook himself to Texcoco, and having convened his councilors and the most distinguished persons of his court, Bk. IX. laid before them the lamentable state in which the court of Mexico found itself through the excessive daring of the Spaniards and the pusillanimity of the king his uncle; the authority which those few strangers were arrogating to themselves; the most grievous insults they had done to the person of the king by imprisoning him as if he were a vile slave, and even to the gods themselves, by introducing into that kingdom the worship of other, foreign deities: he exaggerated the evils that might result from such beginnings against the court and against the kingdom of Acolhuacan. “It is time now,” he said, “to fight for our religion, for our country, for our liberty, and for our honor, before the power of these men increases, whether through new reinforcements come from their own country, or through new alliances contracted in ours.” Finally he bade them declare their opinion freely. The councilors for the most part declared for the party of war, either to please the king or because in fact they were of the same mind; but certain elders of great authority told the king frankly that he should not let himself be carried away so easily by youthful ardor; that before taking any resolution he should consider that the Spaniards were warlike and resolute men, and fought with far superior arms; that he should bear in mind not so much his kinship with Moctezuma as that king’s alliance and friendship with the Spaniards; for such a friendship, of which there were certain and clear proofs, would make him sacrifice to the ambition of those strangers all the interests of blood and of country.

In spite of these representations war was resolved on, and preparations were immediately begun with the greatest secrecy; not with so much, however, that the news did not reach both Moctezuma and Cortés. This general fell into a most grave disquiet, but considering, on the other hand, that all rash undertakings succeeded for him, he resolved to forestall the blow by marching with his troops to make an

informing him of the forces of that court, and of the immense multitude of its inhabitants. Cortés therefore determined to send an embassy to that king, reminding him of the friendship contracted already at Ayotzinco, when he went there to meet him in the name of the king his uncle, and bidding him consider that as easy as it is to undertake a war, so difficult is it to come out of it: that it would be more to his advantage to maintain good relations with the King of

Castile and with the Spanish nation. Cacamatzin replied that he could not regard as friends those who took his honor from him, who oppressed his country, who outraged his blood, and who despised his religion: that he neither knew who the King of Castile was, nor cared to know: that if they wished to avoid the blow that was about to fall upon their heads, they should depart at once from Mexico and return to their own country.

In spite of so harsh an answer, Cortés repeated the embassy; but having been answered in the same tone, he complained to

Moctezuma, and in order to engage him in that affair he pretended to suspect that he had some influence in the hostile designs of his nephew. Moctezuma cleared himself of the suspicion with the most sincere protestations, and offered to interpose his authority. He sent word therefore to Cacamatzin to come to Mexico to visit him: that he would find a way to settle those differences. Cacamatzin, indignant to see Moctezuma more committed to the cause of those who were oppressing his liberty than to that of the one who was exerting himself to restore it to him, replied that if after so much infamy any sentiment of honor had remained in him, he would be ashamed to see himself made a slave by four rascals, who while they lured him with fair words outraged him by their deeds: that since neither zeal for the

Mexican religion and for the Acolhua gods, despised by those strangers, nor the glory of his ancestors, obscured and debased by his cowardice, was enough to move him, he wished to give aid to the religion, avenge [p. 105] the gods, preserve the kingdom, and recover his honor and liberty and those of the whole nation: that therefore he would in fact come, Bk. IX. as Moctezuma begged him, to Mexico, not with folded arms, but with sword in hand, to wipe out with the blood of the Spaniards the disgrace of the Mexicans.

King Moctezuma was dismayed at such an answer, fearing to be

II. 4 nar} [p. 106] === nar} avvenimenti della nostra Storia , sono troppo facili e Lis. IX. triviali per doverci trattenere nel corso della narrazione,

Prince therefore secretly gave orders to certain Mexican officers who served Cuicuitzcatzin. in the guard of the king his nephew to endeavor with all diligence and without delay to seize his royal person and bring him with the greatest caution to Mexico; because this was very important to the public good of the kingdom. He suggested to them the manner of doing it, and perhaps also gave them some gift and promised them some reward to encourage them to the undertaking. These then solicited other officers or servants of King Cacamatzin whom they found more disposed to that plot, and with their help obtained all that Moctezuma wished. Among his other palaces the King of Acolhuacan had built one on the shore of the lake in such a way that boats could enter and leave by a canal that ran beneath it. Here, where King Cacamatzin was then residing, they arranged a good number of boats with armed men, and in the darkness of night, with which the greatest crimes are covered, fell suddenly upon the king, and before any men could come to defend him, put him in a boat and with the greatest speed carried him to Mexico. Moctezuma, without any regard for his character as a sovereign or for his kinship with Cacamatzin, at once handed him over to Cortés. This general, who, as appears from his conduct, had no idea of that respect which is owed to royal majesty even in the person of a barbarian, put him in irons and shut him up under the custody of a strong guard. The reflections to be made on this, as on other extraordinary [p. 106] events of our History are too easy and trivial for us to dwell on in the Bk. IX. course of the narrative.

Cacamatzin, who had begun his unfortunate reign with the dissensions with his brother Ixtlilxochitl, and with the dismemberment of the state, ended it with the loss of his crown, of his liberty, and of his life. Moctezuma, with Cortés’s consent, determined that the crown of Acolhuacan should be given to Prince Cuicuitzcatzin, who had been kept by Moctezuma in his palace, since, to escape the persecutions of his brother Cacamatzin, (g) he had taken refuge in Mexico and placed himself under his protection. In this election wrong was done to the princes Coanacochtzin and Ixtlilxochitl, who, being born of Queen Xocotzin, had a greater right to the crown. The motive which the King of Mexico had for rejecting Coanacochtzin cannot be known, since as regards Ixtlilxochitl it appears that he did not wish to increase the power of so terrible an enemy. However that may be,

Moctezuma, who had not the heart to contradict him, summoned the principal nobility of the court and of the neighboring cities. They all came promptly to receive his orders, and when they had assembled in a great hall of the quarters, with Cortés and some other Spaniards present, the king made them a long speech, in which he declared the love which he bore them as a father, from whom they need not fear that he would propose to them anything that was not just and advantageous. But if Moctezuma’s act was a mere artifice, and he did not intend to carry out what he promised, why, in calling himself the vassal of another monarch, did he feel so much grief that his voice failed him and tears were drawn from him, as the same author says? If he thought of nothing else than getting rid of the Spaniards, there was no need of such a feint.

How many times could he, with a single nod to his vassals, if he had wished, either have sacrificed all the Spaniards to his gods, or else, leaving them their lives, have had them conducted bound to the port, so that from there they might retake the road to Cuba? The whole conduct of Moctezuma was altogether opposed to the intentions which Solís supposes in him; but nothing gives the lie to his accusation so much as the clear testimony given by the court of Spain, which in several rescripts issued in favor of the royal descendants of

Moctezuma, granting them exemptions and extraordinary privileges, declares that such privileges cannot serve as an example to any other house; because no other, it adds, has done

Spain so great a service as that which the Emperor Moctezuma did her in incorporating into that crown, by his voluntary cession, a kingdom as rich and as great as that of Mexico. If the obedience given by Moctezuma to the Catholic King had been such as Solís represents it to us, it would be said that the court of Spain believed the kingdom of Mexico incorporated into the Crown of Castile by means of a feigned and deceitful cession, and of a mere artifice of Moctezuma: which would be a most grave wrong to the Christian rectitude of the

Catholic Kings. Vetancurt, in pt. 2, treatise 1 of his Teatro mexicano, cites the aforesaid rescripts, the originals of which are without doubt in the archive of the Counts of Moctezuma and of Tula. [p. 109] that it cut short his speech and made him substitute tears for words.

Bk. IX. The King’s weeping was followed by such bitter sobs from the whole assembly that they moved the Spaniards to tenderness and pity. The sobs were then succeeded by a melancholy silence, which was broken by one of the most authoritative Mexican lords with these words: “Since, lord,” he said to the king, “the time has come when the ancient oracles are to be fulfilled, and the gods will, and you command us, that we be subjects of another lord, what have we to do but submit to the sovereign dispositions of Heaven, made known to us through your mouth?”

Cortés then thanked the king, and all the lords who were present, for their prompt and sincere submission, and protested that his sovereign did not claim to take the crown from the King of Mexico, but only to have his high dominion over that kingdom acknowledged; that Moctezuma would not only continue to command his subjects, but would even exercise the same authority over all those peoples who should submit to the Spaniards. The assembly being dismissed, Cortés had a public instrument made of that act, with all the solemnities that seemed to him necessary, in order to send it to the court of Spain.

Having thus happily taken this step, he represented to Moctezuma § 11. that since he had already acknowledged the dominion of the King of First       homage of the

Mexicans to the Castile over those countries, it was necessary to show his subordina‐ crown of Castile. tion by some contribution of gold and silver, alleging for this the right which sovereigns had to exact such homage from their vassals in order to maintain the splendor of the crown, to support their ministers, for the expenses of war, and for the other needs of the state. Moctezuma with royal magnificence gave him the treasure of his father Axayacatl, which was kept, as we have already said, in that same palace, from which Cortés had taken nothing until then, although he had been expressly permitted by the king to take from it whatever he wished. All this treasure came into the hands of the Spaniards together with

Disquiet of the Mexican nobility, and a cost, of so many riches, and at having subjected to their sovereign, new fears of without any toil, so great and opulent a kingdom; but their felicity

Moctezuma.

was now excessive, and it was necessary, according to the condition of human affairs, that prosperous events should alternate with adverse.

The Mexican nobility, who until then had kept a respectful silence out of their supreme deference to the will of their lord, seeing him now in such abasement, the King of Acolhuacan and other distinguished persons put in irons, and the nation subjected to the dominion of a foreign monarch whom they did not know, began first to whisper, and then to speak with greater freedom, to blame their own toleration, to hold assemblies, and even, as was said, to raise troops to free their king and their nation from that ignominious oppression.

Some of his favorites spoke to Moctezuma, representing to him the grief which his vassals felt at his misfortune, considering his power diminished and the splendor of his dignity dimmed, and the ferment which was now beginning to be felt no less among the nobility than among the common people, impatient at seeing themselves subjected to a foreign king and condemned to sacrifice to him the fruit of their labors. They exhorted him to shake off the fear that had taken possession of him, and to recover his authority: for if

Moved by so many representations and threats, ashamed that his cowardice should be reproached to him, and softened by the misfortune of his nephew Cacamatzin, whom he had always loved with singular tenderness, and by that of his brother Cuitláhuac and of other persons of the first nobility, although he did not consent to the course of taking the lives of the Spaniards, as some counseled him, he nevertheless resolved to tell them openly that they should leave that kingdom. One day, therefore, he sent for Cortés, who, aware of the secret conferences which in the preceding days the king had had with his ministers, with the nobles, and with the priests, felt a great disturbance in his mind; but dissembling as much as he could, he went at once to the king, accompanied by twelve Spaniards. Moctezuma received him with less affection than he was wont to show him, and frankly disclosed to him his resolution. “You cannot call in doubt,” he said to him, “the great love I have borne you, after so many and such clear demonstrations. Until now I have kept you gladly in my court, indeed I have chosen to remain here to live with you, for the singular pleasure I take in your familiarity and conversation. As far as concerns me,

Eight days after this resolution had been taken, Moctezuma again sent for Cortés, and this general fell into fresh disquiet. The King Bk. IX. told him that it was no longer necessary to build ships, because a short time before eighteen vessels like his own, already destroyed, had put in at the port of Chalchiuhcuecan, in which he might embark with his men: that he should therefore hasten his departure, since this was in the interest of the kingdom. Cortés concealed the joy that he felt at such news, and, thanking God in his heart for having sent him so opportune a relief, replied to the king that if those ships were to make the voyage toward Cuba, he was ready to depart; but that otherwise it would be necessary to continue the building of his own ships. He also saw and examined the paintings of that fleet sent to the king by the governors of the coast, and did not doubt that it was of Spaniards; but, very far from thinking that it had been sent against himself, he rather persuaded himself that his procurators, whom he had sent the year before to the court of Spain, had returned, and that they were bringing with them the royal dispatches and conducting a good number of troops for the conquest.

Cortés made his invincible constancy and magnanimity shine. He found himself on the one hand threatened with the whole power of the Mexicans if he remained at the court; and on the other he saw prepared against himself an army of his own countrymen far superior to his own; but his shrewdness, his singular industry, and his marvelous courage changed into good all the evil that hung over him. He endeavored, both by letters and by certain mediators in whom he most trusted, to win over the mind of Narváez and bring him to reason, making him various offers, and representing to him the advantages that the Spaniards would have if the two armies were united and acted in concert; and, on the contrary, the evils which discord must cause to the one and the other. Narváez, on the advice of three deserters from Cortés, had already landed with his whole army on the coast of Cempoala, and had taken up quarters in that city; the lord of which, knowing that his new guests were likewise Spaniards, and believing that they came to join his friend Cortés, or else fearing their power, received them with the greatest honor, and provided them with everything they needed. Moctezuma, believing at first the same, sent Narváez rich gifts, and gave orders to his governors to show him the same attentions that they had already shown to Cortés; but a few days later he perceived the discord that was between them, in spite of

> Pz tro»

Moctezuma then had the finest opportunity in the world to destroy the one party and the other, if he had harbored in his heart those bloody counsels which several historians have wished to impute to him. Narváez exerted himself to alienate him from Cortés and from those of his party, accusing them all of treachery, and promising to punish their unheard-of rashness in imprisoning so great a king, and to free both the king himself and the whole nation from their oppression; but Moctezuma [p. 115] was so far from plotting anything against Cortés on such suggestions

Bk. IX. that, on the contrary, when this general let him know of his expedition against Narváez, Moctezuma showed great regret at the risk to which he was exposing himself with such inferior troops, and offered promptly to raise a good army to send to his aid.

Cortés had already used every possible diligence to come to a peaceful accommodation advantageous to both armies, with no other effect than that of receiving fresh contempt and threats from the arrogant and haughty Narváez. Seeing himself therefore compelled to make war on his own countrymen, and not wishing, through his distrust, to avail himself of the help which the King of Mexico offered him, he asked the senate of Tlaxcala to equip four thousand men of war to lead with him, and sent to Chinantla one of his soldiers called Tobilla, a man well versed in the trade of war, to ask two thousand men from that warlike nation, and to procure three hundred pikes of the sort which the same Chinantecs used to resist the cavalry of Narváez, since they were longer and stronger than those of the Spaniards. He left in Mexico a hundred and forty (l) Spaniards with all their allies under the command of Captain Pedro de Alvarado, charging them to guard and treat the king well, and to endeavor to keep on good terms with the Mexicans, especially with the royal family and with the nobility. In taking leave of the king he told him that he was leaving in his place Captain Tonatiuh (by this name of the Sun the Mexicans called Alvarado, because he was blond), charged with serving His Majesty in everything: that he begged him to continue his protection of the Spaniards: that he was going to

Cortés left Mexico at the beginning of May of the year 1520, after having been six months at that court, with seventy Spaniards and a number of Mexican nobles, who wished to accompany him for some distance on the road. Several historians have convinced themselves that the Mexicans went to act as spies, and to give the king an account of whatever happened there; but Cortés did not believe them such, although otherwise he did not trust them. He made the journey by way of Cholula, where Captain Velázquez joined him, who was returning from Coatzacoalco, having been sent there with some troops by Cortés to look for a more convenient port for the ships. IX. quietly and without any noise to the great temple of that city, where the enemy had their quarters, he made so furious an assault upon it that before the break of daylight he had already made himself master of the quarters, of all his enemies, of the artillery, of the arms, and of the horses, only four of his soldiers being killed, and fifteen of the enemy, and many on both sides wounded. (n) He had himself acknowledged by all as captain general and supreme magistrate; he put in irons in the fortress of Veracruz both Narváez and Salvatierra, a distinguished person and a sworn enemy of Cortés, and had the sails, the rudders, and the compasses removed from the ships. Scarcely had the light of that day begun (it was Pentecost Sunday, May 27) when the two thousand Chinantecs arrived in good order and well armed, (o) who came only to be witnesses of the triumph of Cortés and of the shame of the partisans of Narváez, seeing themselves vanquished by so few enemies, and less well armed than themselves. The success of this expedition was owing in great part to the incomparable bravery of Sandoval, who with eighty men climbed the temple in the midst of a storm of arrows and balls, assailed the sanctuary where Narváez had fortified himself, and made himself master of his person.

brated with dances of the king and of the nobility, of the priests, and of the people. The nobility begged Captain Alvarado to consent that the king should go to the temple to perform his duty. Alvarado excused himself, either on account of the orders given him by Cortés, or because he feared that the Mexicans might plot some novelty with the king among them, well aware how easily public rejoicings turn into tumults. It was therefore decided to hold that religious dance in the court of the palace, (p) or quarters of the Spaniards, either by the arrangement of that captain or by order of the king himself, so that he might attend it according to their custom. When the day of the festival came, many men of the highest nobility (whose number (q) is not known) assembled in that court, richly adorned with various ornaments of gold, gems, and feathers. They began to sing and to dance to the sound of the instruments, and meanwhile Alvarado had some soldiers occupy the gates. When he then saw the Mexicans more

court of the great temple, but it is not probable that the immense throng of people who gathered there would have allowed so horrible a massacre of the nobility to be committed, especially since the armory was there, whence they could take as many arms as they wished to oppose the rashness of those few strangers; nor can it be believed that the Spaniards would have been willing to expose themselves to so evident a risk of perishing. Cortés and Bernal Díaz make no mention of the place of the dance. Father Acosta says that it took place in the palace, and it could not have been any other than that where the king was then living. The improbability that is seen in the account of those historians, and the judgment and early date of Father Acosta, make us prefer the testimony of this writer alone to that of all the others.

according to other historians, more than a thousand; and according to Monsignor de las Casas, more than two thousand. [p. 119] more heated, and perhaps even wearied by the dance, he gave the signal to his men to assail them, and these threw themselves at once Bk. IX. with fury upon those unfortunate men, who could neither offer resistance, since they were unarmed and weary, nor was it possible for them to escape by flight, because the gates were occupied. Terrible was the massacre, lamentable the cries which the dying sent up to Heaven, and copious the blood that was shed there. This fatal blow was one of the most painful to the Mexicans; for they lost in it the flower of their nobility, and to perpetuate its memory among their descendants they composed upon such a theme mournful songs, or elegies, which were preserved for many years after the conquest. When that tragic and horrible business was ended, the Spaniards stripped the corpses of all the wealth with which they were adorned.

The motive that induced Alvarado to so rash and inhuman a deed is not known. Some say that it was none other than that accursed hunger for gold. (r) Others affirm, and this seems more probable, that having been told that the Mexicans meant at that festival to strike a master stroke against the Spaniards, in order to free themselves from their oppression and to restore to liberty their king and lord, whom the Spaniards held in prison, he forestalled them, thinking true the common saying, he who attacks wins. (s) Whatever the case, his conduct cannot be excused of imprudence and of cruelty.

> Fu terribile la strage, lagrimevoli i gridi, che mandavano al Cielo i moribondi, e copioso il sangue, che vi fi sparse, Questo fatal colpo fu uno de' più sensibili a' Meslicani ; imperciocchè vi perdettero il fiore della lor Nobiltà, e per perperuarne presso i loro discendenti la memoria, composero sopra un tale argomento de’ cantici flebili, o sia elegie, le quali fi conservarono molti anni dopo la conquista . Termipata quella tragica ed orrenda funzione , spogliarono gli o 24 gouoli i cadaveri di rutta la ricchezza, di cui erano tregiati .

Mexican troops assailed the quarters with such impetuosity that they ruined a part of the wall, undermined the palace in various places, and burned the munitions; but they were repulsed by the fire of the artillery and of the muskets, whereby the Spaniards had leisure to repair the wall. That night they rested from the labor of the day, but the next day the assault was so furious that the Spaniards believed they must perish, and in fact not even one of them would have remained alive, as six or seven had already been killed, if the king, showing himself to the throng of the assailants, had not by his authority restrained their fury. Respect for the majesty of their sovereign held the commoners back from assailing the quarters with arms; but it did not turn them from other sorts of hostility: they also burned the four brigantines which Cortés had had built in order to save himself in them, in case he could not escape by the causeways made on the lake, and resolved to destroy the Spaniards by famine, denying them provisions, and endeavoring to prevent their introduction by means of a ditch dug around the quarters.

[p. 121] in the palace of Prince Maxixcatzin. There he reviewed his troops, Bk. IX. and found ninety-six horse and one thousand three hundred Spanish foot, to whom were added two thousand Tlaxcalans furnished by that republic. With this army he entered Mexico on June 24. He met with no opposition at his entry; but he at once perceived the popular ferment, as much from the small number of people to be seen in the streets as from certain bridges that had been raised from the canals. When he entered the quarters, with that jubilation on both sides which is easy to imagine, Moctezuma came to meet him in the court with the most obliging demonstrations of friendship; but Cortés, either made insolent by the victory won over Narváez and by the great force he had under his orders, or persuaded that it was necessary to feign a belief that the king was to blame for the disquiet of his vassals, passed on without so much as heeding him. The king, pierced with the keenest grief at seeing himself so unworthily slighted, withdrew to his apartment, where his sorrow was increased by the news which his servants brought him at once, of the insulting words that the Spanish general had spoken against His Majesty. (t) The historian Solís refuses to believe the slight shown to Moctezuma by Cortés, and in order to defend this general he wrongs Bernal Díaz, who affirms it as an eyewitness, and the chronicler Herrera, who relates it on good documents. He accuses Bernal Díaz undeservedly of partiality against Cortés, and says of Herrera that it may be suspected that he wished to adopt Díaz’s account in order to be able to apply to it a maxim of Tacitus: Ambition, he adds, dangerous among historians; but in no one more than in Solís himself; for every impartial person well instructed in the history of Mexico will see, on reading that of Solís, that this author, instead of fitting his maxims to the narrative, on the contrary fits the narrative to his maxims. Finally, unless he alleges better reasons than those he employs against Bernal Díaz, we must give credit to the testimony of this author, who was present at the event. With the new troops brought to Mexico by Cortés there was an army of nine thousand men, and as they could not all be lodged in the quarters, they occupied also some of the buildings that lay within the enclosure of the great temple, in the part nearest the quarters. With the multitude there grew likewise the scarcity of provisions, already caused by the lack of a market; for out of hatred of the Spaniards the

Mexicans would not hold one. Cortés therefore sent word to

Moctezuma, with great threats, that he should give orders for the market to be held, so that they might supply themselves there with everything they needed. Moctezuma replied that the most authoritative persons, in whom he could trust to have such an order carried out, were, like himself, in prison; that he should set some of them at liberty, so that they might attend to it. Cortés took from prison

Prince Cuitláhuac, Moctezuma’s brother, being very far from foreseeing that the liberty of that prince would cause the ruin of the

Spaniards. Cuitláhuac never returned to the quarters, nor did he restore the market, either because he would not favor the Spaniards, or because the Mexicans did not consent to it; indeed, they forced him to exercise his office of general. In fact it was he who from then on commanded the troops, and directed the hostilities against the

Spaniards, until on the death of his brother he was elected king of

Mexico.

and so many arrows that they covered the whole pavement of the court and the flat roofs of the palace, and the assailants were so many that the ground of the streets could not be seen. It did not seem well to Cortés to remain on the defensive, lest it be ascribed to cowardice, whereby the enemy would take greater courage. He therefore made [p. 123] a sortie against them with four hundred men, part Spaniards and part

Bk. IX. Tlaxcalans. The Mexicans retired with little loss to themselves, and Cortés, after setting fire to some houses, returned to the quarters; but seeing that the enemy continued their hostilities, he sent out Captain Ordaz with two hundred soldiers. The Mexicans pretended to be thrown into confusion and to flee, in order to draw them away from the quarters, as in fact they succeeded in doing; but suddenly the Spaniards saw themselves surrounded on every side by enemies, and attacked by one body of troops in front and another in the rear, though so tumultuously and in such disorder that they got in one another’s way. At the same time a great rabble showed itself upon the flat roofs, which incessantly hurled stones and arrows. The Spaniards then found themselves in great peril, and this occasion was beyond doubt one of those in which the valiant Ordaz made his bravery most conspicuous. The fight was very bloody, but without great loss to the Spaniards, who with their muskets and crossbows cleared the flat roofs, and with their pikes and swords drove back the multitude that flooded the street, and so were at length able to withdraw to the quarters, leaving many Mexicans dead, and of their own not more than eight; but nearly all came out wounded, and Ordaz himself as well. Among the injuries that the Mexicans did the Spaniards on this day was that of setting fire to several parts of the quarters, and in one of them the fire was such that the Spaniards were forced to throw down the wall, and to defend that breach with the artillery and with many men, whom they posted there until night, when the enemy gave them leisure to rebuild the wall and to tend the wounded.

The next day (June 26) the assault was more terrible and the fury of the Mexicans greater. The Spaniards defended themselves with twelve pieces of artillery, which made great slaughter in the throng of the assailants; but since these were in so great a number, they hid the dead under the feet of those who stepped into their place. > La sperienza fece conoscere a Cortès, che il maggior danno veniva alle sue rruppe da' terrazzi , onde per ischivarlo fece fare tra macchine da guerra ( dagli’ Spagnuoli appellate Mantas ) s\/ grandi che ognuna potesse portar venti Soldati armati; coperte con un forte tavolato per difendere i Soldati da’ sassi de' terrazzi, fornite di ruote per agevolare: il moto, e colle loro finestrelle o cannoniere per lo (paro degli schioppi .

streets of the city; he stormed some bridges, set fire to some houses, and after fighting almost the whole day returned to the quarters with more than fifty Spaniards wounded, leaving innumerable Mexicans dead.

Experience showed Cortés that the greatest harm came to his troops from the flat roofs; wherefore, to avoid it, he had three engines of war built (called by the Spaniards Mantas), so large that each could carry twenty armed soldiers, covered with strong planking to protect the soldiers from the stones thrown from the roofs, furnished with wheels to ease their movement, and with their little windows or loopholes for the firing of the muskets.

While these engines were being built, great changes took place at that court. Moctezuma, having gone up on a tower of that palace, had from there observed one of the aforesaid fights, and had seen in the throng of the people his brother Cuitláhuac commanding the

Mexican troops. At the sight of so many lamentable objects his mind was assailed by a crowd of melancholy thoughts. He saw on the one hand the danger he ran of losing crown and life, and on the other there presented themselves to him the destruction of the buildings of the capital, the killing of his vassals, and the happiness of his enemies; and he found no remedy for so many evils save the prompt departure of the Spaniards. In such thoughts he passed that night, and the next day, early, he called Cortés, and spoke to him on the same subject, begging him urgently not to put off any longer his departure from that court. Cortés had no need of such entreaties to resolve upon the journey. He found himself in extreme want of provisions:

food was already being given out by measure to the soldiers, and was so little that it sufficed only to sustain life, not the strength necessary to oppose so many enemies, by whom they were incessantly harassed.

Finally he saw that it was so impossible for him to make himself master of that city, as he would have wished, that he could not even maintain himself in it. On the other

Hardly was this conference ended when the cry to arms was raised The king’s address to the people, and its in the quarters for a general assault by the Mexicans. On all sides they effects. sought to climb the wall in order to enter, while some troops of archers posted at a convenient distance shot an immense multitude of arrows to overcome the resistance of the besieged, and some of the assailants pressed forward so far that, in spite of the fire of the artillery and the muskets, they set foot inside the quarters and fought hand to hand with the Spaniards. These, thinking themselves by now almost beaten and overwhelmed by the multitude, fought like desperate men. Moctezuma, on seeing their conflict and his own peril, resolved to show himself, in order to restrain by his presence and his voice the fury of his vassals. Having therefore put on the royal insignia, and escorted by some of his ministers and by two hundred Spaniards, he went up on the flat roof and presented himself to the people, ordering the ministers to call for silence, so that the voice of the sovereign might be heard. At his appearance the assault ceased, all fell silent, and some knelt to do him reverence. He spoke in a loud voice, and made them in substance this brief speech: “If the motive which induces you to take up arms against these strangers is zeal for my liberty, I hold dear the love and fidelity which you show me; but you are mistaken in believing me their prisoner, since it is in my power to leave this palace of my late father and go to my own whenever I please. If, however, your indignation is caused by their stay in this court, I let you know that they have given me their word to depart, and I assure you that they will certainly depart as soon as you lay down your arms. Let your disquiet cease, then; show me in this your fidelity, unless what I have

The people remained for a little while silent, until a man bolder (u)

> Frattanto i Messicani perfistevano nel loro afsalto, e gli Spagnuoli nella loro difesa , infinattantochè alcuni Nobili

than the rest raised his voice, calling the king a coward and effeminate, and fitter to handle the spindle and the distaff than to rule so courageous a nation as the Mexican, and reproaching him that through his cowardice he had made himself so basely the prisoner of his enemies; and, not content with insulting him in words, taking his bow in hand he shot an arrow at him. The commoners, being so easily moved by the first impulse that is given them, promptly followed his example: insults began to be heard everywhere, and stones and arrows to rain toward the place where the king was. The Spanish historians say that although the royal person was covered with two bucklers, he was nevertheless wounded by a stone on the head, by another on a leg, and by an arrow in an arm. He was then carried by the ministers to his chamber, tormented far more by indignation and rage than by his wounds.
