> Compite finalmente le tre macchine da guerra, uscì con esle a buon'ora Cortès ai 28., o 29. Giugno (x), e s'incamminò per una delle tre strade principali della Città con tre mila Tlascallesi , ed altre truppe ausiliarie, colla maggior parte degli Spagnuoli , e con dieci pezzi d' artiglierìa. Arrivati che furono al ponte, ch'era sul primo canale, apposero alle case le macchine e le scale per iscacciare la ciucma, ch'era sopra i terrazzi ; ma furono tante e sì grofle le saflate quindi tirate contra le macchine, che le fracaslarono, Gli Spagnuoli combatterono coraggiosamenre infin' al mezzo dì senza poter mai espugnar il ponte: per lo che ritornarono vergognati al quartiere , I:sciando un di loro morto, € conducendo seco molti feriti .

The three engines of war being at last completed, Cortés went out with them early on June 28 or 29 (x), and took his way along one of the three principal streets of the city with three thousand Tlaxcalans and other auxiliary troops, with the greater part of the Spaniards, and with ten pieces of artillery. When they arrived at the bridge that was over the first canal, they set the engines and the ladders against the houses in order to dislodge the rabble that was on the flat roofs; but the stones hurled thence against the engines were so many and so large that they shattered them. The Spaniards fought courageously until midday without ever being able to storm the bridge; for which reason they returned shamefaced to the quarters, leaving one of their number dead, and bringing with them many wounded.

This famous fight was one of those in which there was fighting with the greatest courage on both sides; and for that reason both the

Tlaxcalans and the Mexicans represented it in their paintings after the conquest.

Some historians add to this the circumstance of the great danger in which, as they say, Cortés found himself of being thrown down by two Mexicans, who, resolved to sacrifice their own lives for the good of their country, seized Cortés at the edge of the upper court to drag him with them in their fall, believing that they would put an end to the war by the death of that general; but this deed, of which neither

Cortés, nor Bernal Díaz, nor Gómara, nor any other of the older historians makes mention, has become more improbable through the circumstances added to it by some modern writers. (y)

Raynal and Dr. Robertson, moved to pity, as it appears, by Cortés’s peril, supplied him, the latter with I know not what battlements, and the former with a grating, to which he might cling in order to disengage himself from the Mexicans; but neither did the Mexicans ever make gratings, nor were there battlements on that temple. It is a wonder that these authors, so incredulous with regard to what is attested both by the Spaniards and by the Indians, should then believe what is neither found in the ancient authors nor even verisimilar.

The next day, when the engines had been repaired, he sallied out with them and with the greater part of his troops, and set out along the great causeway of Iztapalapa with better success than the first time; for in spite of the vigorous resistance which the enemy made in the entrenchments built by them against the fire of the Spaniards, he stormed the first four bridges, and set fire to some houses of that causeway, and took advantage of their materials to fill the ditches or canals, so that there might be no difficulty in the passage in case the Mexicans should take up the bridges. He left in the stormed posts a sufficient garrison, and returned to the quarters with many soldiers wounded, leaving ten or twelve dead.

On the following day he continued his attacks along the same causeway, stormed the three bridges that remained to him, and, pressing hard upon the enemy who defended them, reached the mainland. tion they had need of the person of a high priest, who had been taken prisoner by the Spaniards when they delivered the assault on the temple. Cortés immediately set him at liberty, and an armistice was agreed upon. This seems to have been a mere stratagem of the electors to recover that head of religion, whose person they needed for the anointing of the new king, whom they had already elected, or were by now about to elect; for hardly had Cortés enjoyed the pleasure of the suspension of arms when some Tlaxcalans arrived there bringing the news that the Mexicans had retaken the bridges and killed some Spaniards, and that a great throng of warriors was coming against the quarters. Cortés went to meet them with the cavalry, and breaking through them with extreme toil and peril in order to make his way, he recovered the bridges; but in the time in which he was storming the last, the Mexicans had already taken from the Spaniards the first four, and had begun to pull out the materials with which they had filled the ditches. Cortés finally returned to storm them, and withdrew to the quarters with all his men weary, battered, and wounded.

Cortés in his letter to Charles V represents to him the great peril he ran that day of losing his life, and ascribes to a particular providence of the Lord his having escaped it amid so great a multitude of enemies. It is certain that from the moment in which the Mexicans rose against the Spaniards, they could have ruined them all together with their allies, if they had observed a better order in fighting, and if there had been greater concord among the subordinate chiefs who directed the attacks; but the chiefs were not in agreement, as we shall see later, and the rabble was borne along only by the impulse of its tumultuary fury. On the other hand it cannot be doubted that the

Spaniards seemed to be made of iron, since they yielded neither to the rigor of hunger, nor to the need of sleep, nor to continual toil, nor to wounds. After having spent the whole day [p. 131] in fighting with their enemies they passed the night burying the dead, tending the wounded, and repairing the damage caused by the Bk. IX. Mexicans during the day in the quarters, and even in the little time that they gave to necessary rest they never laid down their arms, ready at every moment to present themselves to the enemy. But the hardiness of those men will appear still more plainly in the terrible fights which we shall shortly relate.

Moctezuma II. and age, in the eighteenth of his reign, and in the seventh month of his of other lords. imprisonment. Concerning the cause and the circumstances of his death there is such variety and contradiction among the historians that it is utterly impossible to trace the truth. The Mexican historians blame the Spaniards for it, and the Spaniards blame the Mexicans. (z) I cannot persuade myself that the Spaniards resolved to take the life of a king to whom they owed so many benefits, and from whose death they could expect nothing but many evils. His loss was lamented, if we give credit to Bernal Díaz, an eyewitness and a most truthful author, no less by Cortés than by every one of the captains and soldiers, as that of their own father would be. He favored them infinitely, whether altogether out of his own inclination, or partly also from fear; he always showed himself well disposed toward them; at least there is no reason to believe the opposite, nor is it known that he ever spoke ill of the Spaniards, as they themselves declared.

R2                         His

(z) Cortés and Gómara affirm that Moctezuma died of the blow from a stone which his vassals dealt him on the head. Solís says that his death was caused by his not having been willing to have the wound treated. Bernal Díaz adds to such an omission voluntary fasting. The chronicler Herrera says that the wound was not mortal, but that he died of heartbreak and rage. Father Sahagún, and the Mexican and Texcocan historians, affirm that the Spaniards killed him, and one of them states the circumstance that a soldier ran him through the groin with a sword. Among these last historians some say that his death occurred on the night of the defeat of the Spaniards, others affirm that it happened earlier. Acosta, Torquemada, and Vetancurt leave it to the Divine judgment.

Era di buona statura, e di poco buona carnagione , di faccia luaghetta, e d' occhi vivi,

His good and bad qualities may be understood from the account of Bk. IX.

> Lasciò in morendo parecchj} figliuoli , de' quali tre perirono nella infausta notte della sconfirca degli Spagnuoli, o per le mani degli stessi Spagnuoli, come affermano i Meslicani, o per le mani de' Messicani secondo che dicono gli Spagnuoli, Di quelli , che sopravvissero, il più grande fu Jobua- Ucabuatzin , il Huale nel battesimo s' appellò Don Picero Motezuma , e da costui discelero i Conti di Motezuma, e di Tula, Ebbe Motezuma questo figliuolo da MiahuaxochiclI (*)

his actions. He was circumspect, magnificent, liberal, zealous for justice, and grateful for the services of his subjects; but his aloof circumspection made the throne inaccessible to the complaints of his vassals. His magnificence and his liberality rested on the burdens of the people, and his justice degenerated into cruelty. He was exact and punctual in what concerned religion, and very zealous for the worship of his gods and the observance of the rites. (A) In his youth he was inclined to war, and courageous, and remained victor, so it is said, in nine battles; but in the last years of his reign domestic delights, the fame of the first victories of the Spaniards, and above all superstition so abased his spirit that he seemed to have changed his sex, as his subjects said. He took great delight in music and in hunting, and was as skillful in the use of the bow and arrows as in that of the blowgun.

He was of good stature, of not very good complexion, with a longish face and lively eyes.

At his death he left several children, of whom three perished in the ill-fated night of the defeat of the Spaniards, either at the hands of the Spaniards themselves, as the Mexicans affirm, or at the hands of the Mexicans according to what the Spaniards say. Of those who survived, the eldest was Yohualicahuatzin, who at baptism was named

Don Pedro Moctezuma, and from him descended the Counts of

Miahuaxochitl. [p. 133] daughter of Ixtlilcuechahuac, lord of Tollan. By another wife he had Tecuichpotzin, a beautiful princess, from whom descend the two most Bk. IX. noble houses of Cano Moctezuma and of Andrada Moctezuma. Besides these we know that he had another son, who was lord of Tenayuca, who, having escaped and taken refuge in Tepotzotlán when the Spaniards came out defeated from Mexico, was afterwards solemnly baptized, being near death, toward the end of the year 1524 or at the beginning of 1525. (B) The Catholic Kings granted singular privileges to the posterity of Moctezuma in consideration of the incomparable service done them by that monarch in incorporating into the Crown of Castile, by his voluntary cession, a kingdom so great and so rich as that of Mexico. Happy he, if after having ceded his kingdom to the King of Spain he had gained for himself the kingdom of Heaven; but neither the repeated entreaties made to him by Cortés during the whole time of his imprisonment, nor the continual exhortations employed by Father Olmedo, especially in the last days of his life, sufficed to induce him to embrace the faith of Jesus Christ, (C) which was soon afterwards so readily embraced by his vassals. Most lofty counsels of predestination, which cannot be fathomed by mortals.

(C) Diego Muñoz Camargo, a Tlaxcalan noble, says in his manuscripts that Moctezuma was baptized a little before dying, and even names those who held him at baptism, namely, Cortés, Alvarado, and Olid; but this is without doubt false; for it cannot be believed that Cortés would not have made mention of it in his letter to Charles V, when it was of so much importance for his justification. Bernal Díaz, an eyewitness, recalls the sorrow of Father Olmedo at not having been able to bring that king to Christianity. Gómara says that Moctezuma asked for baptism at Carnival of that year; that it was put off until Easter in order that it might be more solemn, and that it was then prevented by the arrival of Pánfilo de Narváez; but it is beyond doubt that by Easter the news of the fleet of Narváez had not yet reached Mexico: baptism could not therefore have been prevented by it.

The nobility, after shedding copious tears over the cold body of their unfortunate king, carried it to a place in the city called by them

Copalco (E), where they burned it with the customary ceremonies, and buried the ashes with the utmost reverence, although there were not lacking some unworthy and abandoned men who insulted it with vile abuse.

Meanwhile the Mexicans continued their attacks with greater ardor. Cortés, although he made great slaughter of them, and had been almost always victorious, nevertheless saw well that more was the blood shed by his soldiers than the advantages arising from his victories, and that in the end the want of provisions and munitions, and the multitude of the enemy, must necessarily prevail over the bravery of his troops and the superiority of his arms. Believing, therefore, the prompt departure of the Spaniards to be absolutely necessary, he called his captains to council to deliberate on the time and the manner of executing it. Their opinions were various. Some said that they ought to depart by day, forcing their way with arms if the Mexicans opposed them. Others wanted it done by night. This was precisely the opinion of a soldier named Botello, who boasted of astrology, to whom Cortés deferred more than was fitting, deceived by having seen certain predictions of his accidentally fulfilled. It was resolved, then, preferring the vain observations of that wretched soldier to the light of military prudence, to go out by night with the greatest possible secrecy, as if all their pains could suffice to conceal from the vigilance of so great a number of enemies the march of nine thousand men with their arms, their horses, their artillery, and their baggage. This was fixed for the night of July 1 (G), a night ill-fated and memorable for the Spaniards on

Bk. IX.

> Ordindò Cartès la sua marcia nel maggior filenzio della

the name of noche triste, by which it is known to this day in their histories. Cortés had a wooden bridge made, which could be carried by forty men, to use for the passage of the ditches. He then had all the gold, the silver, and the gems that they had until then amassed brought out; he took from it the fifth part, which belonged to their king, and delivered it to the officers of His Majesty, protesting the impossibility in which he found himself of keeping and saving it. He left the rest to his officers and soldiers, that each might take what he wished; but at the same time he warned them how much better it would be to abandon everything to the enemy; for, free of that weight, they could save their lives with less difficulty. Many of them, not wishing to remain deprived of the principal object of their desires, and of the sole fruit of their labors, loaded themselves with that precious burden, under whose weight they perished, victims no less of their own avarice than of the vengeance of their enemies.

He gave the vanguard to the invincible Sandoval with other captains, and with two hundred foot and twenty horse, the rear guard to Pedro de Alvarado with the greater part of the Spanish troops. In the main body of the army were conveyed the prisoners, the servants, the baggage; and Cortés with five horse and a hundred foot to give prompt aid wherever the need should be greater. The auxiliary troops of

Tlaxcala, of Cempoala, and of Cholula, in which there were then more than seven thousand men, were divided among the three parts of the army. Having then implored the protection of Heaven, they began to march along the causeway of Tlacopan. The greater part

Il bujo della notte, lo strepito dell'arme, i clamori minacciosi de’ combattenti, 1 lagrimevoli lamemi de’ prigionieri, ed i languidi sospiri de' moribondi fo:mavano un complesso -non men compalslionevole , che orribile . Quì la voce fentivali d'un Soldato , che domandava ajuto a' suoi compagni , e là quella d' un altro, che chiedeva a Dio misericordia, Tutto era confusione , clamori, ferite, ed uccisione. Cortès da buon Generale scorreva intrepidamente quà, e , passando spesso e ripaflando a nuoto i folli, incoraggendo gli uni, ajutando gli altri, e dando agli avanzi del suo scompigliato esercito tutto quell'ordine che petevasi non senza gran rischio- d’ eflere ucciso, o farto prigione. Il secondo fosso s empì a ral segno di cadaveri , che sopra esli passarono queeli della retroguardia, Alvarado, che la comandava, trovossi nel terzo foflo così furiosamente incalzato da' nemici, che . non potendo a loro far fronte , nè passarvi a nuoto senza evidente pericolo di perire per le lor mani, ficcò la Jancia nel fondo del fosso, ed afferrò il piede d' efla colle braccia, e dando uno straordinario impulso al suo corpo, fi lanciò d’ua salto di là dal fosso. Quelto salto stimato da tutti un prodigio d'agilità diede a quel luogo il nome, che fin' ad orta conserva, del Salro d' Alvarado . (1)

; for Cortés affirms that in their retreat they arrived at Tlaxcala on July 10, and from the diary of their march written by this Conqueror it is plain that the defeat could not have happened except on July 1. [p. 137] part of them passed the first ditch, or canal, happily, with the help of the bridge that they carried with them, without meeting any resis‐ Bk. IX. tance but the little that the sentinels, by whom that post was guarded, were able to make; but the priests, who were keeping watch in the temples, having become aware of it, cried to arms, and with their horns roused the people. In a moment the Spaniards found themselves assailed both by water and by land by an infinite number of enemies, who with their very multitude and disorder hindered one another in the attack. The fight at the second ditch was very terrible and bloody, the danger extreme, and extraordinary the efforts of the Spaniards to escape. The darkness of the night, the din of arms, the threatening cries of the combatants, the lamentable wailings of the prisoners, and the languid sighs of the dying formed a whole no less pitiable than horrible. Here was heard the voice of a soldier who called on his comrades for help, and there that of another who asked God for mercy. All was confusion, outcries, wounds, and slaughter. Cortés, like a good general, ran intrepidly hither and thither, passing and repassing the ditches often by swimming, encouraging some, helping others, and giving to the remnants of his scattered army all the order that could be given, not without great risk of being killed or taken prisoner. The second ditch was filled to such a degree with bodies that those of the rear guard passed over them. Alvarado, who commanded it, found himself at the third ditch so furiously pressed by the enemy that, being unable to face them, or to pass by swimming without evident danger of perishing at their hands, he planted his lance in the bottom of the ditch, and clasped its foot with his arms, and giving an extraordinary impulse to his body, leaped with one bound to the other side of the ditch. This leap, esteemed by all a prodigy of agility, gave to that place the name which it still keeps, of the Leap of Alvarado. (I)

Bernal Díaz counts 870 Spaniards dead; but in this number he includes, as he himself affirms, not only those who were killed on that ill-fated night, but also those who perished in the following days until their arrival at Tlaxcala. Solís numbers no more than 200, and Torquemada 290. As to the number of auxiliary troops who perished there, Gómara, Herrera, Torquemada, and Vetancurt are in agreement. Solís says only that more than a thousand Tlaxcalans were lost; but this does not agree with the computation of Cortés, nor with that of other authors.

(M) Cortés affirms that all the prisoners were killed; but Cuicuitzcatzin must be

excepted, whom Cortés had already set on the throne of Acolhuacan; for we know from the account of Cortés himself that this man was a prisoner, although we do not know the reason, and on the other hand it is established for us that he was afterwards killed in Texcoco, as we shall see below.

> Non potè Cortés, malgrado la grandezza del suo cuore, trattener le lagrime a vista di tal calamità, Si mise a sedere sopra una pietra in Popotla, villaggio vicino a Tla» copan, non già per riposar dalle sue fatiche , ma per pianper la perdita de' suoi amici e compagni. In mezzo a tanti disastri ebbe almeno il conforto di sentire, ch’ erano in falvo i suoi più bravi Capitani Sandoval , Alvarado, Olid , Ordaz, Avila, e Lugo, i suoi interpreti Aguilar, 6 Donna Marina , ed il suo ingegniere Martino Lopez, ne’ quali principalmente confidava di poter riparare il suo onore, e conquistar Messico. NL: \ (

Cortés, in spite of the greatness of his heart, could not restrain his tears at the sight of such a calamity. He sat down upon a stone in Popotla, a village near Tlacopan, not to rest from his labors, but to weep for the loss of his friends and companions. Amid so many disasters he had at least the comfort of hearing that his bravest captains, Sandoval, Alvarado, Olid, Ordaz, Ávila, and Lugo, his interpreters Aguilar and Doña Marina, and his engineer Martín López were safe, in whom he chiefly trusted to be able to repair his honor and conquer Mexico.

Lo stesso fenz' altro avranno fatto co' loro parenti , ed amici morti, lasciando in quel giorno nette le strade ed i fosli, e bruciando i cadaveri, prima che infertassero l’aria colla loro corruzione.

Citlaltepec, Xoloc, and Zacamolco, pressed along the whole road by several flying bands of the enemy. At Zacamolco they found themselves so famished, and reduced to such misery, that they ate for supper a horse killed that same day by the enemy, and the general himself had his share. The Tlaxcalans threw themselves on the ground to eat the grass that they found there, imploring the aid of their gods.

§ 22.      The next day, hardly had they set out on the road over the mounFamous battle of tain of Aztaquemecan when they saw from afar, in the plain of Tonan,

Otompan.

not far from the city of Otompan, a numerous and brilliant army, either of Mexicans, as the writers commonly say, or else composed, as I believe, of the troops of Otompan, of Calpulalpan, of Teotihuacan, and of other neighboring places gathered there at the suggestion of the Mexicans. Some historians make this army amount to two hundred thousand men, a number judged by the Spaniards only by eye, and perhaps magnified by their fear. These men persuaded themselves, as Cortés himself attests, that that day was to be the last of their lives. This general drew up his languishing troops, extending the front of that wretched army, so that its flanks might remain in some way covered by the small wings of the little cavalry that was left to him, and with a countenance full of fire said to them: “We find ourselves in such straits that it is necessary to conquer or die. Bk. IX. troops diminish and in great part lose courage, and his enemies come on more proud notwithstanding the damage they received from the Spanish arms, took a bold and most perilous resolution, by which he obtained the victory, and put in safety the remnants of his wretched army. There came to his mind what he had often heard said, namely, that the Mexicans fell into disorder and fled whenever they saw their general dead, or the standard lost. Cihuacatzin, general of that army, clad in a rich military dress with a fine plume on his head, and with a gilded shield on his arm, was carried in a litter on the shoulders of some soldiers. The standard, which according to their custom he carried, was a net of gold fixed on the point of a pike, which he had strongly tied on his back, and which rose about ten palms above his head. (*) Cortés observed it in the center of that great multitude of enemies, and, resolved to deal a decisive blow, commanded his brave captains Sandoval, Alvarado, Olid, and Ávila to keep behind him to guard his back, and with others who accompanied him he hurled himself at the point where the enterprise seemed to him less difficult, with such impetus that he overthrew some to the ground with his lance, and others with his stirrups. Thus he advanced through the enemy ranks until he reached the general, who was accompanied by some officers, and with a thrust of his lance stretched him on the ground. Juan de Salamanca, a brave soldier who accompanied Cortés, dismounting promptly from his horse, put an end to his life, and taking from him the plume, presented it at once to Cortés. (O) The enemy army, as soon as it saw its general dead and the standard taken, was thrown into confusion

> Questa vittoria fu una delle più famose, ch’ ebbero l'ar- _ mi Spagnuole nel Nuovo Mondo, Segnaloss: in ella sopra rutti il Generale Spagnuolo, di cui dicevano poi i suoi “Capitani € Soldati, che non . aveano veduto mai un sì pran coraggio4 ed una sì grande attività , come quella , che fece spiccar in quella giornata; ma ebbe una grave ferita nel“capo, la quale peggiorando vieppiù ogni giorno ridusse ad &stremo pericolo la sua vita. Bernal Diaz loda giustamente la bravura di Sandoval, e fa vedere quanta parte ebbe questo famoso Uffiziale nella vittoria , facendo animo a tutti nod meno. coll’ esempio, che coll' esortazioni, E' stata parimente celebrata dagli Storici Spagnuoli Maria d' Estrada , moglie d'un Soldato Spagnuolo, la quale armata di lancia e rotella correva tra l’ oste nemica ferendo ed uccidendo con una intrepidezza molto strana nel fuo fesso. This victory was one of the most famous that the Spanish arms had in the New World. The Spanish general distinguished himself in it above all, of whom his captains and soldiers said afterwards that they had never seen so great a courage and so great an activity as that which he displayed that day; but he received a grave wound in the head, which, growing worse every day, brought his life into extreme danger. Bernal Díaz justly praises the bravery of Sandoval, and shows how large a part this famous officer had in the victory, giving courage to all no less by example than by exhortations. María de Estrada, wife of a Spanish soldier, has likewise been celebrated by the Spanish historians; armed with lance and buckler she ran amid the enemy host wounding and killing with an intrepidity most strange in her sex. Of the Tlaxcalans Bernal Díaz says that they fought like lions, among whom Calmecahua, captain of the troops of Maxixcatzin, distinguished himself. He took at baptism the name of Don Antonio, and became famous, even more than for his bravery, for his very long life of a hundred and thirty years.

The Spaniards, at length weary of pursuing the fugitives, resumed the road toward Tlaxcala by the eastern part of that plain, where they stayed that night in the open, and the general himself, after the fatigue and the wounds he had received that day, kept guard in person for their greater safety. The Spaniards were by now no more than four hundred and forty. Besides those who had been killed in the fights preceding the night of their ill-fated departure from Mexico, there perished in it and in the six following days eight hundred and seventy, as Bernal Díaz, an eyewitness, often affirms, many of whom, having been taken prisoner by the Mexicans, were inhumanly sacrificed in the great temple of the capital.

1180. In the fights preceding the defeat of the Spaniards in Mexico, he scarcely mentions anyone dead. In the defeat he numbers only 200, and in the account of their journey to Tlaxcala he reports no others than those two or three who died in Tlaxcala of the wounds received at Otompan. Where, then, are, or how did they vanish, the other five hundred and more men who are wanting there to complete the number 1180? Quite another idea of the battle of Otompan is given us by those who were there, as can be seen in the letters of Cortés and in the True History of Bernal Díaz. “Oh, how furious and fearful to behold,” says this author, “was that battle! how they fought hand to hand, and with what fury the dogs (so he calls the enemy by way of insult!) attacked us! What wounds and slaughter they inflicted on us with their lances and swords, etc.,” and after a few lines he says thus: “I repeat that they wounded and killed many of our soldiers.”

The Tlaxcalan women implored Cortés to avenge the death of their sons and relatives, and vented their grief in a thousand imprecations against the perfidy of the Mexicans.

> Poichè ebbero riposato tre giorni in questo luogo, passfarono alla Capitale della Repubblica, quindi distante quindici miglia per curar le loro ferite , delle quali morirono otto Soldati. Il concorso di Popolo nella loro entrata in Tlascallan fu upuale, e forse anche più grande di quello, che vi fu allora , quando la prima volta v' entrarono . L' accoglienza , che loc fece Maxixcatzion, e la cura , che prese di loro, furono degne del suo animo generoso , e della sua fincera amicizia. Gli Spagnuoli fi riconoscevano ogni giorno più obbligati a quella “Nazione , la cui amicizia coltantemente coltivata fu il mezzo più efficace non folo per la conquista della Capitale dell’ Imperio Messicano, ma eziandia per quella di tutre quante le Provincie, che s' opposero ai progrelli dell' armi Spagouole , e per la soggiogazione dei barbari Cicimechi ed Otomiti , da cui furono tanto travagliati i Conquistatori .

Having rested three days in this place, they passed to the capital of the republic, fifteen miles distant from there, to tend their wounds, of which eight soldiers died. The concourse of people at their entry into Tlaxcala was equal to, and perhaps even greater than, that which there was then, when they first entered it. The reception that

Maxixcatzin gave them, and the care that he took of them, were worthy of his generous spirit and of his sincere friendship. The Spaniards recognized themselves every day more obligated to that nation, whose friendship, constantly cultivated, was the most efficacious means not only for the conquest of the capital of the Mexican empire, but also for that of all the provinces that opposed the progress of the Spanish arms, and for the subjugation of the barbarian

Chichimecs and Otomis, by whom the Conquerors were so much harassed.

> Mentre che gli Spagnuoli riposavano in Tlascalla dalle loro fariche, e curavano le loro ferite, i Messicani s' adope[p. 145] ravano per rimediare a' mali della Corte, e del Regno. A questi danni ricevuti dagli Spagnuoli s' aggiunsero quelli, ch'eglino stessi si cagionarono colla guerra civile, la notizia della quale dobbiamo a' manoscritti d' uno Storico Messicano, che fi trovava allora in quella Corte, e sopravvisse; alcuni anni alla ruina dell’ Imperio,

While the Spaniards rested in Tlaxcala from their fatigues, and tended their wounds, the Mexicans were exerting themselves [p. 145] to remedy the ills of the court and of the kingdom. The losses they

IX. had suffered during the past year were indeed great and lamentable; for besides the great sums of gold, silver, gems, and other precious things which they had spent, partly in gifts made to the Spaniards and § 24. partly in homage to the King of Spain, of which they doubtless recov‐ Election    in Mexico,

> Aveano d' uopo i Messicani di mettere alla resta della loro Nazione un uomo capace di ristabilir l’onor d'essa, e di riparar alle perdite avute nell' ultimo anno del Regno di Motezuma. Fu eletto Re di Messico il Principe Cuirlahuarzin O poco innanzi, 0 poco dopo la sconfitta degli Spaguuoli. Era egli, come abbiam già detto, Signor d' Izrapalapan,

and the measures of ered a certain amount, the reputation of their arms had been tar‐ King Cuitláhuac. nished, and respect for the Crown of Mexico diminished; the Totonacs and other peoples had withdrawn from their obedience; their enemies had grown more insolent; the temples were damaged and many houses of the capital ruined, and above all they lacked their king, many persons of the royal house, and a great part of the nobility. To these losses received from the Spaniards were added those which they brought upon themselves by the civil war, of which we owe our knowledge to the manuscripts of a Mexican historian who was at that time at that court and survived the ruin of the empire by some years.

While the Spaniards were in the court, distressed by hunger through the hostility of the Mexicans, several lords of the first nobility, either to favor the Spaniards’ party, or, what seems more probable, to succor their king, who, being among the Spaniards, must have suffered the same want, supplied them secretly with provisions, and perhaps even declared themselves openly in their favor, trusting in their own authority. For this reason so fatal a dissension broke out among the Mexicans that it could not be quenched except by the death of many illustrious persons, and particularly of Cihuacoatl, of Tzihuacpopoca, of Cipocatli, and of Tencuecuenotzin, some of them sons and others brothers of King Moctezuma, according to what the aforesaid historian affirms.

The Mexicans had need of setting at the head of their nation a man capable of restoring its honor and of repairing the losses suffered in the last year of Moctezuma’s reign. Prince Cuitláhuac was elected King of Mexico, either a little before or a little after the defeat of the Spaniards. He was, as we have already said, lord of Iztapalapa,

> Sroria del Messico Tom. 111, #9 Con[p. 146] Consigliere intîimo del Re Motezuma suo fratello, e Tlachs Lis. IX.cocalcail, o fia General d'efercito. Era uomo savio, e di gran talento, siccome ne fa fede il suo nemico Cortès, lìberale, e magnifico, come il suo fratello. Dilettavali assai dell' Architettura , e della coltura de' giardini, come fi vide nel magnifico palazzo, che fabbricò in Iztapalapan , e nel celebre giardino, che vi piantò , de' quali fanno menzione con gran lode quali tutti gli Storici antichi. La sua bravura, e la sua perizia militare gli acquistarono uda grande stima presso i suoi Nazionali , alcuni Spagnuoli bene informati del carattere di lui affermarono, che se egli non fosse statro frastornato dalla morte, non sarebbe stata mai espugnata dagli Spagnuoli la Capitale, (LL) E' da credersi, che i sacrifizj, che fi fecero nella festa della sua incoronazione furono di quegli Spagnuoli, ch'egli stesso fece prigioni nella notte della loro sconfitta. Tosto che furono terminate le feste della sua incorona: zione, s'applicò a rimediar a' mali della Corte, e dell' Imrio, Diede ordine di riparar i tempj danneggiati, e di ri» le case rovinate, aumentò e migliorò le fortificazioni della Capitale, mandò de' messi alle Provincie dell'Imperio, incoraggendole per la comun difesa dello Stato contro a quei nemici stranieri, è promise di rilevar da ogni tributo coloro, che prendessero l’armi in favor della Corona. Mandd altresì degli Ambasciatori alla Repubblica di Tlascallan con un

Privy [p. 146] privy councilor to King Moctezuma his brother, and Tlachcocalcatl, or Bk. IX.

general of the army. He was a wise man and of great talent, as his enemy Cortés bears witness, liberal and magnificent like his brother. He took great delight in architecture and in the cultivation of gardens, as was seen in the magnificent palace which he built in Iztapalapa, and in the celebrated garden which he planted there, both of which are mentioned with great praise by nearly all the ancient historians. His bravery and his military skill won him great esteem among his countrymen; some Spaniards well informed of his character affirmed that if he had not been cut off by death, the capital would never have been taken by the Spaniards. (Q) It is to be believed that the sacrifices which were made at the festival of his coronation were of those

Spaniards whom he himself took prisoner on the night of their defeat.

No sooner were the festivities of his coronation ended than he applied himself to remedying the ills of the court and of the empire. He gave orders to repair the damaged temples and to rebuild the ruined houses, enlarged and improved the fortifications of the capital, sent messengers to the provinces of the empire, encouraging them to the common defense of the state against those foreign enemies, and promised to relieve of every tribute those who should take up arms in favor of the Crown. of King represent to that senate that although the Mexicans and the Cuitláhuac to the

Tlaxcalans. Tlaxcalans had until then been mortal enemies, it was now necessary for them to unite, as natives of one and the same country, as peoples of one language, and as worshipers of the same gods, against the common enemies of the fatherland and of religion; that they had already seen the bloody slaughter which those inhuman and haughty strangers had made in Mexico and in other places, their sacrilegious attempts against the sanctuaries and against the venerable images of the gods, their ingratitude and perfidy toward his brother and predecessor and toward the most respected personages of the Anahuatlacas, and their insatiable hunger for gold, which led them to violate the most holy laws of friendship; that if the republic continued to second the perverse designs of those monsters, it would receive from them in the end the same recompense that king Moctezuma received for the humanity with which he welcomed them to his court and for the liberality with which he favored them for so long; that the Tlaxcalans would be detested by all nations for having given aid to such wicked usurpers, and that the gods would hurl down upon the republic the whole fury of their wrath for its being confederated with the enemies of their worship. If, on the contrary, the Tlaxcalans declared themselves, as he begged them, enemies of those men hated by Heaven and by Earth, the court of Mexico would make a perpetual alliance with them, and would thereafter have free trade with the republic, whereby the latter could escape the misery to which it had until then been reduced; all the nations of Anahuac would be obliged to them for so important a service; and the gods, appeased by the blood of such victims, would send the rain needed in their fields, would make their arms fortunate, and would render the name of the Tlaxcalans famous throughout the earth.

T2 [p. 148] from the audience hall the ambassadors, according to their custom, Bk. IX. remained there to deliberate on that great affair. There were not lack‐

ing some to whom the proposals of the court of Mexico seemed just and conducive to the happiness of the republic, exaggerating the advantages that were offered to them and, on the other side, the disastrous outcome of the Spaniards’ enterprise in Mexico and the slaughter made among the Tlaxcalan troops who had been there under their orders. Among others the younger Xicotencatl raised his voice, who had always been a mortal enemy of the Spaniards, and endeavored with every argument he could to persuade them to the alliance with the Mexicans, adding that it would be much better to preserve the ancient customs of their nation than to submit to the new and extravagant usages of that untamed and imperious people; that he could not imagine another occasion more opportune for freeing themselves entirely from the Spaniards than now, when they found themselves reduced, weakened, and cast down. Maxixcatzin, who on the contrary was sincerely attached to the Spaniards, and was endowed with a better mind for knowing the law of nations and a will better disposed to observe it, rejected the opinion of Xicotencatl, condemning as an abominable perfidy the counsel to sacrifice to the vengeance of the

Mexicans those men harassed by fortune, who had sought their asylum in Tlaxcala, trusting in the protestations and the demonstrations of the senate and of the nation. He added that if they flattered themselves with the advantages which the Mexicans offered, he hoped for greater ones from the bravery of the Spaniards; that if there was reason not to trust the Spaniards, there was still less reason to trust the

Mexicans, of whose perfidy they had so many examples; finally, that no other crime would be capable of so greatly provoking the wrath of the gods and of obscuring the glory of the nation as such wickedness against those innocent guests. Xicotencatl pressed his counsel by presenting to the senators a loathsome portrait of the character and customs of the Spaniards. The altercation was so great, and so heated the minds, that Maxixcatzin, carried away by anger, gave a push to

> La risoluzione , che vi fi prese fu quella di rispondere all’ ambasciata, che la Repubblica era pronta ad accettar la pace ce l'amicizia della Corte di Melssice , qualora non fosse per farsi con un’azione sì indegna, € con un delitto sì) engrme, come quello di facrificar i suoi ospiti ed amici; ma uando fi cercarono gli Ambasciatori per intimar- loro la-riposta del Senato, erano già nascostamente partiti da Tlafcalla, perciocchè avendo oflervato quel popolaccio alquanto inquieto nel loro arrivo, temettero , che volefle far qualche attentato contro il rispetto dovuto al lor carattere, E” però da credersi , che il Senato mandasle degli Ambasciatori Tla-scallesi per portar la risposta a quella Corte. I Senatori procurarono occultar, agli Spagouoli «il motivo dell'ambasciata, e tutto ciò ch'era avvenuto nel Senato; ma a dispetto delle loro diligenze il seppe Cortès, il quale ringraziò, com' e-, ra giusto, Maxixcatzin de'suoi bucni ufficj, è s' esibì a corrispondere alla idea vantaggiosa , che aveva della bravura e dell'amicizia degli Spagnuoli ,

The resolution taken there was to answer the embassy that the republic was ready to accept peace and friendship with the court of Mexico, provided it were not to be made by an action so unworthy and a crime so enormous as that of sacrificing its guests and friends; but when the ambassadors were sought in order to announce to them the senate’s answer, they had already secretly departed from Tlaxcala, because, having observed that rabble somewhat restless at their arrival, they feared that it might attempt something against the respect due to their character. It is to be believed, however, that the senate sent Tlaxcalan ambassadors to carry the answer to that court. The senators took pains to conceal from the Spaniards the motive of the embassy and all that had happened in the senate; but in spite of their diligence Cortés learned of it, and thanked Maxixcatzin, as was just, for his good offices, and offered to live up to the favorable idea he had of the bravery and friendship of the Spaniards.

Giovanni Diaz, Cappellano dell'armata Spagnuola, essendo lor patrini Cortès, ed i suoi priocipali Gapitani , Celebrosh questa funzione colle più gran dimostrazioni di giubilo , tanto degli Spa» gnuoli, quanto de' Tlascallesi. Chiamosli Maxixcatzio nel battesimo D, Lorenzo, Xicorencatl] il vecchio Don Vincenzio, Tlehuexolotzin Don Gonzalo, e Citlalpopoca D. Bartolommeo. (R)

Baptism of the four gave obedience to the Catholic King, and, what is more, the four heads of the lords of Tlaxcala. republic, moved by the grace of the Holy Spirit, renounced idolatry, and after being well instructed were baptized by Father Juan Díaz, chaplain of the Spanish army, with Cortés and his principal captains as their sponsors. This ceremony was celebrated with the greatest demonstrations of joy, both of the Spaniards and of the Tlaxcalans. Maxixcatzin was named at baptism Don Lorenzo, Xicotencatl the elder Don Vicente, Tlehuexolotzin Don Gonzalo, and Citlalpopoca Don Bartolomé. (R)

vered in the faith, because they were not, as was needful, intimately persuaded of the truth of Christianity.

Cortés was already delivered from the danger to which the blow

§ 27. received on the head in the last battle had exposed his life, and the Dismay of some

Spaniards. other Spaniards, except some who died of them, had recovered from their wounds by the aid of the Tlaxcalan surgeons. During the time of his illness Cortés had thought of nothing else but the means to be employed to bring to a good end the great enterprise of the conquest of Mexico, and to attain this he had caused a great quantity of timber to be cut for the construction of thirteen brigantines; but while he was forming these great projects, many of his soldiers were turning over thoughts very different. They saw themselves diminished in number, poor, in bad condition, and stripped of arms and horses.

They could not forget the terrible conflict and the tragic night of July

1, nor did they wish to expose themselves again to such misfortunes.

They fed one another’s ideas and fears, and blamed the obstinacy of their general in so rash an enterprise. From private murmurings they went on to make him a formal petition, wishing to oblige him with many arguments to return to Veracruz, where they could procure reinforcements of troops, arms, and munitions to undertake the conquest with greater forces, which they then thought altogether impossible. Cortés was troubled by this novelty, which upset all his designs; but with that talent which he had of persuading his mentions only that of Maxixcatzin, and Solís adds that of Xicotencatl. Some author makes Father Olmedo the minister of the baptism, and some say that Maxixcatzin received it in his last illness. But it is certain that all four heads of that republic were baptized before the conquest, although Torquemada and Vetancurt do not agree on the time. It is also known that Maxixcatzin did not put off baptism until his last illness, and that the four lords were baptized not by Father Olmedo but by Father

Díaz. Besides other proofs, this is evident from the ancient paintings, made by the

Tlaxcalans, which were in several convents of the Franciscan fathers and were seen by the historian Torquemada. [p. 151] his soldiers to whatever he wished, he made them an effective speech, by which he induced them to desist from their demand. He re‐ Bk. IX. proached them for that cowardice, awakened in their hearts the sentiments of honor, recalling to them in flattering terms their glorious deeds and the protestations, full of ardor and courage, which they had so often made to him; he made clear to them how much more dangerous their return to Veracruz would prove than their stay in Tlaxcala; he assured them of the fidelity of that republic, of which they still showed themselves doubtful; and finally he begged them to suspend their resolution until they should see the outcome of the war which he meant to make against the province of Tepeyacac, in which he hoped to have new proofs of the sincerity of the Tlaxcalans.

The lords of the province of Tepeyacac, bordering on the republic § 28.

War of the Spaniards of Tlaxcala, had declared themselves friends of Cortés and subjects of against the people of

Tepeyacac. the King of Spain ever since that horrible butchery which the Spaniards made in Cholula; but seeing the Spaniards afterward cast down and the Mexicans victorious, they returned to the obedience of the King of Mexico, and to win his favor they killed some Spaniards who were traveling from Veracruz to Mexico, unaware of the tragedy of their companions; they admitted a Mexican garrison into their towns, and occupied the road that led from Veracruz to Tlaxcala, and, not content with this, made some raids into the lands of that republic. Cortés resolved to make war upon them, no less to punish their perfidy than to secure the road from that port for the reinforcements which he expected from there. He was urged to such an expedition also by the younger Xicotencatl, who had already been restored to liberty through the mediation of the same Spanish general, and who, to remove any suspicion that might exist against him on account of what had happened in the senate, offered to aid him in that war with a good army. Cortés accepted the offer; but before taking up arms, he amicably requested some satisfaction from the people of Tepeyacac, and exhorted them to leave the Mexican party, promising to pardon them

Their first expedition was against Zacatepec, a place belonging to the confederation of the people of Tepeyacac. Its inhabitants laid an ambush for the

Spaniards. They fought on both sides with great courage and obstinacy; but the people of Zacatepec were in the end defeated, very many of them remaining dead on the field. (S) Then the army marched against Acatzinco, a city ten miles southeast of Tepeyacac, which the Spaniards entered in triumph after winning a battle little less difficult than that of Zacatepec. From Acatzinco

Cortés sent several detachments to burn some places in those surroundings and to bring others under his obedience, and when it seemed to him time to attack the principal city, he set out with his whole army toward Tepeyacac, which he entered without any resistance from its citizens. There he declared slaves many prisoners taken in that province, and had them branded with a red-hot iron according to the barbarous usage of that century, applying the fifth part to the King of Spain, as was done with everything they acquired, and dividing the rest among the Spaniards and the allies. He founded there, according to the manner of speaking of the Spaniards of that time, a city, which he called Segura de la

Frontera

The Mexican troops that were in the garrisons of that province § 29.

War of withdrew from it, because they had not forces sufficient to resist the Cuauhquechollan. power of their enemies; but at the same time there appeared above the city of Cuauhquechollan (**), more than forty miles from Tepeyacac toward the southwest, an army of Mexicans sent there by King Cuitláhuac to prevent the Spaniards from passing that way to the court, if ever they should attempt it. Cuauhquechollan was a considerable city, where there were some five to six thousand families, very pleasant, and strong no less by nature than by art. It was naturally defended on one side by a high and steep mountain, and on another by two rivers not far apart. The whole city was surrounded by a strong wall of stone and lime, about twenty feet high and twelve wide, with a good parapet all along it, which was almost three feet high. There were no more than four gates by which to enter, in those parts where the ends of the wall were doubled, forming two semicircles, as they are seen represented in the figure we gave in Book VII. The difficulty of the entrance was increased by the elevation of the ground of the city, which was as great as the height of the wall itself, so that to enter it was necessary to climb some quite high steps.

The lord of that city, who was partial to the Spaniards, sent an embassy to Cortés, protesting his vassalage to the King of Spain, who had already been acknowledged lord of that land in the celebrated assembly which King Moctezuma held with the Mexican nobility in the presence of Cortés: that he

Mexicans; that at present there was in Cuauhquechollan a good number of Mexican officers, and as many as thirty thousand men of war, partly in that city and partly in the neighboring places, to prevent any confederation with the Spaniards; therefore he begged him to come to their relief and to free them from the vexations which they suffered from those troops. Cortés welcomed the news, and immediately sent with the same messengers a relief force of thirteen horse, two hundred Spanish foot, and thirty thousand men of auxiliary troops under the command of Captain Olid. The messengers, in accordance with the order of their lord, offered to lead the army by a little-traveled road, and warned the commander Olid that when the army should be already near the city, the people of Cuauhquechollan would assault with armed hand the lodgings of the Mexican officers, and try to seize or kill them, so that when the army of the Spaniards then entered, it would be easier for them to rout the enemy, already deprived of their leaders. But twelve miles before reaching Cuauhquechollan the Spanish commander became suspicious that the Huexotzincas had secretly confederated with the people of Cuauhquechollan and with the Mexicans to ruin the Spaniards utterly. This suspicion, caused by sinister information and made more probable by the multitude of Huexotzincas who had spontaneously joined the army, forced him to return to Cholula, where he had some of the more distinguished Huexotzincas and the messengers of Cuauhquechollan seized, and sent them under good guard to Cortés, that he might make his inquiries concerning the alleged treachery.

Cortés was greatly vexed by such conduct toward friends so faithful as the Huexotzincas. Nevertheless he examined them diligently, discovered the innocence and good faith of both parties, and perceived that the past disasters had made the Spaniards more fearful, and that fear led them, as it usually does, to suspect more than was fitting. He caressed and made gifts, as much as he could, to the

Huexotzincas and the people of Cuauhquechollan [p. 155] and, accompanied by them, he marched at once for Cholula with a

Bk. IX. hundred foot and ten horse, determined to carry out this enterprise in person. He found the Spaniards in Cholula frightened, gave them courage, and then marched for Cuauhquechollan with the whole army, which then consisted of more than three hundred Spaniards and more than a hundred thousand allies. Such was the readiness of those peoples to arm themselves against the Mexicans in order to escape from their domination. Before arriving at Cuauhquechollan Cortés was informed by that lord that all measures had already been taken: that the Mexicans trusted in their sentinels posted on the towers of the city and on the roads; but that these had already been secretly seized by the citizens.

No sooner did the people of Cuauhquechollan see the army that was coming to their relief than they assaulted with armed hand the lodgings of the Mexicans with such violence that before Cortés entered the city they presented to him forty prisoners. When that general entered, three thousand citizens were fighting at the principal lodging of the Mexican officers, who, although much inferior in number, defended themselves nonetheless with such courage that the people of Cuauhquechollan could not take the house, even though they had made themselves masters of the flat roofs. Cortés gave it the assault and took it; but in spite of the pains he took to capture someone from whom to learn the present state of the court, the Mexicans fought with such obstinacy that all were killed, and he could scarcely gain some light from a dying officer. The other Mexicans who were scattered about the city rushed out of it in order to join the main body of the army, encamped in a high place that commanded all the surroundings, which in a moment drew up in battle order and entered the city, setting fire to the houses. Cortés affirms that he had never seen another army of finer appearance, because of the gold and plumes with which it was seen adorned. The Spaniards ran to the defense with their cavalry and many thousands of allies, and forced them to retire to

§ 30.    The army rested three days in Cuauhquechollan, and on the fourth War of Itzocan. marched toward Itzocan (*), a city of three to four thousand families,

situated at the foot of a mountain, about ten miles from

Cuauhquechollan, and surrounded by a deep river and by a small wall.

Its streets were well ordered, and its temples so many that, great and small, they seemed to Cortés to number about a hundred; its climate is hot because it is situated in a deep valley enclosed by high mountains, and its soil, like that of Cuauhquechollan, is most fertile, and shaded by trees with beautiful flowers and excellent fruits. That state was then ruled by a personage of the royal blood of Mexico, to whom

Moctezuma had given it in fief after having put to death, I know not for what cause, the lawful lord who possessed it; and at present there was a garrison there of five to six thousand men of Mexican troops.

Having learned all this from the lord of Cuauhquechollan, Cortés was moved to the expedition against Itzocan. His army had so increased that it amounted, by what he himself affirms, to about a hundred and twenty thousand men. He assaulted the city on that side where the entrance was less difficult. The people of Itzocan, seconded by the royal troops, offered some resistance at first; but being in the end overcome by the far superior forces of the assailants, they were thrown into confusion, and fled by the opposite side of the city, and having crossed the river, they

The lord of Itzocan had absented himself from the city and set out on the road to the court as soon as the enemy army was seen. That sufficed for the nobility, to whom perhaps that lord was not acceptable, to declare the state vacant; whereupon they agreed, with the authority and protection of Cortés, to give it to a son of the lord of Cuauhquechollan and of a daughter of that lord whom Moctezuma put to death; and since he was still a boy of a few years, there were assigned to him as guardians his own father, an uncle of his, and two nobles. This boy was soon instructed in the Christian doctrine and baptized.

The fame of the victories of the Spaniards flew at once throughout the land, and drew several peoples to the obedience of the Catholic King. Besides Cuauhquechollan, Itzocan, and Ocopetlayocan, a large city not far from those two, (V) there came some lords to pay homage to the Crown of Castile from eight places of Coaixtlahuacan (*), part of the great province of Mixtecapan, more than a hundred and twenty miles to the south of Cuauhquechollan, all seeking eagerly the alliance and friendship of men so valiant.

§ 31. Spaniards. The inhabitants of Xalatzinco, a city not far from the road War of Xalatzinco, of Tecamachalco, and of to Veracruz, were conquered by the famous Sandoval, and the princi‐

Tecamachalco, a considerable city of the Popoloca nation, offered great resistance, but in the end surrendered, and two thousand of them were made slaves. Against Tochtepec, a large city on the river

Papaloapan, where there was a Mexican garrison, he sent a captain named Salcedo with eighty Spaniards, of whom not even one remained alive to bring Cortés the news of their defeat. That general was greatly grieved by this loss, which, in relation to the few Spanish troops he then had, was very great, and to avenge it he sent the two brave captains Ordaz and Ávila with some horse and twenty thousand allies, who, in spite of the great courage with which the Mexicans defended themselves, took that city with the killing of many enemies.

The loss of those soldiers was not what most grieved Cortés. The very men who a little before had begged him to return to Veracruz persisted so obstinately in their request that he was forced to grant them permission to return, not to Veracruz to await new reinforcements there, but to Cuba, to be farther from the dangers of war, it seeming the lesser evil to that shrewd commander to diminish his troops than to keep malcontents who by their displeasure would slacken the courage and cool the

Tamazolla, where some months before he had sent some Spaniards to look for mines.

The victories of the Spaniards and the multitude of their allies so § 32.

Havoc wrought by enlarged their name, and gained for Cortés such authority among the smallpox. Death those peoples, that he was the arbiter of their differences, and to him, of King Cuitláhuac

and of Prince as if he were the supreme lord of that land, they came to obtain the Maxixcatzin, and election of King confirmation of the investiture of vacant states, as happened in those Cuauhtémoc. of Cholula and of Ocotelolco in Tlaxcala, both vacant through death caused by smallpox. This scourge of the human race, entirely unknown until then in the New World, was brought there by a Black slave of Narváez. This man gave it to the Cempoalans, and from them the contagion spread through the whole Mexican empire with unspeakable damage to those nations. Many thousands of men perished of it, and some places were left depopulated. Those whose constitution prevailed over the violence of the disease were left so disfigured, and marked with such deep traces of the poison on the face, that they filled with horror all who looked at them. Among the other evils caused by this new disease, there was all too keenly felt by the Mexicans the death of their king Cuitláhuac, after three or four months of reign, and by the Tlaxcalans and the Spaniards that of Prince Maxixcatzin.

The Mexicans elected as king Cuauhtémoc, nephew of the late Cuitláhuac, since there remained no brother of the last two kings. He was a young man of twenty-five years and of great spirit, and although by reason of his age not much practiced in the trade of war, he nonetheless continued the military measures of his predecessor. He married his cousin Tecuichpotzin,

The death of Maxixcatzin was greatly mourned by Cortés, as much for the friendship he had formed with him as also because to him was chiefly due that harmony which existed between the Tlaxcalans and the Spaniards. Accordingly, after having made the road to Veracruz safe, and having sent to the court of Spain Captain Ordaz with a distinct account, written to the Emperor Charles V, of all that had befallen him until then, and Captain Ávila to the island of Santo

Domingo to solicit new reinforcements for the conquest of Mexico, he set out from Tepeyacac for Tlaxcala, and entered it dressed in black, and making other demonstrations of grief for the death of the prince his friend. At the request of the Tlaxcalans themselves, and in the name of the Catholic King, he conferred the vacant state of

Ocotelolco, one of the four principal ones of that republic, upon a son of the deceased prince, a boy of twelve years, who at baptism took the name of Don Juan Maxixcatzin, (*) the name of the father being from then on a surname of the son and of all his illustrious descent; and to do him some particular honor out of regard for the merits of his father, he dubbed him a knight in the manner of Castile.

§ 33. Elevation of Prince     At that same time, though from a very different cause, occurred Coanacochtzin, and the death of Prince Cuicuitzcatzin, whom Moctezuma and Cortés

death of

Cuicuitzcatzin. had placed on the throne of Acolhuacan in place of his unfortunate brother Cacamatzin. He was not permitted to enjoy his counterfeit dignity, because soon the very man who had given him the crown took away his liberty. He left Mexico among the other prisoners on that night of the Spaniards' defeat; but he then had the fortune, or rather misfortune, to escape, since he was soon to lose more ignominiously his

> Sroria Antica del Messico Tom. II. x LL

Bk. IX. Tlaxcala, where he stayed until, either impatient of oppression or eager to recover the throne, he fled secretly to Texcoco. There reigned then at that court his brother Coanacochtzin, to whom, Cacamatzin being dead, the crown belonged according to the law of that kingdom. No sooner had Cuicuitzcatzin presented himself there than he was made prisoner by the royal ministers, who gave prompt notice of it to the king, then absent in Mexico. He let King Cuauhtémoc his cousin know of it, who, thinking that fugitive prince a spy of the Spaniards, was of opinion that he should be put to death. Coanacochtzin, either to please that monarch, or rather to remove from Cuicuitzcatzin the occasion of wishing to recover the throne to the prejudice of his own right and of the peace of the kingdom, had him put to death without delay. Thus ended that unfortunate prince, whose exaltation served for nothing but to make his fall greater and more resounding. (Z)

[p. 163] be employed in the siege of Mexico; and when it seemed to him that it was time to march, he reviewed his troops, which consisted of forty Bk. X. horse and five hundred and fifty foot. He divided that small cavalry into four parts, and the infantry into nine companies, armed some with muskets, others with crossbows, others with sword and buckler, and others with pikes. From his horse, on which he was drawing up his troops, he made them this address: “Friends and comrades of mine, any discourse that I might wish to make to animate your bravery is altogether superfluous, since we all acknowledge ourselves obliged to repair the honor of our arms and to avenge the death of our Spaniards and allies. Let us go to the conquest of Mexico, the most glorious enterprise of any that can ever be offered to us in all our life. Let us go to punish at one stroke the perfidy, the pride, and the cruelty of our enemies, to enlarge the dominions of our sovereign by adding to them a kingdom so great and so rich, to smooth the road for the Gospel, to open the gate of Heaven to so many millions of souls, to secure by the toil of a few days the comfort of our families, and to make our name immortal: incentives capable of encouraging even the most cowardly minds, let alone hearts so noble and generous as yours. I see no difficulty that your bravery cannot overcome. It is true that our enemies are many; but we are superior to them in courage, in discipline, and in arms. Besides, we have under our orders so great a number of auxiliary troops that, helped by them, we could conquer not only one but many cities equal to that of Mexico. Let it be as strong as you please; but it is not so strong that it can resist the attacks which we must give it by land and by water. Finally, God, for whose glory we fight, has declared that he will second our designs. His providence has preserved us in the midst of so many perils and disasters, has sent us new companions in place of those whom we have lost,

The Tlaxcalans, who strove to imitate the discipline of the

Spaniards, wished also to review their troops in the presence of

Cortés. The army began with military music of cornets, conch trumpets, and other wind instruments of the kind, behind which came the four heads of the republic armed with shield and sword, and adorned with most beautiful plumes that rose more than two feet above their heads. They wore their hair bound with golden ribbons, in their lips and ears pendants of gems, and on their feet shoes of great price.

Behind them came four squires of theirs armed with bow and arrows.

After these came the four principal standards of the republic, each with its own ensign made of feathers. Then began to pass, in well-ordered files, the troops of archers, twenty abreast, the particular standards of their companies being seen at certain intervals, each company composed of three or four hundred men; these were followed by the troops armed with sword and shield, and at the end by those of the pikemen. Herrera and Torquemada affirm that the archers were sixty thousand, the pikemen ten thousand, and the others armed with sword forty thousand. (b)

(b) Solís, following Bernal Díaz, as he says, counts in the review of the Tlaxcalans

no more than 10,000 men, and he censures Herrera because, departing from Bernal

Bernal Díaz makes no mention of the review of the Tlaxcalans; he says only that when Cortés asked the senate for ten thousand men, the senate replied that it was ready to furnish a much greater number of troops.

Herrera does not count 80,000 men, as Solís says, but 110,000, as may be seen in his

Dec. 2, bk. 2, ch. 20. Herrera was followed in this reckoning by Torquemada and

Vetancurt. Ojeda, who was present there and was commander of the allied troops, affirms that they were 150,000 men; but in this reckoning he included the

Huexotzincas, the Cholulans, and the people of Tepeyacac.

Xicotencatl the younger also made his speech, in imitation of Cortés, in which he told his troops that on the following day, as was well Bk. X. known to them, they were to march with the brave Spaniards against the Mexicans, their mortal enemies: that although the mere name of the Tlaxcalans sufficed to terrify all the nations of the earth, they should nonetheless strive to win new glory by their deeds.

> AA OVRIOUNMNA 10% I RUTE] 1A!

Cortés for his part summoned the principal lords of the allied states, and exhorted them to constant fidelity toward the Spaniards, exaggerating to them the advantages which they should hope for from the ruin of the Mexicans, and the evils which they should fear if ever, through the suggestion of the Mexicans, or through fear of the war, or through inconstancy of mind, they should fail in the faith given. Then he published a military edict for the regulation of his troops, which contained the following articles:

I. Let no one blaspheme against God, nor against the Blessed Virgin, nor against the saints.

II. Let no one quarrel with another, nor lay hand to sword or other weapon to wound him.

III. Let no one gamble away his arms, nor his horse, nor his iron gear.

IV. Let no one force any woman, under penalty of death.

V. Let no one take the property of others, nor punish any Indian unless he is his slave.

VI. Let no one go out on raids without our permission.

VII. Let no one take any Indian prisoner, nor plunder his house, without our permission.

VIII. Let no one maltreat the allies; on the contrary, let every means be used to maintain their friendship.

And because it is of no use to publish laws if zeal for their observance is lacking and offenders are not punished, he had two Blacks, slaves of his, hanged because they had stolen a turkey and two cotton mantles. By these and other such punishments he made his orders respected, so necessary for the preservation of his troops.

When he had made all the dispositions which seemed to him conBk. X.

ducive to the good outcome of his enterprise, he finally marched with all his Spaniards and with a good number of allies on December 28,

1520, after having heard Holy Mass and invoked the Holy Spirit. He did not then wish to take with him the whole army of allies which had been reviewed the day before, as much on account of the difficulty there would be in maintaining so great a number of troops in

Texcoco, as because he thought it more necessary to leave the greater part of them in Tlaxcala for the security of the brigantines, when it should be time to transport them. (c) Of the three roads there were for going to Texcoco, Cortés took the most difficult, prudently persuading himself that since the Mexicans would not have to wait for him on it, his march would prove safer. He set out accordingly by way of Tetzmellocan, a village belonging to the state of Huexotzinco. On the 30th they observed from the highest summit of those mountains the beautiful valley of Mexico, partly with jubilation, because there was the object of their desires, and partly with some displeasure because of the memory of their disasters. As they began to descend toward the valley they found the road obstructed with many trunks and branches of trees laid across it on purpose, and had need to employ a thousand Tlaxcalans in clearing it. As soon as they reached the plain, they were attacked by some flying squadrons of the enemy; but some of them having been killed by the Spaniards, the others were put to flight. That night they lodged at Coatepec, a place eight miles distant from Texcoco, and the next day, making their way to that court, anxious about the disposition of the Texcocans, but equally resolved not to turn back without having taken vengeance on their enemies, they saw coming toward them four persons of authority, unarmed, one of them with a small golden banner in his hand, and Cortés, recognizing that this was

80,000. [p. 167] was a sign of peace, advanced to confer with them. These four were messengers sent by King Coanacochtzin to compliment the Spanish Bk. X. general, to invite him to betake himself to his court, and to beg him not to commit any hostility in his states; they presented to him the little banner, which had thirty-two ounces of gold. Cortés, in spite of these tokens of friendship, reproached them with the death dealt a few months before by the inhabitants of the village of Zoltepec to forty-five Spaniards, five horses, and three hundred Tlaxcalans who were accompanying them, laden with gold, silver, and arms for the Spaniards who were then in Mexico, a death carried out with such inhumanity that they had hung up as trophies in the temples of Texcoco the skins of the Spaniards with their arms and garments, and those of the horses with their shoes. He added that since it was not possible for them to make up the loss of those people, they must at least repay him the gold and silver stolen: that if they did not give him due satisfaction, for each Spaniard killed he would put to death a thousand Texcocans. The messengers replied that the Texcocans were not guilty of that, but the Mexicans, by whose orders the people of Zoltepec had done it; that nevertheless they offered to use every possible diligence that everything should be restored to them, and having taken courteous leave of the Spanish general, they returned in haste to Texcoco with the news of the speedy arrival of the Spaniards at that court.

Cortés entered Texcoco with his army on the last day of that year. Some nobles came to meet him, and led him to one of the palaces of the late King Nezahualpilli, which was so large that not only were § 2.

[p. 168] of that court. Not to increase the distrust of the citizens, and not to Bk. X. expose his men to some disaster, he published an edict in which, on

pain of death, he forbade his soldiers to leave their quarters without his permission. After dining they observed from the roofs of the palace that a great number of people were leaving the city, some making their way to the neighboring woods and others to various places on the lake. The following night King Coanacochtzin himself slipped away, betaking himself to Mexico in a boat, in defiance of Cortés, who wished to seize him, as he had already done with his three brothers Cacamatzin, Cuicuitzcatzin, and Ixtlilxochitl. Coanacochtzin could take no other course; for how could it be possible that he should consider himself safe among the Spaniards after seeing what they had done to his brothers and to King Moctezuma his uncle, and especially since he feared that many of his own subjects might thereupon take occasion to declare themselves his enemies, some through fear of the Spaniards or for the particular interest of their families, others to avenge the death of Cuicuitzcatzin, and others again to set

Ixtlilxochitl upon the throne.

Mexico, in whose dominions much better lands would be assigned to them; but those lords, instead of being frightened by the reprimand or yielding to the promises, seized the messengers and sent them to Cortés. He asked them the reason for their embassy, and they replied that, knowing that those lords were in his favor, they had come to beg them to be willing to act as mediators for peace between the Mexicans and the Spaniards. Cortés, pretending to believe what they said, set them at liberty and charged them to tell their sovereign that he did not want war, nor would he ever wage it unless compelled by the hostility of the Mexicans; that he should therefore take heed, and guard against doing any harm to the Spaniards or to their allies, because otherwise they would behave as enemies and would infallibly ruin his cities.

> Sam ——

The alliance of those three cities was indeed of great importance to Cortés; but more than anything else he needed to win over the court of Texcoco itself, both for the great nobility that was there and for its influence on the other cities of the kingdom. Ever since he had entered that court he had constantly sought to win hearts by courtesy and good manners, and had urged the same upon his men, strictly forbidding every kind of hostility toward the citizens. He recognized at the outset a party among the nobility favorable to Prince Ixtlilxochitl, whom he was keeping, I know not for what reason, in Tlaxcala. He had him brought to the court by a good number of Spaniards and Tlaxcalans, presented him to the nobility, and obtained that he be recognized by them as king and crowned with the same ceremonies and demonstrations of joy that they were accustomed to show toward their legitimate sovereigns. Bk. X. their usages and manners. He was instructed in the Christian religion and baptized with the name of Don Fernando Cortés Ixtlilxochitl, out of regard for the Spanish general, who was his godfather. He had upon the throne nothing but some semblance of majesty; for rather than lord of his subjects he was a minister of the will of the Spaniards, to whom he rendered great services, not only in the conquest of Mexico, in which he served with his person and with his troops, but also in the rebuilding of that capital, for which he furnished some thousands of architects, masons, and laborers. He died quite young in 1523, and his brother Don Carlos, of whom we shall afterward make honorable mention, succeeded him in the lordship of Texcoco. With the elevation of Ixtlilxochitl, and with the courtesies which Cortés showed him, the Spanish party grew considerably, and all those Texcocan families that had absented themselves from the court for fear of the Spaniards’ hostilities, now rendered secure, returned gladly to their homes.

Cortés had resolved to make his quarters in Texcoco, and so had taken pains to fortify that royal palace where his troops were lodged. He could not have taken a counsel more suited to his purpose. Texcoco, as capital of the kingdom of Acolhuacan and so large a city, abounded in every sort of provisions for the sustenance of the army; it had good buildings for their lodging, good fortifications for their defense, and a plentiful supply of every kind of artisan for all the work they needed. The dominions of Texcoco, moreover, bordering on those of Tlaxcala, made the necessary communication with that republic easier for the Spaniards; the proximity of the lake was of great importance for the construction of the brigantines; and the advantageous situation of that court made the Spaniards aware of all the movements of their enemies without exposing them to their hostilities.
