Spaniards, more than three thousand Tlaxcalans (e), and many

Texcocan nobles. Before reaching Iztapalapa, some troops of the enemy came to meet them, pretending to oppose their entry, and fighting partly on land and partly in the water, but in fighting they kept retiring toward the city, making a show of being unable to withstand their attack. Thus the Spaniards and Tlaxcalans, drawn on in pursuing them, entered the city, whose houses they found largely deserted, because the citizens had taken refuge with their wives, their children, and the greater part of their goods in the houses which they had on the little islands of the lake; but there too they were pursued by their enemies, who fought even in the water. The night was already far advanced when the Spaniards, delighted with the victory which they believed they had won, were busy plundering the houses, and the

Tlaxcalans setting fire to them; but their rejoicing was soon changed to terror, for by the very light of the fire they observed that the water of the canals was gushing out and beginning to flood the houses. The danger recognized, the retreat was sounded, and the city was abandoned in haste to take again the road to Texcoco; but in spite of their diligence they came to a place where there was so much water that the Spaniards crossed it with difficulty, and some of the Tlaxcalans were drowned, and most of the booty was lost. Not one of them would have remained alive, according to Cortés’s statement, if they had stayed three hours longer in the city, because the citizens, wishing to drown all their enemies, broke the dike of the lake and flooded the city. Spaniards. ings gave him by means of their ambassadors, alleging, in order to obtain his favor, that, though they had been urged by the Mexicans to take up arms against the Spaniards, they had never consented. Cortés, as one who was continually acquiring greater authority the more his party grew, required of them as a necessary condition for obtaining his alliance that they should seize all the messengers who might be sent them from Mexico, and all the Mexicans who might come to their cities. They offered to do so, though not without great difficulty, and from then on were constantly faithful to the Spaniards.

This confederation was immediately followed by that of Chalco, a considerable city and state on the eastern shore of the fresh-water lake; for Cortés, knowing that the Chalcas wished to adhere to his party but dared not declare themselves for fear of the Mexican garrisons that were in their state, sent Sandoval there with twenty horse, two hundred Spanish foot, and a good number of allies, and gave him orders first to escort certain Tlaxcalan troops who wished to carry to their homeland that portion of the booty of Iztapalapa which they had saved, and then to turn upon Chalco to drive the Mexicans out of that state. Sandoval gave the vanguard to the Tlaxcalans; some Mexican troops that had put themselves in ambush rushed suddenly upon them, threw them into confusion, killed some of their men, and took the booty from them; but when the Spaniards came up they defeated

La cagione di ribellarsi sì facilmente tanti popoli di quell’ Imperia era negli uni la paura dell’ armi Spagnuole, e della possanza de' loro alleati ,e negli altri l'odio della dominazione messicana. Non è possibile , che fia costante la fedeltà de' sudditi , qualora nella subordinazione infiaisce più il ter rore, che la beneficenza . Non v'è trono più vacillante ché quello che fi sostiene più colla forza dell’ armi, che coll'amor de’ Popoli. Cortès , dopo avere accarezzato ì due giovani Chalcheli , divise fra loro quello Stato, 0 a richiesta di loro medesimi , o per suggestione della Nobiltà . urne al più

marched toward Chalco, but long before reaching the city the main body of the Mexican garrison came to meet him, which, according to some historians, was composed of twelve thousand men. A battle was fought, which lasted two hours and ended with the killing of many

Mexicans and the flight of the rest. The Chalcas, informed of the victory, came with great rejoicing to meet the Spaniards, and led them in triumph into the city. (f) The lord of that state, dead of smallpox a little earlier, had in the last moments of his life warmly recommended to the two sons he left that they should ally themselves with the

Spaniards, cultivate their friendship, and have Cortés for a father. In consequence of his last will those two young men betook themselves to Texcoco, accompanied by the Spanish army and by many Chalca nobles; they presented to Cortés the value of a hundred and fifty sequins in gold and established the alliance, in which they remained constantly faithful. The reason why so many peoples of that empire so easily rebelled was in some the fear of the Spanish arms and of the power of their allies, and in others hatred of the Mexican domination. It is not possible for the fidelity of subjects to be steadfast when in their subordination terror has more influence than beneficence.

There is no more unstable throne than one that is sustained more by force of arms than by the love of its peoples. Cortés, after showing favor to the two young Chalcas, divided that state between them, either at their own request or at the suggestion of the nobility. He gave the elder

Diede per ranto loro il’consiglio di confederarsi cogli Huexotzinchi , co' Cholollesi, e-co' Quauhquechollesi . Appena erano partiti i Chalchesi , che arrivarono opportunamente a Tezcuco tre messaggieri di Huexotzineo e di Quauhquechollan, ‘mandati da que' Signori a Corrtès per fignificarglii la loro sollecitudine per cagione di certi fummi , indizj non oscuri di guerra, offervati dalle sentinelle, ch’ eglino aveano sulle cime delle montagne, e per offerirgli le loro truppe pronte a’ suoi ordini , qualora se ne volesse servire. Profictosi Cortès di sì bella occasione per confederar quegli Stari con quello di Chalco, obbligandoli a rinunziare pel bene comune ai particolari loro risentimenti. Fu ferma questa alleanza, che d' allora innanzi s' ajutazono scambievolmente contro ‘i Messicani.

Meanwhile the Mexicans did not cease to make raids into the states that had allied themselves with the Spaniards, but Cortés’s diligence in sending them relief rendered their efforts for the most part useless. Among others, within a few days the Chalcas themselves came to Texcoco to implore the aid of the Spaniards; for they had learned that the Mexicans were preparing to strike a great blow in that state, lately withdrawn from their dominion. Cortés could not this time comply with their requests; because, having now finished the work of the masts, the planks, and all the fittings of the brigantines, he needed his troops to have them transported safely to Texcoco. He therefore gave them the counsel to ally themselves with the Huexotzincas, the Cholulans, and the people of Cuauhquechollan. The Chalcas refused such a confederation because of their ancient enmity with those peoples; but in the end they accepted it, moved by Cortés’s urging and compelled by necessity. The Chalcas had hardly departed when three messengers from Huexotzinco and from Cuauhquechollan opportunely arrived at Texcoco, sent by those lords to Cortés to make known to him their concern on account of certain smokes, by no means obscure signs of war, observed by the sentinels which they had on the summits of the mountains, and to offer him their troops, ready at his orders, should he wish to make use of them. Cortés took advantage of so fine an occasion to confederate those states with that of Chalco, obliging them to renounce for the common good their particular resentments. This alliance was firm; from then on they helped one another mutually against the Mexicans.

Spaniards, many of them killed and others made slaves. Thence

Sandoval marched to Tlaxcala, where he found everything ready for the transport of the worked materials of the brigantines. The first brigantine was made by Martín López, a Spanish soldier, who served as engineer in Cortés’s army, and was tried out in the river Zahuapan.

On its model the other twelve were built by the Tlaxcalans. The transport was carried out with the greatest display and rejoicing of the Tlaxcalans, who found light that burden which was to contribute to the ruin of their enemies; eight thousand Tlaxcalans carried on their backs the beams, the sails, and the other gear required for the construction of the brigantines, two thousand came laden with the provisions, and thirty thousand armed men for the defense, under the orders of three principal chiefs, Chichimecatl, or Chichimecatecuhtli,

(*) Ayotecatl, and Teotepil, or Teotlipil. This convoy occupied, according to Bernal Díaz, more than six miles. When they left Tlaxcala,

Chichimecatl commanded the vanguard; but as soon as they set foot outside the dominions of that republic, Sandoval gave him the rear guard, because he feared some attack from the enemy. § 6.

Hardly had the general Chichimecatl arrived when, without wish‐ Expeditions against the cities of Xaltocan ing to rest from the fatigue of the journey, he begged Cortés to em‐ and Tlacopan. ploy him and his troops against the enemy. Cortés, who was waiting for nothing else than the arrival of the auxiliary troops from Tlaxcala to carry out an expedition which he had been meditating for some time, leaving in Texcoco a good garrison, and having given the proper orders concerning the completion of the brigantines, set out on the march at the beginning of spring of 1521 with twenty-five horse and six small cannon of artillery, with three hundred and fifty Spanish foot, thirty thousand Tlaxcalans, and a part of the Texcocan nobility; and because he feared that the Texcocans, whom he did not yet trust, might give some secret warning to the enemy and upset his plans, he left Texcoco without disclosing the object of his expedition. The army marched twelve miles toward the north, and spent that night in the open. The next day it went to attack Xaltocan, a strong city situated in the midst of a small lake, with a causeway leading to it that was cut, like those of Mexico, by several ditches. The Spanish infantry, aided by a good number of allies, crossed the ditches amid a dense cloud of darts, arrows, and stones, by which many were wounded; but the citizens, unable to bear longer the slaughter which the Spanish arms were making among them, abandoned the city and saved themselves by flight. The victors plundered the houses and burned some of them.

Thence they passed to Tenayuca and to Azcapotzalco, and because they met with no resistance in those three cities, they did them no harm. Finally they arrived at the court of Tlacopan, the goal which

> ‘9 Motezuma , sacrificata alle vostre voglie? Entrate pure,

Cortés had set himself, in order to seek there some accommodation with the court of Mexico, and, if that should never succeed, to inform himself more closely of their designs and preparations. He found the inhabitants of that city disposed to resist their entrance. These attacked the Spaniards with their usual fury, and fought courageously for a good while; but at last, unable to withstand the fire of the muskets and the impetus of the horses, they withdrew to the city. The

Spaniards, because it was late, lodged in a great house of the suburb.

The next day the Tlaxcalans set fire to many houses of the city, and in the six days that the Spaniards stayed there they had continual skirmishes, and there were some famous duels between the Tlaxcalans and the people of Tlacopan; but both sides fought with singular bravery, and vented the hatred they bore one another in a thousand insults. The people of Tlacopan called the Tlaxcalans the damsels of the

> » entrate nella Corte , dove fi farà di tutti voi un gran sa- » crifizio a'nostri Dei. ,, Nelle zuffe, ch’ebbero in questi giorni gli Spagnuoli , entrarono in quella farale strada , € [p. 179] s accostarono; a que' memorabili fossi, ne' quali nove mesi ==innanzi erano stati sconfitti . Vi trovarono una terribile re- Lu. X. sitenza, e rutti in una volta furono per perire; perchè impegnati nel perseguitare certe truppe messicane , ch' eran venute a bella;posta ad insultarli per tirarli al pericolo fi trovarono improvvisamente aflaliti dall'una e dall'altra banda della strada da un, sì gran numero di nemici, che a stento retrocedettero, combattendo furiosamente fin'a terra ferma,

Spaniards, without whose protection they would never have dared to advance as far as that city. The Tlaxcalans in turn answered them that the title of women was owed rather to the Mexicans and to all their partisans, since, though so superior in number to the Tlaxcalans, they had never been able to subdue them. Nor were the Spaniards exempt from such insults. They invited them in mockery to enter Mexico to command there as lords and to enjoy all the pleasures of life. “Does it seem to you, Christian,” they said to Cortés, “that things will go now as they did the other time? Do you think that another Moctezuma reigns in Mexico, sacrificed to your desires? Enter, enter by all means into the court, where of all of you a great sacrifice will be made to our gods.” In the fights which the Spaniards had in those days, they entered that fatal causeway, and [p. 179] approached those memorable ditches in which nine months before they had been defeated. There they met a terrible resistance, and all Bk. X. at once were on the point of perishing; for, engaged in pursuing certain Mexican troops that had come on purpose to insult them in order to draw them into danger, they found themselves suddenly assailed on both sides of the causeway by so great a number of enemies that they retreated with difficulty, fighting furiously as far as the mainland. In this conflict five Spaniards were killed, and many wounded. Many of the Mexicans were left dead in this and in the other fights. Cortés, displeased at the ill success of his expedition, returned with his army by the same road to Texcoco, receiving on his march fresh insults from the enemy, who ascribed his retreat to fear and cowardice. (g) The Tlaxcalans who accompanied the Spaniards on that expedition, having amassed a great sum of spoils, asked Cortés for permission to carry it to their homeland, and Cortés granted it willingly. (g) Solís, wishing to give the lie to Bernal Díaz, says thus: “Whatever our historian may say to discredit this expedition (to Tlacopan), it was so important to the principal end that scarcely had Cortés returned to Texcoco when the caciques of Tucapan, of Mascalzingo, and of Auhtlan (so he calls Tuzapan, Mexicaltzinco, and Nauhtlan), and other peoples of the northern shore, came to him as suppliants to give obedience: which shows that the Spaniards returned with reputation, etc.” But setting aside the ambiguous expression northern shore, which readers unacquainted with the geography of that kingdom will perhaps understand of the shore of the lake, though it must be understood of that of the sea, and the error in saying that the lords of those places came to Texcoco, whereas we know from the testimony of Cortés that they sent their ambassadors there, it is certain that those lords could not have been induced to send such an embassy by the news of what had happened at Tlacopan, because their ambassadors arrived at Texcoco four days after that expedition, as Bernal Díaz, an eyewitness, affirms, and their cities were distant from that court more than 200 miles.

Yacapichtla. knowing that the greatest harm was done to that city by the

Mexicans who were in the garrison of Huaxtepec, a city situated on the mountains fifteen miles south of Chalco, he set out thither. On their march they were assailed by two large bodies of the enemy, but promptly defeated them, which was in great part due to the innumerable multitude of allies whom the Spaniards led with them. These entered Huaxtepec, and lodged in certain large houses to rest and tend the wounded; but immediately they had a fresh assault from the

Mexicans, which compelled them to take up arms again to repel them, as they did, pursuing them for more than three miles until they left them wholly routed. Then they returned to the city, where they rested two days. Huaxtepec was then a city famous no less for its excellent cotton manufactures than for its marvelous garden, of which we have already made mention.

From Huaxtepec Sandoval sent messengers to offer peace to the inhabitants of Yacapichtla, a very strong place six miles distant, situated on the summit of a mountain almost inaccessible to cavalry, and defended by a sufficient garrison of Mexicans; but his proposals having been rejected by them, he marched toward that city, determined to deal it a blow that should blunt their pride, and free the and that same avarice which made so many Spaniards perish in their exit from

Bk. X. quarter. The Tlaxcalans and the other allies were frightened at the sight of the difficulty and the danger; but Sandoval, animated by that great courage which shone in all his actions, resolved to die or conquer. He began to climb with his infantry, having at the same time to overcome both the roughness of the mountain and the multitude of enemies who defended it with a cloud of darts, of stones, and even of huge rocks, which although they broke in striking against the crags in between, yet their fragments wounded the Spaniards; but nothing was able to stop them until they entered the city, bathed in sweat and in blood, and the allies did the same after their example. The fatigue and the wounds so inflamed their anger, and with such fury did they hurl themselves against the enemy, that many, fleeing from the swords, threw themselves headlong down the cliffs of the mountain. So great was the blood that was shed there that it dyed a stream that ran there, and so fouled its waters that for more than an hour the victors could not use them to appease the great thirst that tormented them. (i) “This was,” says Cortés, “one of the most signal victories, in which the Spaniards gave the greatest proofs of their courage and of their constancy.” This day cost the life of Gonzalo Domínguez, one of the bravest soldiers of Cortés, whose loss was very keenly felt by all.

Irritated by the slaughter at Yacapichtla (*), the Mexicans armed promptly

(i) Bernal Díaz makes fun of Gómara for this account of the waters clouded with blood, and adds that they had no need to drink that water, since there were some springs of good water; but if these springs were in the same place as the fight, it is to be believed that they too remained stained with blood; if they were distant from that place, the Spaniards were not in a state to seek them. Bernal Díaz was not present on that expedition, and we ought to give more credence to the account of Cortés: “So great,” he says, “was the butchery which our Spaniards made of the enemy, and such the slaughter which the enemy made of themselves, throwing themselves headlong from that summit, that all those who were present affirm that a stream which encircled almost all that place remained tinted with blood for more than an hour, so that they could not drink of it.”

The Chalcas implored, as at other times, the aid of the Spaniards, and their messengers arrived just as Sandoval was returning from Yacapichtla with his army, exhausted, battered, and wounded. Cortés, ascribing with too great levity the repeated hostilities of the Mexicans against the Chalcas to negligence on the part of that incomparable commander, without wishing first to inform himself of his conduct, nor to hear him, nor to allow him a moment’s rest, commanded him to march at once to Chalco with those soldiers who were least wounded, to give aid to those allies. Sandoval was exceedingly vexed by this affront from his general, at a time when he should have expected from him the greatest praises; but so great was his prudence in dissembling the injury, and so great his promptness in obeying, as his courage had been in that arduous expedition.

est of the spoils, or, as I believe, for both, came from various places to serve in that war. Then, keeping always, as is to be believed, to that route which the Chalcas had represented in their painting, they set out through the southern mountains toward Huaxtepec, and saw near the road a very steep mountain, whose summit was occupied by a great multitude of women and children, and its foot by very many warriors, who, confiding in the natural strength of that place, mocked the Spaniards with howls and whistles. Cortés, unable to bear that mockery, had an assault made on the mountain from three sides; but they had scarcely begun to climb with great difficulty amid a storm of darts and stones when he called a retreat; for besides perceiving that the undertaking was rash, and more difficult than fruitful, an army of enemies was seen that was marching toward that quarter with the intent of assailing the Spaniards from behind while they should be most engaged in the assault. Cortés went to meet them with his troops well ordered. The battle lasted little, because the enemy, recognizing themselves inferior in force, quickly abandoned the field. The

He observed on a slope of the mountain two cavaliers, or commanding crags, defended by many warriors; but these, believ‐ Bk. X. ing that the Spaniards intended to make the assault from the opposite side, abandoned the crags and ran to where the danger seemed greater. Cortés, as one who knew well how to profit by all the conjunctures which fortune, or the heedlessness of his enemies, presented to him, ordered one of his captains to try to occupy with a competent number of soldiers one of those two crags, while he himself engaged the besieged on the opposite side. He began, then, to climb with the utmost toil; but when he reached a post as high as that where the enemy were, he saw the Spanish banner raised on one of the crags or cavaliers. The enemy, finding themselves attacked on two sides, and having already begun to feel the damage which the firearms did them, surrendered. Cortés received them with singular humanity; but required of them, as a necessary condition for obtaining pardon, that they should induce likewise to surrender those who occupied the first mountain, as in fact happened.

§ 10. Huaxtepec, Yauhtepec, and Xiuhtepec for the great and pleasant city Conquest of of Cuauhnahuac, (*) capital of the Tlahuica nation, more than thirty Cuauhnahuac. miles distant from Mexico toward the south. This city was very strong by its situation; for on one side it was surrounded by precipitous mountains, and on the other by a ravine about seven perches deep, where a stream ran. Cavalry could not enter it except by two roads, unknown at that time to the Spaniards, or by the bridges, if they had not been raised, when they appeared there.

Terror drew the citizens back from the defense, and put them to headlong flight toward the mountains; so that the allies burned without any opposition a good part of the city. The lord of it, who had fled with the others, fearing to be overtaken in the mountains by the Spaniards, took the resolution to surrender, protesting that he had not done so before because he was waiting for the anger of the Spaniards to be spent in the city, and, satisfied with other hostilities, to refrain from raging against his person.

Bk. X. the city of Xochimilco. This beautiful city, the largest after the courts of all those of the Mexican valley, was founded on the shore of the § 11. lake of Chalco, little more than twelve miles from the capital. Its Conquest       of

Xochimilco. population was very numerous, its temples many, its buildings magnificent, and singularly beautiful its gardens floating on the lake, whence it had the name of Xochimilco. (*) Like the capital, it had many canals, or ditches, and now, for fear of the Spaniards, they had made many entrenchments. As soon as they saw the army coming, they raised the bridges from the canals to make the entrance more difficult. The Spaniards divided the army into three squadrons to assail the city from as many sides; but everywhere they found great resistance, and could not storm the first ditch except after a terrible fight of more than half an hour, in which two Spaniards were killed and many wounded; but having at last overcome these obstacles, they entered the city, pressing hard upon the Xochimilcas, who from the boats in which they had taken refuge continued fighting until night. There were heard at times among the combatants certain voices asking for peace, but the Spaniards, being convinced that such voices were aimed at no other end than to gain time to put their families and goods in safety, and to receive the relief they were expecting from Mexico, pressed them harder, until, finding no resistance, they withdrew to rest and tend the wounded; but they had hardly begun to breathe when they saw themselves assailed by a great number of enemies, who came in battle order by that same street by which the Spaniards had entered. These were reduced to the greatest straits, and Cortés himself ran great danger of remaining a prisoner of the enemy; for his horse having fallen from exhaustion, as he says, or been thrown to the ground by the blows of the Xochimilcas, as other historians affirm, he continued fighting

Spaniards had leisure to rest somewhat from the toils of the day, in which some of their soldiers were killed, and almost all wounded, and their general himself, and the principal captains, Alvarado and Olid.

Four Spaniards taken prisoner were conducted to the capital, and without delay sacrificed, and their arms and legs sent to various places to encourage the subjects against the enemies of the state. There is no doubt that on this as on many other occasions Cortés could easily have been killed by his enemies, if they had not had that foolish eagerness to take him alive to sacrifice him to their gods.

The news of the capture of Xochimilco threw the court of Mexico into great consternation. King Cuauhtémoc summoned some military chiefs, and set before them the damage and the danger caused to

Mexico by the loss of so considerable a place, the service they would render to the gods and to the nation by recovering it, and the courage and the forces needed to defeat those bold and pernicious strangers.

Orders were therefore given at once to arm an army of twelve thousand men to be sent by land, and another to be sent by water; and this was carried out with such promptness that the Spaniards had scarcely rested from the fatigue of the day before when Cortés was warned by his sentinels of the march of

X. three columns, and gave his captains the most opportune orders; he left some troops as a garrison in the quarters, and commanded that twenty horse with five hundred Tlaxcalans should pass through the enemy to occupy a neighboring hillock, and there await his further orders to attack. The Mexican commanders came full of pride, displaying certain European swords taken from the Spaniards in the defeat of July 1. The battle was fought outside the city, and when it seemed good to Cortés he ordered the troop posted on the hillock to assail the Mexicans from behind. These, seeing themselves attacked on every side, fell into confusion and fled, leaving five hundred dead on the field. The Spaniards, returned to their quarters, learned that the troop left there had been in great danger because of the multitude of Xochimilcas who had fought it. Cortés, after having been three days in Xochimilco in frequent fights with the enemy, had fire set to the temples and houses, and went to the market, which was outside the city, to order his men for the march. The Xochimilcas, persuading themselves that their departure was an effect of fear, attacked the rear guard with loud cries; but they were so thoroughly beaten by the Spaniards that they did not dare to assail them again.

Cortés advanced with his army as far as Coyoacán, a large city situ‐ § 12. ated on the shore of the lake, six miles distant from Mexico toward March of the the south, with the intention of observing all those positions the bet‐ Spaniards   around the

He found the city deserted, and the next day went out from it to reconnoiter the road that led from that city as far as the causeway of Iztapalapa. He found there an entrenchment made by the Mexicans, and ordered the infantry to attack it, and in spite of the terrible resistance of the enemy who defended it they stormed it, ten Spaniards being wounded and some Mexicans killed. Tlacopan, being harassed on the way by some flying troops of the enemy, who attacked the baggage. In one of these fights, in which Cortés ran great danger, two of his servants were taken prisoner, who, being led to Mexico, were at once sacrificed. Cortés arrived at Tlacopan afflicted by such a misfortune; but his grief was increased when from the upper court of the great temple of that court he contemplated, together with other Spaniards, that fatal causeway on which some months before he had lost so many of his friends and soldiers, and considered attentively the great difficulties that must be overcome in order to make himself master of the capital. Some suggested to him that he should send his troops along that causeway to commit some act of hostility against the Mexicans; but he did not wish to expose them to so great a risk, and so, without remaining longer in that city, he returned by way of Tenayuca, Cuauhtitlan, Citlaltepec, and Acolman to Texcoco, having in this journey gone around all the lakes of the Mexican valley, and observed all that was needed in order to carry out successfully the great enterprise which he was meditating.

[p. 191] with those who a few days before had come from Spain in a ship that

Bk. X. put in at the port of Veracruz, laden with horses, arms, and munitions of war. Everything seemed to point to a happy outcome, when the enterprise fell into the greatest danger of being ruined. Certain Spanish soldiers, partisans of the governor of Cuba, moved by hatred of Cortés, or by envy of his glory, or, what seems more likely, by fear of the perils that awaited them in the siege of the capital, agreed secretly to take the life of Cortés, of his captains Alvarado, Sandoval, and Tapia, and of all those whom they saw more attached to the party of that general. The conspirators had not only determined the time and the manner of carrying out the blow safely, but had even chosen those on whom the vacant offices of general, judge, and captains were to be conferred; but one of the accomplices, repenting of his crime, opportunely revealed the treachery to Cortés. The general immediately had Antonio de Villafaña, the head of the conspiracy, seized and committed the examination of the culprit to a judge; and when the culprit frankly confessed his crime, he was hanged by sentence of justice from a window of the quarters. Toward the accomplices Cortés prudently dissembled, pretending not to believe them guilty and attributing to the malice of Villafaña the infamy that resulted against them from his confession; but so that in the future his life might not be so exposed to such dangers, he created a bodyguard composed of several soldiers, of whose fidelity and courage he was well assured, who accompanied him by day and by night and kept constant watch over the preservation of his person.

The conspiracy having thus been prevented by the punishment of § 14. its principal culprit, Cortés applied himself with greater activity to Last   preparations for

the siege of Mexico. giving the last touch to his great enterprise. was followed by the singing of the Te Deum with the music of the military instruments. All these demonstrations were owing to the great confidence that Cortés had in the brigantines for the success of his enterprise, without which, perhaps, he could never have brought it to a good end. He then held a review of his army, and found in it eighty-six horse and more than eight hundred Spanish foot, three large iron cannon, fifteen smaller ones of copper, a thousand Castilian pounds of musket powder, and a great quantity of balls and of arrows, the number and the strength of his little army having been doubled by the reinforcements that had come to him that year from Spain and from the islands of the Antilles. To encourage them he made them an address like the one he had already made when he left Tlaxcala. He sent messengers to this republic, to Cholula, to Huexotzinco, and to other cities, letting them know that the work on the brigantines was already finished and begging them to send him within ten days as many picked troops as they could, since the time had now come to lay siege to that proud court, which for so many years had oppressed their liberty. On Whit Monday (May 20) Cortés assembled his men in the main square of that court, to make the division of the army, to name the commanders, and to assign to each of them the place where he was to pitch his [p. 193] camp, and the troops that were to be under him, and to publish anew the military edict already published in Tlaxcala. He ordered Pedro de Bk. X. Alvarado to encamp in the city of Tlacopan, to prevent any relief

§ 15. from entering by that side for the Mexicans, and assigned him thirty Disposition of the horse, a hundred and sixty-eight Spanish foot, distributed in three army     in the siege of

the capital. companies under as many captains, and twenty-five thousand Tlaxcalans with two cannon of artillery. Cristóbal de Olid was named master of the camp and head of the division destined for the city of Coyoacán, and there were assigned to him thirty-three horse, a hundred and sixty-eight Spanish foot, under three other captains, with two cannon, and more than twenty-five thousand allies. To Gonzalo de Sandoval were given twenty-four horse, a hundred and sixty-three Spanish foot under two captains with two cannon, and the allies of Chalco, Huexotzinco, and Cholula, who numbered more than thirty thousand; and Cortés ordered him to go first to ruin the city of Iztapalapa, and then to encamp in whatever place should seem to him most suitable for the purpose of pressing the Mexicans. Cortés, in spite of the remonstrances made to him by his captains and soldiers, took command of the brigantines, since he judged his own assistance more necessary in them. He distributed among the thirteen brigantines three hundred and twenty-five Spaniards and thirteen falconets, assigning to each brigantine a captain, twelve soldiers, and as many rowers; so that the whole army destined to begin the siege of the capital consisted of nine hundred and seventeen Spaniards and more than seventy-five thousand men of auxiliary troops (q), whose number shortly after

(q) Herrera and Solís count a hundred thousand allies assigned to the three camps; Bernal Díaz, on the contrary, counts no more than twenty-four thousand, eight thousand for each camp. We give greater credence to Cortés, as one who better than anyone else knew the number of troops assigned to each commander. Solís says that Bernal Díaz complains many times that the allies gave them more hindrance than help; but this is false, for on the contrary the said Díaz often boasts of the great help they had from the allies, and of their courage in fighting against the Mexicans. Our friends the Tlaxcalans, he says in ch. 151, helped us very well throughout the whole war, like courageous men. His whole History is full of such expressions, as may also [p. 194] increased, as we shall see, to two hundred thousand and more. All the other

§ 16.

Olid and Alvarado departed together from Texcoco with their troops to go Execution of to the posts assigned them by the general. Among the most distinguished Xicotencatl. Tlaxcalans who accompanied Alvarado were the younger Xicotencatl and his

cousin Piltecuhtli. The latter was wounded in a quarrel that arose by a

Spaniard, who, imprudently disregarding the orders given them by the general and the respect due to that personage, might have brought about by his attack the desertion of the Tlaxcalans. The outrage greatly vexed them, and they made their indignation plain in certain demonstrations. Ojeda, their leader, tried to calm them, and gave Piltecuhtli leave to go and be treated in his native city. Xicotencatl, to whom, no less because of his position than because of his kinship, such an injury was more keenly felt than to anyone else, finding at the time no other way of avenging himself, secretly abandoned the army, and together with other Tlaxcalans took the road to his native city.

Alvarado promptly gave notice of it to Cortés, and the latter ordered Ojeda to overtake and seize him, and when he had been seized had him hanged publicly, either in the same city of Texcoco, (r) as Herrera and Torquemada say, or be seen from the letters of Cortés and the narrative of other historians. Bernal Díaz only says that in their retreats along the causeway of Tlacopan they were hampered by the auxiliary troops; but any numerous troop that wishes to make its retreat along a narrow road is hampered by its very multitude.

(r) Cortés makes no mention of this event of Xicotencatl: it may be believed that he had

some particular reason for passing over it in silence. Bernal Díaz affirms that Xicotencatl was going to Tlaxcala to seize the state of Chichimecatl while the latter was at the war; but this is altogether improbable. There are authors who say that he was drawn to Tlaxcala by the love of a lady. In my account of this event I follow Torquemada and Herrera, because they wrote on the manuscripts of Ojeda and of Camargo, who were quite well informed. To Solís it seems incredible [p. 195] or in a place near it, as Bernal Díaz affirms, a crier having first published the cause of his sentence, which was that of having deserted Bk. X. and of having stirred up the Tlaxcalans against the Spaniards. It is to be believed that Cortés did not risk the execution of such a punishment without having first obtained, as Herrera expressly affirms, the consent of the senate of Tlaxcala; which was not difficult, considering their severity in punishing crimes even in the most conspicuous persons, and the particular hatred they bore that prince, whose pride they could no longer endure. So resounding a punishment, which should naturally have stirred up the minds of the Tlaxcalans against the Spaniards, so terrified both them and the other allies that from then on they observed the laws of military service more punctually and kept themselves more subordinate to those foreign leaders, the Spaniards drawing profit even from their own faults; but the Tlaxcalans did not fear to make some demonstrations of esteem and veneration toward their prince, weeping for his death, distributing among themselves his garments as precious relics, and celebrating, as is to be believed, his obsequies with due magnificence. The family and goods of Xicotencatl were adjudged to the King of Spain and carried to Texcoco. In the family there were thirty wives, and among the goods a great quantity of gold.

that Xicotencatl was put to death in Texcoco: “because it would have been too great a risk for Cortés to resolve upon so violent an execution under the eyes of so great a number of Tlaxcalans, to whom the ignominious punishment inflicted on one of the foremost men of their nation must necessarily have been distressing;” but Cortés risked far more in imprisoning King Moctezuma in his own court, and under the eyes of an incomparably greater number of Mexicans, to whom that great affront done to the first man of their nation must without fail have been distressing. Meanwhile, while Alvarado and Olid were busy filling in some ditches that were on the shore of the lake and repairing some passes for the convenience of the cavalry, the commander (*) Sandoval, with the aforesaid number of Spaniards and with more than thirty-five thousand allies, set out from Texcoco on May 31 with the purpose of taking by assault the city of Iztapalapa, against which Cortés was particularly bent. Sandoval entered it, making a terrible slaughter with fire in the houses and with arms upon the inhabitants, who in terror sought to save their lives in the boats. Cortés, in order to attack at the same time that part of the city which was in the water, after having had the whole lake sounded, embarked with his men in the brigantines and sailed with sails and oars toward Iztapalapa. He cast anchor near an isolated hillock, not far from that city, whose summit was occupied by many enemies resolved

(s) Cortés landed there, and overcoming with a hundred and fifty men the roughness and difficulty of the ascent and the resistance of the enemy, he took the hill by storm, with the killing of all who defended it. (t) But hardly had they taken it when they saw a great fleet of boats (u) coming against them, summoned by the signals of the smoke that at the first appearance of the brigantines had been made both on that hill and in some temples of those surroundings. The Spaniards embarked at once and stood on the defensive without moving until, aided by a strong wind that opportunely arose, and increasing the speed of the brigantines by the impulse of the oars, they dashed against the boats, breaking some and capsizing others by the shock. Some of the enemy perished wounded by the balls, and many were drowned. All the other boats fled, pursued for more than eight miles by the brigantines as far as the capital.

have already said, at that angle which the causeway of Coyoacán formed with that of Iztapalapa. He fought by water and by land, and in spite of the bravery with which the Mexican garrison that was there defended itself, he nevertheless took it by storm, and with two great cannon of artillery made a horrible slaughter in the multitude that filled the lake and the causeway. That place, called Xoloc by the

Mexicans, seemed very advantageous to Cortés (x) for establishing his camp there, and in fact it was not easy to find another more suited to his designs; for in it he made himself master of the principal causeway, and of that part of the lake by which greater relief could enter the city, and besides, of the causeway of Coyoacán, for communication with Olid’s camp. The short distance of that place from the camps of Coyoacán and of Tlacopan was of great importance to

Cortés, in order to give his orders promptly and to bring aid wherever it was needed. Finally, the nearness to Mexico helped to facilitate the assaults. (y)

There he gathered the brigantines, and, abandoning the expedition against Iztapalapa, took the resolution to begin the assaults at once. He therefore had half the troops of Coyoacán brought to his camp, and fifty picked foot from the troops of Sandoval. That night a great crowd of enemies was heard coming toward that camp. The

Spaniards, knowing that the Mexicans were not accustomed to fight at night unless they were sure of victory, were terrified at first; but although they suffered some damage from the enemy, they

(x) Father Sahagún in his manuscript History of the conquest says that Cortés, by

means of certain persons of note among his prisoners, summoned the king and the nobility of Mexico to a place called Acachinanco, and he sets down the harangue that he made, setting forth to them the motives of the war; but such a conference seems to me neither true nor probable. Cortés, who relates in detail what he said to the

Mexicans and what the Mexicans said to him, would certainly not have omitted a thing so notable.

(y) Vetancurt gives it to be understood that Cortés encamped inside the city; but

this is altogether contrary to the truth, and to the account of Cortés himself, who affirms that his camp was half a league distant from the city. [p. 199] they nevertheless forced them, with the fire of the artillery and mus‐ Bk. X. kets, to retire to the city. The next day they found themselves assailed by a prodigious multitude of warriors, who with frightful shouts magnified their number in the imagination of the Spaniards. Cortés, the relief that he was awaiting from Coyoacán having opportunely arrived, made a sortie with his men drawn up in battle order. They fought on both sides with great courage and obstinacy; but the Spaniards and their allies took a ditch and an entrenchment, and with the artillery and the horses did the Mexicans so much harm that they obliged them to take refuge in the city; and because on the side of the lake that lay to the west of the causeway they were troubled by the Mexican boats, Cortés had a ditch of the causeway widened so that the brigantines could pass through it, and these hurled themselves impetuously against them, pursued them as far as the city, and set fire to some houses of the suburbs.

Meanwhile Sandoval, having happily completed, though not without great risk, the expedition of Iztapalapa, marched with his troops toward Coyoacán. On the road he was attacked by the troops of Mexicaltzinco; but he defeated them, and had fire set to their city. Cortés, aware of his march and of a great ditch that had recently been made in the causeway, sent him two brigantines to facilitate the passage of the army. The latter marched toward Coyoacán, and Sandoval went with ten horse to the camp of Cortés. When he arrived there he found those Spaniards in combat with the Mexicans. The fatigue of the journey and of the battle of Mexicaltzinco did not suffice to keep him from the fray. He fought as usual with courage, but in the fighting his leg was pierced by a dart, and along with him many other Spaniards were also wounded. These advantages gained by the Mexicans are not to be compared with the loss that they suffered that day, nor with the fear that the fire of the artillery caused them, which was so great that for many days they did not dare to approach the camp of the Spaniards. [p. 200] fights: the brigantines, circling around the city, set fire to many hous‐

Bk. X.

es of the suburbs, and in their forays discovered a large and deep canal by which they could enter the city at ease; which was of great advantage to the Spaniards in the sequel.

Alvarado for his part pressed the Mexicans as hard as he could, taking in frequent skirmishes some ditches and entrenchments of the causeway of Tlacopan; but some of his men were killed and many wounded. He observed that by the causeway of Tepeyacac, situated toward the north, relief was continually introduced into the city, and he perceived that by that causeway escape would be easy for the besieged, whenever they should find themselves unable to resist the besiegers any longer. He promptly made this known to Cortés, and the latter commanded Sandoval to go with a hundred and eighteen

Spanish foot and a very great number of allies to occupy that place, and thereby prevent the relief that came to the enemy. Sandoval obeyed, though still suffering from the wound in his leg, and took possession of that place without opposition, every communication by land with the other cities being from then on cut off for the

Mexicans. (*)

Bk. X. causeway with his numerous army well ordered and flanked by the brigantines, and having scarcely gone a little way he came upon a wide and deep ditch and an entrenchment more than ten feet high. The Mexicans courageously opposed their passage, but, driven back by the artillery of the brigantines, the Spaniards passed on, pressing them as far as the city, where they found another great ditch and a strong and high entrenchment. The force of the water in this ditch, the throng of enemies who had gathered to the defense, their frightful and threatening cries, and the thick rain of arrows, darts, and stones that they shot, held up for some time the resolution of the Spaniards; but having finally, with the discharge of all the artillery and of all the firearms, driven from the entrenchment those who defended it, the army passed over it, and advanced taking other ditches and entrenchments as far as a principal square of the city, which was full of people. In spite of the slaughter that they saw being made in the multitude by a great cannon planted at the entrance of the square, the Spaniards did not dare to enter it, until the general himself, reproaching them for that ignominious fear, and hurling himself intrepidly against the enemy, put courage into his soldiers. The Mexicans, terrified by so great an intrepidity, fled into the enclosure of the great temple, and seeing themselves still assailed there, took refuge in the upper courts of the temples, where they were likewise pursued; but suddenly the Spaniards found themselves attacked from behind by other Mexican troops, and put in such a strait that, being unable to sustain the fury of the enemy either within the enclosure of the temple or outside in the neighboring square, they were forced to retire to the causeway by which they had entered the city, leaving the cannon of artillery in the power of the enemy. Shortly after, three or four horse arrived opportunely in the square, and the Mexicans, persuaded that all the cavalry was coming against them, were thrown into confusion by the fear they had of those great and fiery beasts, and abandoned ignominiously

Spaniards. Ten or twelve Mexican nobles had fortified themselves in the upper court of the great temple; but in spite of their obstinate resistance they were overcome and killed by the assailants. The Spanish army in its retreat set fire to the largest and finest houses of the causeway of Iztapalapa, though not without very grave danger from the impetuosity with which the Mexicans fell upon the rear guard, and from the harm that they did it from the flat roofs. Alvarado and

Sandoval with their troops made a great slaughter of the Mexicans, and the allies earned on that day great praises from the Spanish general.

Bk. X. divided among the camps of Sandoval and of Alvarado. This aid from the Texcocans was soon followed by the confederation of the Xochimilcas and of the mountain Otomis with the Spaniards, which new troops increased Cortés’s army by twenty thousand men.

Nothing more was wanting to this general for the completion of the siege except to prevent the relief that was being introduced into the city by water. Keeping therefore seven brigantines, he sent the other six toward that part of the lake that lay between Tlacopan and Tepeyacac, so that from there they could easily give aid to the camps of Sandoval and of Alvarado, whenever those commanders should require it; and while not employed by them, should go cruising two by two, and try to capture all the boats that carried provisions or troops to the city.

Cortés, now finding himself with so great a number of allied troops, determined to make within three days an entry into the city. He gave therefore the necessary orders, and on the appointed day marched with the greater part of his cavalry, with three hundred Spanish foot, with seven brigantines, and with an innumerable multitude of allies. They found the ditches opened, the entrenchments rebuilt, and the enemy well prepared to resist; nevertheless, with the aid of the brigantines they took all the ditches and entrenchments that were there as far as the principal square of Tenochtitlan. There the army halted, Cortés not permitting them to advance further without leaving leveled all the difficult passes that he had taken; but while ten thousand allies were occupied in filling the ditches, the others applied themselves to burning and ruining some temples, houses, and palaces, and among others that of King Axayacatl, where the Spaniards had formerly had their quarters, and the celebrated palace of the birds of King Moctezuma. After these hostile acts, accomplished with great difficulty and with grave danger because of the efforts the Mexicans made to prevent them, Cortés sounded the retreat, which was carried out happily,

Alvarado and Sandoval did the same on their part. This day was without doubt one of great fatigue for the Spaniards and their allies, but also of unspeakable grief for the Mexicans, as much for the loss of so many fine buildings as for the taunts with which they were insulted by their own vassals confederated with the Spaniards, and by the

Tlaxcalans, their mortal enemies, who in fighting showed them the arms and legs of the Mexicans whom they had killed, and threatened to eat them that night at supper, as in fact they did.

Cortés sallied from his camp in the same manner as the day before; but in spite of his diligence the Mexicans had already rebuilt the greater part of the destroyed fortifications, and defended them with such obstinacy that the army of the besiegers could not take them except after a furious fight of five hours. The army advanced and took two ditches of the causeway of Tlacopan; but as the day was now about to end, it withdrew to its camp, still fighting the enemy troops, who were pressing upon the rear guard. The same combats that

Cortés’s army had were had by those of Sandoval and of Alvarado, the besieged having to fight at one and the same time against three most numerous armies, superior to them in arms, in horses, in brigantines, and in military discipline. Alvarado on his part had already ruined all the houses that stood on either side of the causeway of Tlacopan; (A)

for the population of the capital continued on that side up to the

Confederation of sevincreasing, who at this very time received one as advantageous to eral cities of the lake them as it was harmful to the enemy. The inhabitants of the cities sit‐ with the Spaniards. uated on the shore and on the islets of the lake of Chalco had until then been enemies of the Spaniards, and could have done much harm to Cortés’s camp if their troops had assailed it from one side of the causeway at the same time that the Mexicans assailed it from the other; but they had attempted no hostility against the Spaniards, perhaps because they reserved it for a more opportune occasion. The Chalcas and other allies, to whom the neighborhood of so many enemies was not convenient, tried to draw them to their party, now with promises and now with threats and vexations, and so much did their importunity avail, and perhaps also the fear of vengeance from the Spaniards, that there came to Cortés’s camp to confederate with him the nobles of Iztapalapa, of Mexicaltzinco, of Colhuacan, of Huitzilopochco, of Mixquic, and of Cuitláhuac, which cities were a considerable part of the Mexican valley. Cortés rejoiced infinitely at that alliance, and asked of them not only that they should help him with their troops and their boats, but also that they should bring materials for making huts along that causeway, because, it being the rainy season, his men suffered too much from lack of shelter.

All this was so well carried out by them that they immediately placed Bk. X. under Cortés’s orders a considerable body of troops, whose number is

not stated, and three thousand boats to help the brigantines in their course, in which they promptly transported the necessary materials, and built so many huts that all the Spaniards could stay in them comfortably, together with two thousand Indians employed in their service; for the bulk of the allied troops was encamped at Coyoacán, four miles distant from Xoloc; and, not content with such great aid, they brought to Cortés’s camp many provisions, and chiefly fish and cherries in great quantity.

Cortés, finding himself thus with his forces so increased, entered the city with them two or three days in succession, making a considerable slaughter of the citizens. He persuaded himself that the besieged must surrender, seeing themselves faced with so excessive a number of troops and experiencing the pernicious effects of their obstinate resistance; but he was deceived, for the Mexicans were resolved to lose their lives before their liberty. He resolved, however, to make continual entries into the city in order to compel them by incessant hostilities to ask for the peace that they refused. He formed of his vessels two flotillas, each composed of three brigantines and of fifteen hundred boats, ordering them to approach the city, to set fire to the houses, and to do the Mexicans all the harm possible. He ordered Sandoval and Alvarado to do the same on their part, and he himself, with all his Spaniards and, as it seems, with eighty thousand allies (B), marched as usual along the causeway of Iztapalapa toward the city, without being able to obtain, either on this or on other entries of those days, any other advantages than that of gradually diminishing the number of the enemy, ruining some buildings, and

prowess of in which from then on he maintained a garrison in spite of the violent Tzilacatzin. assaults of the Mexicans. He had likewise taken some ditches and entrenchments, and knowing that the greatest strength of the enemy was in Tlatelolco, where King Cuauhtémoc resided, and where an infinite number of people from Tenochtitlan had taken refuge, he directed his operations toward that quarter; but although he fought with all his forces by land and by water, he could not advance as far as he wished, because of the stubborn opposition of the besieged, in which fights many perished on both sides.

In one of the first skirmishes a sturdy and courageous Tlatelolca showed himself, disguised as an Otomi, with an Ichcahuepilli, or cotton cuirass, and without other arms than a shield and three stones, and running very swiftly toward the besiegers he hurled the three stones in succession with such dexterity and such force that with each one he struck down a Spaniard, causing no less indignation to the Spaniards than fear and wonder to their confederates. They used every diligence to get him into their hands; but they could never catch him, because in all the fights he appeared differently dressed, and in all did great harm to the besiegers, having moreover as much speed in his feet to save himself as strength in his arms to attack. The name of this celebrated Tlatelolca was Tzilacatzin.

Alvarado, puffed up by some advantages gained over the Mexicans, wished one day to advance as far as the market square: he had already taken some entrenchments and some ditches, and among others one that was more than fifty feet wide and more than seven deep, and, forgetting in his good fortune to have it filled up, as his general had ordered him, he advanced with forty or fifty Spaniards and some allies.

This misfortune greatly vexed Cortés, as one that was bound to increase the spirit and the pride of the enemy, and he betook himself at once to Tlacopan to reprove Alvarado severely for his disobedience and his rashness; but being informed of the courage with which he had conducted himself on that day and of the fact that he had made himself master of the most difficult posts, he contented himself with a gentle admonition, impressing his orders on him concerning the manner of making the entries.

They sent a secret embassy to King Cuauhtémoc, protesting their inviolable fidelity to the crown, and complaining of the Spaniards, who forced them to take up arms against their natural lord, and adding that they wished on their first entry to unite with the Mexicans against those enemies of the country to kill them all, and thus put an end to so many calamities. The king praised their purpose, assigned them the posts they were to occupy, and even sent them gifts in return, to reward their pretended fidelity. These traitors entered the city, as they were wont to do, and feigning at first to turn their arms against the Spaniards, they then began to sack the houses of the

It was now twenty days that the Spaniards had been making con‐

§ 24. tinual entries into the city; whence some captains and soldiers, weary Victory of the

Mexicans. of so many fights, the fruit of which they still saw far off, complained to the general and entreated him to venture all the great forces he had on one decisive stroke, which would finally draw them out of so many perils and hardships. Their design was to advance as far as the center of Tlatelolco, where the Mexicans had gathered their forces, in order to ruin them utterly in a single day, or at least to induce them to surrender. Cortés, who knew very well how dangerous such an enterprise was, tried to dissuade them from it with the most effective arguments; but, nothing availing, and being unable besides to resist a counsel that had become almost general, he yielded at last to their importunate entreaties. He ordered the commander Sandoval to go with a hundred and fifteen foot and ten horse to join Alvarado, to place the cavalry in ambush and have the baggage removed, feigning to depart and to abandon the siege of the city, so that the Mexicans, lured into pursuing them, should be attacked from behind by the cavalry; that with the six brigantines he should try to make himself master of that great ditch where Alvarado had been defeated, having it filled and leveled; that he should not take a step forward without leaving the way well prepared for the retreat, and that he should strive to enter the market square by force of arms.

On the appointed day for the general assault Cortés marched with twenty-five horse, with all his infantry, and with more than a hundred thousand allies. His brigantines, with more than three thousand auxiliary boats, formed the wings of his army on either side of the causeway. He entered the city without any opposition, and at once divided his army into three parts, so that by as many streets they might arrive at the same hour at the market square. The command of the first division was given to Julián de Alderete, the king’s treasurer, who

Ancient History of Mexico, Vol. III.       Dd [p. 210] had been the one who with greatest zeal had urged Cortés to underBk. X. take this expedition, and he was ordered to proceed by the main and

widest street with seventy Spanish foot, seven horse, and twenty thousand allies. Of the other two streets that led from the main causeway of Tlacopan to the market square, the less narrow was assigned to the captains Andrés de Tapia and Jorge de Alvarado (brother of Pedro de Alvarado) with eighty Spanish foot and more than ten thousand allies, and Cortés himself took charge of the other, narrower and more difficult, with a hundred Spanish foot and the bulk of the auxiliary troops, leaving at the entrance of each street the cavalry and the artillery. All entered at one stroke, fighting courageously. The

Mexicans made at first some resistance, but then, feigning cowardice, they retired, abandoning the ditches to the Spaniards, in order that the latter, lured by the hope of victory, might advance to greater perils. Some Spaniards pressed on to the streets nearest the market square, incautiously leaving behind a wide ditch badly filled, and when, being more encouraged, they were vying to be the first to enter that square, they heard the formidable sound of the horn of the god

Painalton, which was sounded by the priests in cases of public and pressing need to rouse the people to take up arms. There ran up at once so great a multitude of Mexicans, and fell with such fury upon the Spaniards and the allies, that it threw them into confusion and forced them to turn precipitately back as far as the ditch (C), apparently filled with fascines and other light materials, and, wishing to pass over it, they sank through the weight and the violence of the crowd. [p. 211] of the fugitives; for, being unable to swim across and defend themselves at the same time, they were wounded and taken by the Bk. X. Mexicans. Cortés, who with the diligence proper to a good general had come to the ditch when the routed troops arrived there, tried to stop them with his shouts, so that they should not by their disorder facilitate the slaughter begun to be made by the enemy; but what voices are capable of restraining the flight of a confused multitude, to which fear lends speed? Pierced by the keenest grief for the loss of his men, and heedless of his own danger, he approached the ditch to rescue those he could. Some came out unarmed, others wounded, and others half drowned. He tried to put them in order and to start them toward the camp, remaining himself behind with twelve or twenty men to guard their rear; but he had scarcely begun to march when he found himself in a narrow pass surrounded by the enemy. That day would have been his last, in spite of the extraordinary courage with which he defended himself, and together with his life all hope of the conquest of Mexico would have been lost, if the Mexicans, instead of giving him death, as they easily could, had not been intent on taking him alive, to honor with so illustrious a victim their gods. They had already taken him, and were leading him without delay to the sacrifice, if his men, warned of his captivity, had not promptly come to free him. Cortés owed his life and his liberty chiefly to a soldier of his guard called Cristóbal de Olea, a man of great courage and singular skill in arms, (*) who on another occasion had delivered him from a like danger, and in this one saved him at the cost of his own life, cutting off with a stroke of his sword the arm of that Mexican who had seized him. Cortés was also indebted for his liberty to the prince Don Carlos Ixtlilxochitl, and to a brave Tlaxcalan called Temacatzin.

At length the Spaniards got out, though with great difficulty and Bk. X.

with not a few wounds, onto the wide causeway of Tlacopan, where

Cortés was able to put them in order, taking the rear guard himself with the cavalry; but the boldness and fury with which the Mexicans pursued them were such that it seemed to them impossible to escape with their lives. Those who had entered by the other two streets had had terrible fights; but because they had been more diligent in stopping up the ditches, their retreat was less difficult, when Cortés gave them the order to march to the great square of Tenochtitlan, where they assembled. From there they saw, to their very great distress, rising from the braziers of the great temple the smoke of the copal that the Mexicans burned in thanksgiving for the victory won; but their grief increased further when they saw some heads of Spaniards thrown toward them by the Mexicans to dishearten them, and heard it said that the commanders Alvarado and Sandoval had been killed.

From the square they took the causeway of Iztapalapa to their camp, pressed continually by a great multitude of enemies.

Alvarado and Sandoval had striven to enter the market square by a street that led from that of Tlacopan to Tlatelolco, and had happily advanced their operations as far as a post not far from that square; but having seen the sacrifices of some Spaniards, and heard from the

Mexicans that Cortés and his captains had been killed, they retired with the utmost difficulty; for to those enemies who had been fighting them before were added those who had defeated Cortés’s troops.

The loss that the besiegers suffered that day was seven horse, many arms and boats, and a cannon of artillery, more than a thousand allies, and more than sixty Spaniards, partly killed in the battle and partly taken prisoner and immediately sacrificed in the great temple of Tlatelolco in sight of Alvarado’s men. The captain of a brigantine was also killed. Cortés received a wound

The Mexicans celebrated the victory for eight continuous days with illuminations and music in the temples; they made the fame fly through the whole kingdom, and had the heads of the slain Spaniards carried through the provinces to frighten those that had rebelled against the crown and to recall them to their obedience, as in fact they obtained it from some. They dug out the ditches anew, repaired the entrenchments, and restored the city, except the temples and the houses ruined by the enemy, to the state in which it had been before the siege began.

soon as they saw the boats, ran after them, but just when they were most engaged in pursuing them, the brigantines struck against the stakes, and at the same moment the thirty large boats came out and assailed them on every side. The Spaniards ran great danger of losing their lives together with their vessels; but while with the fire of their muskets they held the enemy back, some skillful swimmers found time to pull up the stakes, and so, freed from that encumbrance, they were able to use their artillery to put the boats to flight. The brigantines were left badly damaged, and the Spaniards wounded; and of the two captains who commanded them, one was killed in the fray, and the other died within three days of his wounds. The Mexicans repaired their boats to repeat the stratagem; but Cortés, secretly informed of the place where they lay in ambush, prepared an ambush of his own of six brigantines, and, profiting by the enemy's example, ordered that one brigantine should approach the place where the boats were lying in ambush and, when it discovered them, should take to flight toward the spot where the Spaniards were hidden. It all happened as Cortés had planned; for the Mexicans, seeing the brigantine, promptly came out of ambush, and just when they thought themselves surest of their prey, the other five brigantines came out against them and at once began to play their artillery, with whose first discharge they overturned some boats and threw the rest into disorder. Se ad una tal risoluzione fossero stati ridotti non già dalla superstizione, ma dall’ onore, © dall'amor della patria, e della propria libertà, non farebbono (tati tanto biasimzvoli , perchè quantunque incvitabile prevedéfsero la loro rovina, continuando la guerra,

Spaniards did not enter that court to commit hostilities, it would suffice merely to cut off their relief to make them die [p. 215] of hunger; that they could still avoid the disasters that threatened them; that if they consented to the proposals of peace, he would at Bk. X. once cause all hostilities to cease, the king would remain in peaceful possession of the crown, with all the greatness, all the power, and all the authority which he had hitherto enjoyed, and his subjects would remain free and masters of all their goods, without his requiring anything more from His Majesty or from his subjects than the homage due to the King of Spain, as supreme lord of that empire, whose rights had already been recognized by the Mexicans themselves, as resting on the ancient tradition of their ancestors; that if on the contrary he persisted in the war, he would be deprived of the crown, the greater part of his vassals would lose their lives, and that fine and great city would be utterly ruined. The king consulted his councilors, the generals of the army, and the heads of religion; he laid before them the subject of the embassy, the state of that court, the scarcity of provisions, the affliction of the people, and the still greater evils that threatened them, and commanded them to say freely what they thought. Some, foreseeing the outcome of the war, inclined toward peace; others, spurred by hatred of the Spaniards or by the incentive of honor, advised war. The priests, whose authority in this matter as in others was held in the highest respect, strongly opposed peace, alleging several pretended oracles of their gods, whose anger was to be feared if they yielded to the demands of those cruel enemies of their worship, and whose protection had to be sought with prayers and sacrifices. This opinion prevailed in the end, through the superstitious fear that had taken possession of their minds, and in accordance with it the Spanish general was answered that he should continue the war, since they had resolved to defend themselves to their last breath. Had they been brought to such a resolution not by superstition but by honor, by love of their country and of their own liberty, they would not have been so blameworthy, because although they foresaw their ruin as inevitable by continuing the war,

they

they had no hope of improving their fortune by peace. The experience of past events did not allow them to trust the promises that were made to them, so that it had to seem to them more consonant with their ideas of honor to die with arms in hand in defense of their country and of liberty than to abandon that same country to the ambition of those strangers, and to reduce themselves by their surrender to a sad and wretched servitude.

Malinalco, who, as these messengers asserted, wished to ally themselves with the Cohuixcas, a rather numerous nation, in order to destroy Cuauhnahuac, because it had allied itself with the Spaniards, and then to cross the mountains and come with a great army to attack Cortés's camp. This general, although he was in a position to ask for help rather than to give it, nevertheless, for the reputation of the

Spanish arms, and to forestall the blow with which he was threatened, sent Captain Andrés de Tapia with the messengers, with two hundred

Spanish foot, ten horse, and a good number of allies, giving him orders to unite with the troops of Cuauhnahuac and to do whatever he should judge conducive to the service of his king and to the safety of the Spaniards. Tapia carried out what was enjoined upon him by his general, and in a small place situated between Cuauhnahuac and

Malinalco he fought a great battle with the enemy, routed them, and pursued them to the foot of the high mountain on which stood the city of Malinalco. He could not assault it, as he would have liked, because the mountain was inaccessible to cavalry; but he laid waste the countryside, and since the term of ten days prescribed to him was nearly complete, he returned to Cortés's camp.

Matlatzincas, a powerful and warlike nation of the [p. 217] same valley, who were making continual war upon them, had burned one of their towns and had taken many of them prisoner, and who, Bk. X. besides this, had agreed with the Mexicans to attack Cortés's camp with all their forces from the mainland side at the same time as the Mexicans should attack it from the side of the city. On entering Mexico, the Spaniards had sometimes heard the Mexicans threaten them with the power of the Matlatzincas, and Cortés now perceived, from the report of the Otomis, the great danger he would run if he gave the enemy time to carry out their design. He would entrust this important expedition to no one but the brave and invincible Sandoval. This tireless man, although he had been wounded on the day of Cortés's defeat, had in the days that followed acted as general, going ceaselessly around all three camps and giving the most opportune orders for their security. Scarcely fourteen days had passed since the defeat when he marched toward the Valley of Toluca with eighteen horse, a hundred Spanish foot, and sixty thousand allies. On the way they saw some signs of the slaughter made there by the Matlatzincas, and when they entered the valley they found a place freshly ruined, and saw the enemy troops going laden with spoils, which they abandoned as soon as the Spaniards appeared, wishing to be less encumbered for the battle. They crossed a river that traverses the valley, and remained on its bank to await the Spaniards. Sandoval crossed it intrepidly with his army, attacked the enemy, put them to flight, and pursued them for a good nine miles to a city where they took refuge, leaving more than a thousand Matlatzincas dead on the field. Sandoval besieged the city and forced the enemy to abandon it and to take shelter in a fortress built on the top of a steep mountain. The victorious army entered the city, and after sacking it they set fire to the buildings; and because it was late and the troops were too weary, the assault on the fortress was put off until the next day, when, expecting to have

Ancient History of Mexico, Vol. III.   Ee [p. 218] a great struggle, they found the fortress empty. Sandoval resolved to Bk. X.

pass, on his return, through some places that had likewise declared themselves hostile; but he had no need to use arms against them, for, frightened at seeing so great an army come against them, swelled with numerous Otomi troops, they surrendered at once. Sandoval received them with the utmost kindness, and asked of them that they induce the Matlatzinca nation to make friendship with the Spaniards, pointing out to them the advantages they could hope to have from them and, on the contrary, the evils that enmity would bring upon them.

These expeditions were of the greatest importance; for four days after Sandoval had returned there arrived at Cortés's camp several lords of the Matlatzincas, of Malinalco, and of the Cohuixcas (E) to ask pardon for their hostilities and to establish a confederation, which was as useful to the Spaniards as it was harmful to the Mexicans.

The Spaniards no longer had enemies to fear on the side of the mainland, and Cortés had at his disposal so excessive a number of troops that he could have employed in the siege of Mexico many more people than Xerxes sent against Greece, had the situation of that capital not made so great a multitude of besiegers rather an encumbrance. The Mexicans, on the contrary, found themselves abandoned by their friends and by their subjects, surrounded by enemies, and afflicted by famine. That unfortunate court had against it, besides the Spaniards, the kingdom of Acolhuacan, the republics of Tlaxcala, of Huexotzinco, and of Cholula, almost all the cities of the Valley of

Mexico, and the very numerous nations of the Totonacs, the Mixtecs, the Otomis, the Tlahuicas, the Cohuixcas, the Matlatzincas, and others; so that besides

§ 28. against the Matlatzincas, the Tlaxcalan Chichimecatl also gave proof A memorable deed of of his own against the Mexicans. This famous general, when he saw General

> “. 2s. Fatro memo-rabile del Generale Chichiîmecarl ,

Chichimecatl. that the Spaniards after the defeat were keeping on the defensive, resolved to make an entry into Mexico with his Tlaxcalans alone. He left, then, the camp of Alvarado, where he had always been since the beginning of the siege, accompanying the Spaniards in all the fights and ever making his bravery conspicuous. This time he carried all the ditches that were on the causeway of Tlacopan, and, leaving four hundred archers on guard at the most dangerous one, so that they might secure the passage on the retreat, he entered the city with the main body of his troops, where he had a terrible fight with the Mexicans, in which many were killed and wounded on both sides. The Mexicans flattered themselves that they could defeat him at the passage of the ditch, and pressed him hard in his retreat; but thanks to the archers posted on the other bank of the ditch, he crossed back happily with his Tlaxcalans, and returned full of glory to their camp.
