(F) Bernal Díaz says that after the defeat the Spaniards were left abandoned by their allies, who, out of the fear that the Mexicans put into them with certain threats which they made them in the name of their gods, all went away to their homes; that in Cortés's camp there remained no one but the prince Don Carlos with forty Texcocans; in Sandoval's, a lord of Huexotzinco with fifty men; and in Alvarado's, General Chichimecatl with eighty Tlaxcalans. But this cannot be, because two days after that defeat Captain Tapia set out from Cortés's camp to make war on the people of Malinalco, and took many allies with him, as the same Bernal Díaz affirms. Twelve days after Tapia, Commander Sandoval set out from the same camp with sixty thousand allies, as Cortés says. At the time when Sandoval was making war on the Matlatzincas, that is, sixteen or eighteen days after the defeat, General Chichimecatl made his famous entry, and he could not have made it without many thousands of Tlaxcalans. It is certain that not all the allies went away, and that if some did go away they returned at once, because within a few days there was in the three camps, and especially in Cortés's, a number of them far greater than there had been before the defeat. Cortés says nothing of such a desertion, and it is not very likely that he would have omitted it in recounting his misfortunes to the king.

Alvarado's camp one night; but having been heard in time by the sentinels, the Spaniards and the allies ran to arms. The fight lasted three hours, during which time Cortés, having heard a cannon shot from his camp, and suspecting what it in fact was, thought this a fitting occasion to make an entry into the city with his men, who were by now healed of their wounds. The Mexicans who had gone to Tlacopan, being unable to overcome the resistance of the Spaniards, returned to the city, where they found Cortés's army; they fought with ardor, but without any considerable advantage on either side.

At this same time, when the need of arms and munitions was greatest, a ship put in at Veracruz that brought the Spaniards a fresh relief, with which they were placed in a position to continue their operations. Prince Don Carlos Ixtlilxochitl had advised the Spanish general not to engage in new assaults, in which his army would have to suffer too much; that without exposing himself to so many ills, and without ruining the beautiful buildings of that capital, he could make himself master of it merely by preventing the entry of provisions; for the greater the number of the besieged, the sooner they would consume the few provisions they had. This wise counsel, all the more valuable as it was the less to be expected from a prince who by his age and his intrepidity longed for occasions to make his courage shine, pleased Cortés so much that, unable to restrain himself, he ran to embrace him, signifying his gratitude to him in singular expressions. He held to such counsel for some days; but then, weary of the length of the siege, he returned to the former hostilities; but before continuing them he offered peace anew to the Mexicans, making them a comparison of the forces of the one side and of the other, and repeating the reasons which he had already on another occasion proposed to them.

and the bravery of side and the other of the street, both to avoid the harm which the flat some women. roofs did to his troops, and to constrain the besieged by such hostilities to accept his proposals. He therefore solicited, and obtained from the allied lords, some thousands of peasant laborers provided with the necessary tools for demolishing the buildings and filling the ditches. In the following days he made several entries into the city with his Spaniards and brigantines, and with more than a hundred and fifty thousand allies, destroying buildings, filling ditches, and diminishing by slaughter the number of his enemies, though not without grave danger to his own person and to his men; for he very nearly was taken prisoner, and would have been had his soldiers not come to his aid, and his troops were at times obliged to withdraw by flight from the fury of the Mexicans; some Spaniards and allies perished there; and two brigantines were already almost overwhelmed by a fleet of canoes, but another brigantine that came up drew them out of the danger.

The bravery of some Spanish women (*) became famous in these entries; they had voluntarily accompanied their husbands to the war, and by the continual hardships they suffered, and by the examples of valor which they had ever before their eyes, they had become soldiers. They stood guard, they marched with their husbands armed with cotton corselets, with buckler and sword, and they threw themselves intrepidly into the midst of the enemy, increasing, in spite of their sex, the number of the besiegers.

From a Mexican lady taken in the last assault the Spanish general learned the miserable state of the city, owing to the want of provisions and the discord that existed among the besieged; for the king, his relatives, and many nobles had determined to die rather than surrender, but the people were disheartened and weary of the siege. This was confirmed by two deserters of middling rank, who, driven by hunger, came to Cortés's camp.

On these tidings Cortés resolved to let no day pass without entering the city until he should carry it or ruin it; so he returned there on the 25th with his army, and carried a broad street in which there was a ditch so great that in the whole day it could not be filled or stopped up. They demolished or burned all the houses that were in that part, in spite of the resistance of the enemy. The Mexicans, seeing the allies employed in tearing down the buildings, said to them: “Ruin them, you traitors, ruin those houses, for afterwards you will have the labor of rebuilding them.” “We,” the allies answered, “shall surely rebuild them, if you are the victors; but

X. your enemies may live in them.” Now, unable to repair the buildings, the Mexicans made some small wooden fortifications in the streets, in order to harm the besiegers from them, as they had harmed them before from the flat roofs, and to hinder the cavalry they filled the square with stones; but the besiegers made use of them to fill up the ditches.

In the entry made there on the 26th, two great ditches which the Mexicans had newly made were carried. Alvarado for his part was advancing every day farther into the city; and on the 27th he went so far, carrying several ditches and entrenchments, that he came to occupy two towers near the palace where King Cuauhtémoc resided; but he could not thence pass farther, as he wished, because of the extreme difficulty he found in the ditches and the vigorous resistance of the enemy, who forced him to retire, pressing furiously upon his rear guard. Cortés, having observed an extraordinary smoke that rose from those towers, and suspecting what had in fact happened, entered the city, as he was accustomed to do, and spent the whole day in repairing all the bad passages. He now lacked no more than one canal and one entrenchment to enter the market square. He determined to advance as far as that, as in fact he accomplished, and that was the first time since the siege began that his troops joined with those of Alvarado, with unspeakable joy on both sides. Cortés entered that square with some cavalry, and found there an innumerable people lodged in the porticoes, because they could not be contained in the houses of that ward. He climbed the temple, from which he observed the city, and saw that of its eight parts only one remained to be carried. He had fire set to the high and beautiful towers of that temple, in which, as in the greater one of Tenochtitlan, the idol of the god of war was worshiped. The Mexican commoners, on seeing that great flame, which seemed to rise to heaven, raised a great lament. Cortés, moved to pity at seeing so numerous a people

again to the besieged, that they might surrender; but they replied that they would never do so, that in case a single Mexican remained alive, he would continue the defense till death.

> (H) Sì disse, secondochè scrive Cortés, che tosto che quel Signore fi presentò a Quauhbtemotzin per esporgli le proposizioni di pace , fu sacrificato per ordine di quel Re; ma siccome questo fatto non ha altro fonda» mento, the quel rumore vago, non è degno della nostra fede.

After four days had then passed without fighting, Cortés entered

§ 30. the  city anew, and there he came upon a great throng of wretched The lamentable state of the Mexicans. men, of women, and of children, weak, emaciated, and almost dying of hunger, which was so great that many lived only on herbs and marsh roots, on insects, and even on the bark of trees. Moved to pity, that general commanded his troops that they should do them no harm; he passed to the market square, and found the porticoes filled with disarmed people: a manifest sign of the dejection of the people, and of the displeasure with which they endured the obstinacy of the king and of the nobility. The greater part of that day was spent in negotiations for peace; but Cortés, seeing that this availed nothing, gave order to Commander Alvarado to advance by force of arms along a great street where there were more than a thousand houses, and he himself with all his army went to assail them from another side. So great was the slaughter which they made that day among the besieged that, between dead and prisoners, there were more than twelve thousand. The allies were so cruel against those unhappy victims that they spared them neither for age nor for sex, the severe orders of the general not sufficing to restrain their cruelty.

The next day Cortés returned with all his forces; but he commanded that no harm should be done to the besieged, both for the compassion which the sight of their miseries caused him, and for the hope he had of inducing them to surrender. The Mexicans, seeing so great a number of troops coming against them, and among them their own subjects, who had formerly served them and now threatened them with death, finding themselves now reduced to such misery and calamity, and having before their eyes so many lamentable objects, for [p. 225] they had nowhere even to set foot except upon the corpses of their fellow citizens, they vented their rage in horrible cries, and demanded Bk. X. death as the only remedy for their ills. Some commoners begged Cortés to confer with certain nobles who were defending an entrenchment, in order to treat of some accommodation. Cortés went to them, although he had little hope of success. These were precisely some of those who could no longer bear the hardships of the siege; so that when they saw the Spanish general approach them, moved by despair they said to him: “If you are the son of the Sun, as some imagine, why, when your Father is so swift that in the brief space of a day he completes his course, do you take so long to free us from so many ills by death? We wish indeed to die, in order to go to heaven, where our god Huitzilopochtli awaits us to give us rest from our labors and the reward of our services.” Cortés proposed to them various reasons to move them to surrender; but as they answered that this was neither in their power nor had they any hope of being able to persuade the king, he withdrew, in order to urge him by means of a distinguished personage whom he had made prisoner three days before, and who was an uncle of the king of Texcoco. That man, although wounded, was charged with betaking himself to Tlatelolco to treat of that business with the king; but no other fruit of his embassy was seen than the reiterated outcries with which the people demanded death. (H) Some Mexican troops hurled themselves desperately against the Spaniards, but they were so weakened by hunger that the harm they did was slight, and too great that which they received from their enemies.

Cortés returned the next day to the city, expecting at every moment that the Mexicans would surrender, and, without permitting any harm to be done them, he addressed himself to

certain principal men who were in an entrenchment, already known to him since the first time he was at that court, and asked them why

§ 31. they wished to defend themselves so obstinately, when they could no Vain efforts toward the surrender of the longer resist and found themselves in such a state that with a single

Mexicans. blow he could take the lives of all. They replied that they saw very well that their ruin was inevitable, and would have wished to prevent it, but they could not, because it was not for them to deliberate.

Nevertheless they offered to beg the king to be willing to hear the proposals of peace. In fact they went at once to the palace, and after a little while returned, saying that, because it was late, the king could not come, and that they did not doubt that the day following he would be with Cortés in that same square. In the center of it there was a great square platform of earth, where the Mexicans held their theatrical representations, as we have said elsewhere. On this stage

Cortés had carpets and low platforms placed for holding the desired conference, and had a good meal prepared for the king and for the nobility who were to accompany him. When the day came, he sent word to the king that he was awaiting him in that place; but the king sent him five very authoritative personages, excusing himself from coming in person on account of a certain indisposition that he had, and because he did not trust the Spaniards. Cortés received them with the utmost kindness, gave them a stately banquet, and sent them back to the king, that they might beg him in his name to be willing to come to that place without fear; since he pledged his word to respect, as was fitting, his royal person; that his presence was absolutely necessary, and without it nothing could be concluded; and he accompanied this embassy with a gift of provisions, which was then the most valuable thing. The ambassadors, after having made known at the meal the great need they suffered, went away, and two hours later returned, bringing Cortés a gift of very fine garments which the king sent him, and repeating the aforesaid excuses. Three days passed in these negotiations without any fruit.

[p. 227]

> Cortès avea dato ordine agli alleati di starsene ‘fuori della Città , perchè i Messicani l' aveano pregato di non per. Lis Xmettere , che v' interveniflero , allorchè si tenesse la conferenza col Re; ma ora avendo perduta ogni speranza d' ac- Teibil comodamento, richiamò tutte le truppe del suo Campo, nel. conflitto, le quali cerano più di cencinquanta mila uomini , e quel. Gore le ancora del campo d'Alvarado, e con tutte queste forza de' Mel insieme fi mile a combattere certi fossi e trinciere, ch” erano ficani, le maggiori fortificazioni, che restavano a' Messicani, e ad un ora Sandoval col suo esercito afsalì la Città dalla banda di Tramontana + Questa fu la giornata più infaulta per quella Cictà , nella quale fi sparse più copiosamente che mai il sangue Messicano, non avendo ormai quegli infelici Cittadini nè ar» mi per rispignere la moltirudine e la furia de' lor nemici, nè forze per difendersi, nè anche terra per combattervi , Il suolo della Città era coperto di cadaveri, e l’acqua de' fofsi è de'canali era tinta di sangue . Non fi vedeva altro, che rovina & strage, nè altro sì sentiva, che pianti lagrimevoli, e clamori di disperazione . Gli Alleati incrudelirono talmente contra quella gente miserabile, che più .s' affaticavano gli Spagnuoli nel contener la lor crudeltà, che nel combattere co' loro nemici . La strage, che in quella giornata fì fece ne’ Messicani fu sì grande, che tra morti e prigionieri, per quel che dice lo steslo Cortès, oltrepassò le quaranta mila persone .

Cortés had given orders to the allies to stay outside the city, be‐

Bk. X. cause the Mexicans had begged him not to permit them to take part when the conference with the king should be held; but now, having § 32. lost all hope of an accommodation, he recalled all the troops of his A      terrible conflict,

and horrible slaughcamp, in which there were more than a hundred and fifty thousand ter of the Mexicans. men, and those also of Alvarado's camp, and with all these forces together he set himself to attack certain ditches and entrenchments which were the greatest fortifications that remained to the Mexicans, and at the same hour Sandoval with his army assailed the city from the north side. This was the most disastrous day for that city, on which Mexican blood was shed more copiously than ever, those unhappy citizens having by now neither arms to repel the multitude and the fury of their enemies, nor strength to defend themselves, nor even ground to fight upon. The soil of the city was covered with corpses, and the water of the ditches and of the canals was tinged with blood. Nothing was seen but ruin and slaughter, nor was anything heard but lamentable weeping and cries of despair. The allies raged so cruelly against that wretched people that the Spaniards labored more to restrain their cruelty than to fight with their enemies. The slaughter that was made of the Mexicans on that day was so great that between dead and prisoners, by what Cortés himself says, it exceeded forty thousand persons.

The intolerable stench of so many unburied corpses then forced § 33. the besiegers to withdraw from the city; but the next day (August 13) Last assault, and capthey returned to it to give the last assault to that corner of Tlatelolco ture of the city and

of the kings. which still remained in the power of the Mexicans. Cortés brought with him three cannon and all his troops. and above all that they should endeavor to take King Cuauhtémoc, since that would suffice to make them masters of the city and to put an end to the war; but before coming to this decisive stroke, he made new attempts to bring the besieged to some accommodation. He was induced to this not only by compassion for so many wretched people, but even by the desire to make himself master of the treasures of the king and of the nobility; for if that last part of the city were taken by assault, the Mexicans, deprived of every hope of saving their riches, might throw them into the lake, in order that the victors should not enjoy them, and in case they did not do so, they would be seized by the allies, who, being innumerable and more familiar with the houses, would leave little or nothing to the Spaniards in the disorder and confusion of the assault. He therefore spoke again, from an eminent place, to certain Mexicans of rank who were well known to him, representing to them their extreme danger, and begging them to make new entreaties to the king, that he should yield to that conference so much desired by him for the good of the king himself and of all his subjects; for if he still persisted in his resolve to defend himself, he was determined not to leave a single Mexican alive that day. Two of those nobles undertook to persuade the king, but they had scarcely departed when they returned, accompanying the Cihuacoatl, or supreme magistrate of the court. He was received by Cortés with singular demonstrations of honor and cordiality, but he, with a lordly air, by which he seemed to wish to show his spirit superior to all calamities, spoke thus to Cortés: “Spare yourself, O General, the trouble of soliciting a conference with my king and lord Cuauhtémoc. He is resolved to die rather than appear before you. I could not tell you how much such a resolution grieves me; but there is no remedy. Take, then, whatever counsel pleases you best, and act according to your designs.” Cortés told him to go and prepare [p. 229] the minds of his citizens for the death that they would soon have to

In the meantime numerous troops of women, of children, and of wretched people had come to give themselves up to the Spaniards, hastening in rivalry to escape from that extreme peril, and some of those who strove to cross the ditches by swimming were drowned, through their great weakness. Cortés commanded that no harm should be done to those who surrendered; indeed he stationed at several posts some Spaniards, in order that by their authority they should restrain the barbarous cruelty of the allies; but in spite of his orders more than fifteen thousand men, women, and children perished at the hands of those inhuman and furious troops.

> Mellacelle male a coloro che s' arrendevano; an-,

The nobles and the military men who had held obstinately to the resolution of defending themselves to the last breath occupied the flat roofs of the houses and some paved streets. Cortés, seeing that it was late and that they would not surrender, had the artillery play upon them, and this not sufficing, he gave the signal for the assault with an arquebus shot. The besiegers all assailed at one hour, and pressed the weak and afflicted citizens so hard that, there being left to them in the city no place where they could defend themselves from the fury of so great a number of enemies, many threw themselves into the water, and others came to give themselves up to the victors. The Mexicans had made ready some boats in order to escape by flight from the power of the Spaniards; but Cortés, having perceived such a subterfuge, had given orders to Sandoval to take possession with the brigantines of the harbor of Tlatelolco and to seize the boats. In spite of Sandoval's extreme diligence many boats escaped, and among others precisely the one that carried the royal persons. That active commander, having noticed it, ordered García Holguín, captain of the swiftest brigantine, to give chase to it; he made such haste that in a short time he overtook them, and as the Spaniards made ready to fire upon the fugitives, these stopped their oars and threw down their arms as a sign of surrender. There were on that great boat, or piragua, the king of

[p. 230]

Mexico, Cuauhtémoc, the queen Tecuichpotzin his wife, the king of Bk. X.

Acolhuacan Coanacochtzin, and the king of Tlacopan

Tetlepanquetzaltzin, with other personages. The brigantine came alongside, and the king of Mexico, advancing toward the Spaniards, said to that captain: “I am, O Captain, your prisoner, nor do I ask any other favor of you than that you show to the queen my wife and to her maidens that regard which is due to their sex and to their rank”; and taking the queen by the hand, he passed with her into the brigantine. Then, observing that the Spanish captain was anxious about the other boats, he told him not to doubt that all, as soon as they should know that their sovereign was a prisoner, would come to die with him.

Captain Holguín conducted those illustrious prisoners to Cortés, who was then on the flat roof of a house in Tlatelolco. He received them with every demonstration of honor and humanity, and had them sit down. Cuauhtémoc, with great spirit, said to him: “I have done, O valiant General, both for my own defense and for that of my subjects all that the honor of my crown and zeal for my people required of me; but because the gods were against me, I now see myself deprived of the crown and of liberty. I am your prisoner; dispose of my person at your pleasure”; and placing his right hand upon a dagger which Cortés wore at his belt, he added: “Take from me with this dagger a life that I did not lose in the defense of my kingdom.”

Gli

Cortés strove to console him with kind reasons, protesting to him that he did not consider him his prisoner, but the prisoner of the greatest monarch of Europe, in whose clemency he ought to trust that not only the liberty which he had unhappily lost, but also the throne of his most illustrious ancestors, which he had so worthily occupied and defended, would be restored to him. But what comfort could he have from such protestations, or what faith could he give to the words of Cortés, he who had always been his enemy, having seen that to King Moctezuma it was not enough to be his [p. 231] friend and protector to avoid losing his crown, his liberty, and his life? He demanded of Cortés that no harm be done to his subjects, and Cortés in turn de‐ Bk. X. manded of him that he command all his subjects to surrender. Each gave his orders, and both were promptly obeyed. It was likewise ordered that all the Mexicans should leave the city without arms and without baggage, and, according to what a most truthful eyewitness affirms, (*) for three days and three nights all three causeways were seen full of men, women, and children, weak, emaciated, and filthy, who were leaving by them to take refuge in other places. The stench that so many thousands of putrefied and unburied bodies gave off was so intolerable that it caused some indisposition to the general of the Conquerors. The houses, the streets, and the canals were full of disfigured corpses; (I) the ground of the city was found dug up in some parts by the citizens, who sought roots under the earth to feed upon, and many trees were seen stripped of their bark to meet the extremity of hunger. The general had the corpses buried, and an immense quantity of wood burned throughout the city, both to purify that infected air and to celebrate his victory.

(I) “It is true, and I swear it, amen, that the whole lagoon, and the houses, and the barbacoas were full of bodies and heads of dead men, so that I do not know in what manner to write it; for in the streets, and in the very courts of Tlatelolco, there was nothing else, and we could not walk except among bodies and heads of dead Indians. I have read of the destruction of Jerusalem; but whether in that there was such mortality as in this, I do not know,” etc. Bernal Díaz in ch. 156 of his history. Such expressions from an eyewitness so truthful, and one who did not know how to exaggerate, give some idea of that horrible slaughter. I suspect that the corpses were left unburied by the Mexicans on purpose, to drive off the besiegers with the stench; nor can I persuade myself otherwise, considering the extreme solicitude of those nations in the obsequies of their dead. [p. 232] allies returned to their countries exceedingly joyful over the booty, Bk. X.

Charles V. All the rest of the gold, which was melted down, scarcely amounted to 19,200 ounces, (K) both because the Mexicans threw the greater part of it into the lake, (L) and because individuals,

Spaniards as well as their allies, in sacking the city sought to recompense themselves secretly for their labors.

The capture of that great court took place on August 13, 1521, a hundred and ninety-six years after it was founded by the Aztecs, and a hundred and sixty-nine years after it was raised into a monarchy, which eleven kings ruled. The siege of Mexico, comparable in its misfortunes and in its slaughter with that of Jerusalem, lasted seventy-five days, in which time several thousand of the more than two hundred thousand allies perished, and more than a hundred of the nine hundred Spaniards. The number of the Mexicans who died is not known; but in view of the account of Cortés and of Bernal

Díaz,

380,000 pesos, which seems to be more. Among the spoils that were sent to Charles

V there were pearls of enormous size, most precious gems, and marvelous works of gold. The ship on which they were sent was captured by Jean Florin, a famous French corsair, and the treasure was sent to the court of France, which authorized such robberies under the pretext, no less celebrated than frivolous, that the Most Christian

King is a son of Adam just as the Catholic King is.

(L) Bernal Díaz says that he saw some things of gold taken out of the lake, and

among others a sun like that which King Moctezuma sent to Cortés when the latter was on the shore of Chalchiuhcuecan.

As for those who died of hunger, or of sickness caused by the brackish water which they drank, or by the infection of the air, Cortés himself affirms that they were more than fifty thousand. The city remained almost wholly ruined. The king of Mexico, notwithstanding the magnificent promises of the Spanish general, was after a few days ignominiously put to the torture (which he endured with unconquered constancy) in order that he should declare where the immense riches of the court and of the temples were; (M) and three years later he was hanged, on certain suspicions, together with the kings of Texcoco and of Tlacopan. (M) The torture that was given to King Cuauhtémoc was that of burning his feet little by little after anointing them with oil. A close private friend of his accompanied him, and died in the torments. Bernal Díaz adds that the king of Tlacopan was also tormented along with him. Cortés, against his will, took up so unworthy and barbarous a resolution in order to yield to the urgings of some greedy Spaniards, who suspected that he did not wish to put the king to the torture in order to profit secretly by the whole royal treasure.

(N) Cuauhtémoc, king of Mexico, Coanacochtzin, king of Acolhuacan, and Tetlepanquetzaltzin, king of Tlacopan, were hanged from a tree by sentence of Cortés in Izancanac, capital city of the province of Acallan, on one of the three days preceding Lent of the year 1525. The cause of their death was a certain conversation which they had among themselves about their misfortunes, in which they suggested how easy it would be for them, if they wished, to kill Cortés and all the Spaniards, and to recover their liberty and their crowns. A Mexican traitor, to win the favor of the Spanish general, gave him an account of everything, altering the sense of the words, and representing as an organized conspiracy what had been merely talk in the air. Cortés, who was then journeying toward the province of Comayagua with a few Spaniards weakened by fatigue, and with more than three thousand Mexicans whom he was leading with him, became convinced that there was no other remedy for avoiding the danger by which he believed himself threatened, except that of putting the three kings to death. This execution, says Bernal Díaz, was most unjust, and blamed by all of us who traveled with him that day. It caused Cortés great melancholy and some sleepless nights. The same author adds that Father Juan de Varillas, a friar of the Order of Our Lady of Mercy, confessed and comforted them at the execution; that they were good Christians, and that they died well disposed; whence it is manifest that they had been baptized; but among so many historians of Mexico there is not one who makes mention of an event so notable and so glorious as that of the baptism of these three kings, while otherwise filling so many pages and so many [p. 234] the nations that contributed to their ruin remained, in spite of the Bk. X. Christian and most humane dispositions of the Catholic Kings, aban‐

Don Fabrizio Pignatelli d'Aragon, etc., 9th Duke of Monteleone, 9th Duke of Terranova, 11th Marquis del Valle, Grandee of Spain, Prince of the Holy Roman Empire, etc., married to Donna Costanza Medici, of the Princes of Ottaviano. Their son was ═══

IX.

Don Ettore Pignatelli d'Aragon, etc., 10th Duke of Monteleone, 10th Duke of Terranova, 12th Marquis del Valle de Oaxaca, Grandee of Spain, Prince of the Holy Roman Empire. He lives at present in Naples, married to Donna N. Piccolomini, of the Dukes of Amalfi.

From that most noble couple, whom we have placed under number VI, were born four sons, Diego, Ferdinando, Antonio, and Fabrizio, and as many daughters, Rosa, Maria Teresa, Stefania, and Caterina. 1. Don Diego was the heir of the marquisate of the Valle, or of the Vaglio, as they say in Naples, and of the duchies of Monteleone and of Terranova. 2. Don Ferdinando married Donna Lucrezia Pignatelli, Princess of Strongoli, whose son Don Salvatore took Donna Giulia Mastrilli, of the Dukes of Marigliano. 3. Don Antonio married in Spain the only daughter of the Count of Fuentes. From that marriage was born Don Gioacchino Pignatelli d'Aragon, Moncayo, etc., Count of Fuentes, Marquis of Coscojuela, Grandee of Spain, Prince of the Holy Roman Empire, Knight of the Golden Fleece and of Santiago, etc., Ambassador of the King of Spain at the courts of England and of France, and President of the Royal Council of the Military Orders, whose son Don Luigi, now living, has married the only daughter and heiress of Casimiro Pignatelli, Count of Egmont, Duke of Bisaccia, etc., Knight of the Fleece, and Lieutenant General of the Armies of the Most Christian King. 4. Don Fabrizio took to wife Virginia Pignatelli, sister of the Princess of Strongoli, whose son Don Michele is Marquis of Salice and Guagnano. 5. Rosa was given in marriage to the Prince of Scalea. 6. Maria Teresa to the Marquis of Westerloo, a Bohemian lord. 7. Stefania to the Prince of Bisignano. 8. Caterina to the Count of Acerra.

M I S TA K E S OV E R L O O K E D I N T H E F I R S T T WO

VO L U M E S .

In vol. I, p. 126, where it is said, speaking of the migration of the Toltecs, that it began in the year I Tecpatl, that is, in 596 of the common era, it should read thus: in the year I Tecpatl, that is, in 544 of the common era, as is found in my Spanish original and in my dissertations; the other was a mistake in the translation. On the same page, where it is said that the monarchy of the Toltecs began in the year VIII Acatl, that is, in 667 of the common era, it should say in the year VII Acatl, etc., since the year 667 was not VIII, but VII Acatl. In vol. 2, p. 59, where it is said that every four years the Mexican year was advanced by one day on account of the intercalary day of our leap year; so that in the last years of the Mexican century it began on February 14, etc., it should say, it began on February 13.

On p. 16 of the same vol. 2, where it is said that three festivals were held for the goddess Centeotl in the third, eighth, and eleventh months, it should say, in the fourth, eighth, and eleventh months, as is seen in the account of the festivals, p. 68, and in the Calendar, p. 236.

In the aforesaid Calendar, p. 239, where one reads Festival of Maculitochtli, it should say, Festival of Macuiltochtli, and at the end of the Calendar, where it says, The following year II Acatl begins with II Mizquili, it should say, with II Miquiztli.

T H E P R I N T E R’ S N O T I C E .

The volume of the dissertations will probably not be published until the month of August of this year (1781), but every possible effort will be made so that it may come to light sooner.
